 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for Ghost Operator 

 Inspiration 

 Local-service businesses lose real revenue when calls go unanswered, but deploying an automated front desk is consequential. The owner understands the business constraints; an agent excels at structured setup work. Ghost Operator gives both of them one shared, auditable workspace. 

 What it does 

 The owner enters industry, weekly call volume, missed-call rate, average job value, and desired coverage. Through WebMCP, an agent can read those values, update approved inputs, calculate calls at risk, recommend coverage, draft a constrained call policy, and open the completed plan for review. Every action appears in a visible activity ledger. 

 The human-agent boundary is deliberate: there is no tool for final approval, deployment, purchasing, calling, or messaging. The owner must inspect the visible plan and click Approve & save personally. Even then, the demo only saves locally and confirms that no external system changed. 

 Why WebMCP 

 This workflow combines structured inputs, deterministic calculations, editable shared state, and a consequential handoff. Browser automation alone would need to infer form semantics and scrape changing output. WebMCP gives the agent six precise operations connected to the same logic and session the owner sees, making the workflow faster, more reliable, and easy to audit. 

 People and agents can now collaborate on a launch plan in plain language while keeping authority visible and constrained—something that previously required brittle UI automation or a separate integration disconnected from the page under review. 

 How we built it 

 Ghost Operator is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. It registers six imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a narrow JSON input schema, read/write annotations, application-level validation, structured results, and an abortable lifecycle. Tool handlers reuse the same deterministic state and calculation functions as the human UI. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel, tested with Vitest, and published under the MIT License. All challenge code was created after the challenge opened on August 25, 2026; the public commit history documents the work. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest design decision was not exposing every UI action as a tool. We intentionally omitted approval and deployment operations so the agent can accelerate the work without silently crossing the human authorization boundary. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is strongest when the page remains the shared source of truth. The best agent experience is not invisible automation—it is structured collaboration where the person can see state, understand changes, and retain final control.

about_excerpt: One circuit, two native interfaces: people edit visually while agents inspect, author, highlight, and simulate the exact same design through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Electronic design is naturally visual, but agents are usually forced to guess their way through pixels or work in a separate text-only model. That creates two competing versions of the circuit. Circuit Sim explores a better model: one authoritative circuit that a person can see and edit while an agent can inspect, change, simulate, and explain through structured browser-native tools. What it does Circuit Sim is a collaborative schematic workbench for people and agents. A user works in the visual editor while an agent uses four WebMCP tools exposed directly by the live page: inspect_circuit discovers instructions, the component catalog, exact terminal keys, project state, ERC findings, and simulation freshness. author_circuit applies a validated complete circuit graph using an optimistic project hash. highlight_components focuses the same objects in the human-visible schematic for explanation and review. simulate_circuit runs the selected SPICE engine and returns measurements tied to the exact circuit snapshot. The demo shows Codex designing a beta-100 NPN bias stage from a natural-language target, creating the complete connected schematic, highlighting the bias network, running ngspice, and reporting node voltages and branch currents. It then changes the emitter resistor from 1 kΩ to 2 kΩ and simulates again to explain the stability-versus-headroom tradeoff using measured evidence. Why WebMCP is the right fit Without WebMCP, an agent would have to click through a dense CAD interface, infer component geometry, and scrape results from pixels. With WebMCP, the page advertises its capabilities and schemas directly. The agent can make precise, validated edits while every result remains visible to the user in the same workbench. This creates a workflow that was previously difficult: a person can describe design intent, watch an agent turn it into a real schematic, inspect exactly what changed, and challenge the design with another simulation—all without copying netlists between tools or maintaining a hidden agent-only circuit. How we built it The browser editor is React and TypeScript. Effect Schema defines and validates the canonical CircuitProject , edit operations, WebMCP inputs, and simulation responses. The page registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Agent edits cross the same domain validation used by the human interface. Connectivity and the SPICE netlist are derived from the saved project; the server runs ngspice in an isolated process and returns a validated simulation run associated with the project snapshot hash. IndexedDB persists validated projects and runs. The app is containerized and deployed on Render. The project is intentionally human-in-the-loop: hashes prevent stale agent writes, ERC findings stay visible, simulation evidence is inspectable, and component highlighting connects the agent’s explanation to the schematic. Challenges and learning The hardest part was keeping a visual editor, structured agent tools, connectivity extraction, and SPICE results consistent without creating a second source of truth. We learned that WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose domain operations and evidence—not a thin wrapper around UI clicks. Accomplishments Circuit Sim delivers a working deployed product rather than a mockup: four live WebMCP tools, validated authoring, shared human/agent state, ERC feedback, ngspice simulation, snapshot identity, undo/redo, persistence, and an end-to-end demonstration inside the Codex in-app browser. title: OpenMemoz
pitch: A personal content library where AI agents are the writers and you're the editor. 35 WebMCP tools let any AI curate news from open & allowed sources, lives in your browser, no backend needed.
about_excerpt: A personal content library where AI agents are the writers and you're the editor. 35 WebMCP tools let any AI curate news from open & allowed sources, lives in your browser, no backend needed. Like Comment Story Updates 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 Inspiration Content discovery is fragmented. The same story surfaces across multiple apps, each optimizing for engagement rather than what the reader actually wants. Long-form content on YouTube has incredible depth, but finding the right video takes longer than watching it. And none of these platforms are agent-native. The vision was a consolidated personal content library where AI agents curate open sources and the reader decides what to read. Not another algorithmic feed, but a place where agents search the web, summarize videos, discover discussions on Bluesky and Mastodon, and organize it all into a newspaper the reader can actually use. WebMCP made it possible. Chrome 150 shipped document.modelContext.registerTool() , which lets a web page expose structured tools to any AI agent visiting it. No extensions, no API keys. The browser becomes a User-Agent Generated Content (UAGC) platform — users direct, agents curate. What it does OpenMemoz exposes 36 WebMCP tools to any visiting AI agent. The agent reads the current edition, searches stories, discovers content from YouTube, Bluesky, and Mastodon, writes original articles, embeds videos, manages reader preferences, and reshapes the newspaper layout. Everything happens through the browser's native tool-calling protocol. The reader experience is a newspaper: a hero story with an embedded YouTube video, a sidebar with text stories, a mid-row section, a video feature row, and a below-fold masonry grid. Thirteen color palettes, four visual styles (flat, glass, neumorphic, paper), two layout modes. The agent experience is a structured workflow. Here is what a typical interaction looks like: User tells ChatGPT: "Discover trending YouTube videos, read the transcript of the best one, write a summary, and add it as my hero story." Agent calls discover_youtube_content to find trending videos Agent calls get_youtube_video to read the full transcript of the top result Agent writes an original summary from the transcript, calls add_story with pinAsHero: true The newspaper layout recalculates instantly: new hero with embedded video, sidebar adjusts, masonry reflows The page is the interface. The agent is the editor. The reader stays in control. How we built it The entire system runs client-side as a Next.js PWA. There is no backend for content curation. The AI agents visiting the page are the backend. Server-side API routes exist only as thin CORS proxies for YouTube, Bluesky, and Mastodon. The flow above shows one real interaction: the user asks for trending content → the agent discovers document.modelContext and its 36 tools → calls discover_youtube_content → picks the best video → calls get_youtube_video to read the full transcript → writes an original summary → calls add_story → source validation checks the allowlist (~90 approved) and banned list (~280 blocked) → edition data updates in localStorage → the layout rule engine rescores and reflows → the page updates instantly, live. The agent can also use its own web search to find content from any source and call add_story directly — the discover tools are convenience shortcuts, not the only path. Personalized interests via AI conversation Tell the agent what you want to learn — "This week I want to learn about LLMs and quantum computing" — and it sets your topic interests via set_user_interests . The interests persist in localStorage and influence what the agent curates next. The agent can search anywhere on the web, write original articles in its own words, and add them via add_story . WebMCP tools Every tool is registered through the browser's document.modelContext.registerTool() API. The registration function runs on page load and registers all 36 tools in parallel: // src/lib/webmcp.ts const modelContext = document.modelContext ?? (navigator as any).modelContext; // Chrome 146-149 compat if (typeof modelContext?.registerTool !== "function") return; modelContext.registerTool({ name: "openmemoz.add_story", description: "Add a new story. Page updates IMMEDIATELY.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { headline: { type: "string" }, excerpt: { type: "string" }, section: { type: "string" }, sourceName: { type: "string" }, youtubeVideoId: { type: "string" }, pinAsHero: { type: "boolean" }, }, required: ["headline", "excerpt", "section", "sourceName"], }, execute: (args) => { /* validate source, create story, update edition */ }, }, { signal: abortSignal }); Tool descriptions do double duty as agent instructions. When search_stories returns zero results, its description guides the agent to discover tools. When discover_youtube_content finds a video, its description tells the agent to read the transcript with get_youtube_video and write an original summary before adding. The descriptions chain tools into workflows — they need the same care as system prompts. Source validation OpenMemoz only accepts content from approved sources. Every add_story call validates the source URL against two lists before the story is accepted: // src/lib/curatedSources.ts export const APPROVED_SOURCES = [ { domain: "nasa.gov", licenceBasis: "public-domain-usgov" }, { domain: "youtube.com", licenceBasis: "youtube-embed-tos" }, // ~90 total across government, CC, open API, video, social ]; export const BANNED_DOMAINS = ["nytimes.com", "wsj.com", /* ~280 total */]; Layer Sources Legal basis Government SEC, Fed, NASA, NOAA, BLS, NIH, CDC Public domain (17 USC 105) Creative Commons The Conversation, Global Voices, VOA, Wikipedia CC licence terms Open APIs Hacker News, YouTube, Bluesky, Mastodon Permissive API / embed ToS Provenance tiers Every story carries a provenanceTier in its data schema. Tier 1 means the text comes directly from the source (a government press release, a CC-licensed article). Tier 2 means the AI synthesized the summary. The agent knows the difference. // src/lib/types.ts export interface Story { storyIdentifier: string; headline: string; excerpt: string; section: string; provenanceTier: 1 | 2; // 1 = source text (quotable), 2 = AI-synthesized sourceName: string; sourceUrl: string; licenceBasis: string; // legal basis for redistribution youtubeVideoId?: string; isHeroPinned?: boolean; } Layout rule engine The layout engine assigns stories to slots the way a newspaper editor would. No empty space, no mixed-height rows. The hero is scored automatically based on visual impact: // src/lib/layoutRuleEngine.ts function scoreHeroCandidate(story: Story, index: number): number { if (story.isHeroPinned) return 100; let score = 0; if (story.youtubeVideoId) score += 5; if (story.imageUrl) score += 3; if (story.provenanceTier === 1) score += 2; return score; } The engine produces a structured layout: hero + sidebar, then a uniform mid-row (all-thumbnail or all-text to avoid dead space), then brief strips in full rows of 4, a video feature row, and a below-fold masonry grid packed with a greedy shortest-column algorithm. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new and barely documented. Chrome 150 shipped document.modelContext.registerTool() with no tutorials and few examples. We discovered edge cases through trial: tools fail silently when descriptions are too long, agents call tools in unexpected orders, and Chrome 146 through 149 used navigator.modelContext instead of document.modelContext . Our code handles both entry points. AI agents are unpredictable editors. The first time we asked ChatGPT to "add some tech stories," it added 47 stories in a row, all in the Tech section, most from banned domains. We built guardrails layer by layer: source validation against ~90 approved and ~280 banned domains, duplicate detection by headline slug, and rate guidance baked into tool descriptions. The agent still needs coaching, but it cannot publish from the New York Times. Newspaper layout is harder than it looks. Our first layout was a 3-column masonry grid. It looked like a Pinterest board, not a newspaper. Real newspapers have hierarchy: the hero is visually dominant, sidebar stories complement it, mid-row stories are uniform height, and the below-fold grid fills every pixel. We built a rule engine that enforces these constraints automatically. YouTube video verification is a rabbit hole. We curate static editions with YouTube video embeds. Matching video IDs to story topics turned out to be fragile. A story about the Federal Reserve was showing a Linkin Park music video. The fix was YouTube oembed API verification and strict video-to-topic matching. Accomplishments that we're proud of 36 WebMCP tools under the openmemoz.* namespace, making this one of the most comprehensive WebMCP implementations built so far Zero backend for content curation. AI agents visiting the page are the editorial team Personalized int

title: LedgerRehearsal
pitch: Rehearse before agents act.
about_excerpt: Rehearse before agents act. Like Comment Story Updates Deterministic receivables baseline — Three fictional accounts and three safe agent tools before approval. Approval changes the tool surface — One uniquely scoped execution capability appears after human review. Stale permission disappears — Drift applies nothing and removes the approved execution capability. Exact rehearsal before action — Complete simulated ACME reminder, Jones assignment diff, and Smith policy block. Receipt separates proposed, authorized, executed, and blocked — The final record explains what happened and whether reality changed. Rehearsal against current reality — ACME is no change, Jones remains proposed, and Smith remains blocked. Short description LedgerRehearsal is a WebMCP accounts-receivable demo where a human and an agent review the same exact business transition before the webpage exposes a one-time capability to execute it. If reality changes after approval, the page removes that capability and requires a fresh rehearsal. Inspiration Approval interfaces often live beside an agent rather than inside the interface the agent can actually use. A screen may say “approved” while the agent’s available actions remain unchanged. LedgerRehearsal asks a narrower question: what if the WebMCP tool surface itself became shared interface state between a person and an agent? The project uses a familiar accounts-receivable scenario because the stakes are easy to understand. An overdue reminder may be reasonable when an invoice is unpaid and wrong seconds later if a payment arrives. The interesting moment is not generating the reminder; it is proving that a previously reviewed permission disappears when its factual basis changes. What it does The agent begins with three safe tools: inspect_accounts , propose_collection_actions , and rehearse_transition . The first rehearsal proposes an overdue reminder for ACME, proposes assigning Jones to Maya Chen, and blocks a final notice for Smith because the invoice is disputed. The human reviews the complete simulated message, exact before/after values, effects, and blocked reason in the webpage. Human approval then makes one uniquely named, zero-argument execution capability appear. Before the agent uses it, the human simulates ACME’s payment. That state change invalidates the reviewed transition, so stale execution applies no business mutation, creates no outbox effect or receipt, and removes the capability. The agent rehearses again against current reality. ACME becomes NO_CHANGE , Jones remains PROPOSED , and Smith remains BLOCKED . A second human approval creates a distinct capability. Using it applies only the stored Jones assignment, adds one simulated outbox effect, writes one receipt, and consumes the capability so replay cannot duplicate the change. All customers, balances, messages, and effects are fictional. There is no real email, payment provider, financial API, or external financial operation. How it was built LedgerRehearsal is a React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vinext for Cloudflare Sites. A D1-backed transition store keeps deterministic fictional account state, reviewed manifests, expected account versions, exact typed changes, simulated effects, blocked items, and lifecycle events. The browser uses top-level imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , with the current Chrome compatibility path at navigator.modelContext . Each approved execution registration receives an AbortSignal so it can be removed when authorization expires, drifts, or is consumed. The execution tool accepts zero mutation arguments. The agent cannot substitute an account, owner, message, or value after review. On execution, the server claims the transition with compare-and-swap semantics, rechecks stored preconditions, applies only stored after-values, appends simulated effects, and records the receipt. Competing callers observe the transition as no longer available, so exactly one wins inside this application boundary. How LedgerRehearsal uses WebMCP LedgerRehearsal explores the WebMCP tool surface itself as shared interface state. Human approval makes one reviewed execution capability appear; changing business reality removes it; successful use consumes it. The choreography is visible in actual tool enumeration: 3 safe tools → 4 with reviewed execution → 3 after drift → 4 with replacement execution → 3 after consumption Human approval is deliberately not an agent tool. The consequential capability appears only after a person reviews the concrete transition in the webpage. Human-agent collaboration The agent is good at inspecting state, proposing work, and explaining exact effects. The person owns the consequential approval. The webpage connects those roles by changing what the agent can do only after the person reviews a specific transition. That division also makes disagreement legible. Smith is not silently omitted; the rehearsal shows the blocked action and its policy reason. When ACME pays, the system does not reinterpret the old approval. It revokes it and asks the agent and person to review the smaller current transition together. Creativity and ambition The project does not claim a new security primitive. Human approval, dry runs, optimistic concurrency, capability-based security, version checks, and single-use authorization all have prior art. The contest contribution is the shared-page experience: approval, drift, replacement, and consumption are reflected directly in the live WebMCP surface rather than only in a status label. Impact Agents become more useful when people can see not just what they plan to do, but exactly when permission exists, what that permission covers, and why it disappears. The pattern is relevant anywhere a reviewed action can become stale: finance operations, customer support, fulfillment, compliance, and other consequential workflows. Challenges The hardest part was keeping browser capability state, server authorization state, and business state aligned. Removing a tool from the browser is not enough if a stale handle can still reach the server, so the server rechecks the reviewed account versions and lifecycle on every execution. Another challenge was making the scenario comprehensible without hiding the mechanics. The interface exposes exact diffs, complete simulated messages, blocked actions, lifecycle events, outbox effects, and receipts while keeping the main story readable. Accomplishments A real 3 → 4 → 3 → 4 → 3 capability lifecycle in supported WebMCP runtimes. Zero-argument execution tied to a reviewed manifest rather than agent-supplied mutation values. Drift detection that applies zero stale business mutations and creates zero stale effects or receipts. Single-use application-boundary execution with replay and competing-caller coverage. Deterministic fictional data, visible reset, and judge-accessible public deployment with no signup. A 32-test suite covering registration, drift, replay, concurrency, blocked-action exclusion, outbox integrity, receipt integrity, and reset behavior. What I learned The most important lesson was that approval is not just a record; it can be part of an interface lifecycle. WebMCP makes that lifecycle observable to both sides of the collaboration. The browser registration still needs authoritative server checks, because a removed UI capability does not prove that no stale caller exists. I also learned that blocked work deserves first-class representation. A rehearsal is more trustworthy when it explains what will not happen and why, instead of showing only the actions that survived filtering. What’s next The next step would be to generalize the choreography carefully without turning the demo into a generic workflow engine: stronger audit export, additional accessibility testing, and more supported-runtime acceptance evidence. Real email, real payments, authentication, customer data, and external finance APIs are intentionally outside this challenge build. Testing instructions Open the live app in the ChatGPT desktop in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and Chrome restarted. Use Reset demo and verify three initial tools. Ask the agent to inspect accounts, propose current collection actions, and rehearse them without execution. Review the exact changes and approve them in the webpage. Verify a unique fourth execution tool appears. Click Simulate payment received before execution. Invoke the old execution handle. Verify drift, zero business mutations, zero outbox additions, zero receipts, and return to three tools. Inspect, propose, and rehearse again. Verify ACME NO_CHANGE , Jones PROPOSED , and Smith BLOCKED . Approve the smaller transition. Verify a distinct fourth tool appears. Invoke it once. Verify only Jones changes, exactly one simulated outbox effect and receipt exist, and the tool list returns to three. Attempt replay and verify no duplicate mu
video_transcript_excerpt: Ledger rehearsal is a web MCP receivables workspace where a human and an agent rehearse consequential business changes together before the web page allows execution. The agent begins with three safe tools. It finds Acme overdue with no reminder, Jones needing a follow-up owner, and Smith in an active billing dispute. The page rehearses exact effects before anything changes. I can read the complete simulated Acme reminder, see Jones move from unassigned to Maya Chan, and see why policy blocks Smith. Approval stays a human web page action. Once I approve this exact review, a uniquely scoped execution capability appears. The tool surface changes from three to four. No reality changes before execution. A visible payment sync records Acme's invoices paid in full. The overdue reminder no longer makes business sense. I approved this when Acme was overdue, but Acme paid before the agent acted. So, the page removes that capability instead of letting the agent use stale approval. Nothing executes. The agent must rehearse against current reality. Acme's reminder is gone. Jones is still valid, while Smith remains blocked because the dispute has not changed. I approve the smaller replacement transition. A new distinct execution capability appears, again changing the page's web MCP surface from three tools to four. The agent supplies no targets or replacement values. The application rechecks current state and applies only the stored Jones assignment. Smith's blocked action never executes. Successful use consumes the one-time capability. It disappears. The tool count returns to three and a replay cannot duplicate the change or simulated effect. The receipt records what was proposed, what the human authorized, what actually executed, what remained blocked, and whether reality changed after rehearsal. Rehearse before agents act. Approval changes what the page lets the agent do. Changing reality revokes that permission.

title: PCMCP
pitch: Start on Mac. Continue on Windows. Send it back. Nothing gets lost.
about_excerpt:
Start on Mac. Continue on Windows. Send it back. Nothing gets lost.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 PCMCP lets a person or AI agent hand a live task from one computer to another, even across different operating systems, without losing the task state. 

 Why WebMCP fits: the browser exposes explicit tools for sending and receiving the task capsule, so an agent can move the task through the web interface instead of remote-controlling another machine. 

 User experience: start with a task on Mac, send it, continue on Windows, change the state, and send it back. The receiving computer rehydrates the same task state for its destination. 

 People and agents can now collaborate on cross-device task handoff through simple WebMCP tools rather than screen sharing, manual copying, or platform-specific workflows. 

 Implementation: the web app registers WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). A small relay stores the latest neutral capsule/state. Each browser can send, receive, and apply that state locally while showing a destination-specific representation.

title: Cleansheet
pitch: A WebMCP-powered spreadsheet cleaner where agents find defects and propose fixes, while people control every write.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered spreadsheet cleaner where agents find defects and propose fixes, while people control every write. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Cleansheet logo Cleansheet word mark A 3,290-row finance export: 25 defect classes across 37,479 cells, found server-side in one pass. the diffs. /review with before-and-after pairs and a destructive tag visible. the tool surface. /activity with the extension panel visible if you can fit it, showing live and withdrawn tools with their reasons. Inspiration I chose spreadsheet cleaning because spreadsheets still sit behind a large amount of daily work. People use them for budgets, forecasts, inventory, finance reports, operations, and planning. Fixing a few cells sounds easy, but a large file can turn that job into hours of repetitive checking. I wanted to test whether an agent could do the inspection without being trusted to silently rewrite the file. Cleansheet gives the agent access to the sheet, but keeps the final write decision with the person using it. What I built Cleansheet accepts a CSV upload and checks it for common data problems. It reports the defect type, the number of affected cells, an example, and a possible fix. The bundled finance export contains 3,290 rows, 25 defect classes, and 37,479 damaged cells. The app exposes 11 tools through WebMCP. An agent can read the sheet, inspect a column, preview a transformation, stage a proposal, and request a review. The available tools change with the state of the sheet. During review, tools that could write are removed. The agent can explain a proposed change, but it cannot apply one. The Apply button is the only writer. There is also a switch that turns WebMCP off. With tools enabled, the agent uses the tool surface. With tools disabled, it has to operate the interface. The page measures both cases using real tool-call and DOM-interaction counters. How I built it The frontend is static. Three Node functions handle parsing, transforming, and exporting the CSV. Uploaded files are processed for the session and are not retained. src/core.mjs contains the state machine without DOM or network access. toolAvailability() is the single place that decides which tools may be called. resolveReview() is the only function that can write to a row. After each state change, the browser layer reconciles the registered tools with that core state. scripts/proof.mjs uses the same core as the browser. That lets me test the important behavior without relying on a browser test. Problems I ran into Deduplication nearly shipped as a data-loss bug twice. At first, the key columns were hardcoded. A file with different headers could cause every row to fall into one duplicate group. I changed the ranking to look at how well columns actually distinguish rows. When no reliable key set exists, Cleansheet reports that and does not offer deletion. I also found a mismatch between preview and Apply. The preview said 61 rows would be dropped, but Apply would have removed 116 because blank-key rows were handled differently. The proof script caught it. I changed both paths to use the same decision logic. The WebMCP client landscape also changed while I was building. Chromium renamed navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext and removed the old name in version 150. One in-app browser could render the page and register tools but could not invoke them. The page now registers against whichever supported entry point the browser exposes. The work meter was wrong for a while too. It counted clicking the WebMCP switch as work avoided, which made the result look better than it was. The counters now attribute each event to the system that performed it. What I learned The most useful part of this project was deciding what the agent should leave alone. Blank fields stay blank. Free-text fields are not automatically title-cased. Deduplication is only offered when the file contains reliable matching keys. I also learned that the interface should enforce the safety boundary. A refusal message can be ignored. A tool that was never registered cannot be called. The on/off switch made the comparison measurable. Instead of estimating how many interactions an agent might use, I could count the actual events on the page. What's next I want to add Excel workbook support. For now, the app returns a clear 415 response instead of treating the workbook ZIP as plain text. Other planned additions are reversible applies, saved cleaning recipes, a manual key picker for deduplication, and support for larger files. The current limits are 8 MB and the first 20,000 rows. title: Tripster
pitch: Plan your weekends or trips based on your needs with ease. Don't just go to the same old place, use tripster.
about_excerpt:
Plan your weekends or trips based on your needs with ease. Don't just go to the same old place, use tripster.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration
Planning group trips often turns into a chaotic mix of scattered tabs, conflicting budgets, and endless group chat messages. While modern AI trip planners promise convenience, they often introduce new problems: weak budget reasoning, fabricated venue suggestions, poor route planning, and slow response times. We wanted a better approach.
Tripster combines the flexibility of AI assisted planning with the reliability of deterministic algorithms. Instead of relying on a model to guess the best trip, we use structured optimization logic to generate realistic, budget aware itineraries quickly and consistently. 

 What it does
Tripster is a trip planning app that helps groups create better travel plans based on their constraints. It supports multi origin trip planning for group members, budget aware itinerary generation, terrain and effort preference handling, spatially balanced destination selection, venue rerolling and itinerary refinement, interactive visual planning through a map and timeline, optional submission of new trip spots into the planning system, and agent style integration through browser native tool execution. 

 How we built it
We built the frontend with React and Vite, used Leaflet and React Leaflet for maps, applied custom CSS for styling, and relied on Supabase for the data layer. The planning logic is powered by a custom deterministic engine for itinerary generation, route optimization, and constraints handling. For agent integration we added a browser side WebMCP bridge for tool interoperability. This stack keeps the app fast, lightweight, and cost efficient while still supporting an interactive planning experience. 

 Challenges we ran into
We had to figure out how to find a fair group midpoint across multiple starting locations, balance travel distance with budget and venue suitability, handle edge cases where no venues fit perfectly within the provided constraints, keep route generation realistic while avoiding over optimization, and synchronize UI state with planning actions without breaking the user experience. 

 Accomplishments we are proud of
We built a functioning trip planning app focused on real constraints instead of generic AI suggestions. We created a structure that blends deterministic planning with interactive user experience, designed a system that is lightweight, fast, and easy to extend, and integrated map based planning and itinerary visualization in a single interface. 

 What we learned
The best travel planning experiences do not come from forcing AI to solve everything with raw generation. They come from combining AI interaction with well defined optimization logic. For structured tasks like trip planning, deterministic heuristics and route aware algorithms are often more reliable than purely generative approaches. 

 What is next for Tripster
We plan to add real time shared itinerary updates, better transit aware route planning, more venue verification and review workflows, offline support for saved itineraries, and improved personalization and recommendation engines.

pitch: What if a child’s wall drawing could start moving and become part of a story? Kids can play and create stories together, then make their favorite creations into real keepsakes through Shopify
about_excerpt: What if a child’s wall drawing could start moving and become part of a story? Kids can play and create stories together, then make their favorite creations into real keepsakes through Shopify Like Comment Story Updates drawing webmcp agents web room changing draw together make an invite draw together Inspiration My eight years old daughter loves drawing everywhere. on paper, on the wall, and on her iPad. I love seeing her imagination, but like many parents, I also worry about how much time children spend only looking at screens. I started wondering what if screen time could begin with something a child created with their own hands? What if their drawing could leave the paper, become a character, and continue its story in a 3D world? That question became WallAlive. What it does WallAlive turns a child’s drawing into a movable 3D character. A child can draw inside the app or photograph a paper drawing. WallAlive separates the character from the background, detects its visible parts, builds a movable rig, and places it inside an interactive, storybook, wizard, or museum world. Children can paint the 3D character with brushes, spray paint, oil paint, and colorful splashes. They can make it walk, dance, wave, and join stories with characters created by friends. A browser agent can help plan stories, suggest painting activities, inspect what each character can do, and prepare a creator collection. Children still control the creative actions, and an adult must approve any Shopify product draft. drawing 3d model How we built it I used several small on-device computer-vision models for drawing isolation, face and body-part detection, pose estimation, and character topology. Three.js renders the characters, animations, paint effects, and interactive 3D worlds. WebMCP gives the browser agent structured tools for understanding the current scene and helping with the next step. The available tools change according to what the user is doing, such as drawing, checking the character, painting, storytelling, collaborating, or preparing a Shopify product. This makes the agent more reliable than asking it to understand the interface by guessing. Shopify’s API is used to read the connected catalog and create an unpublished product draft from approved artwork. Vercel hosts the public application, while Cloudflare D1 supports shared drawing rooms. I used Codex during development and gstack by Garry Tan to challenge the idea, review the experience, test the implementation, and find weak points. Challenges we ran into Turning a paper drawing into a believable 3D character was the hardest technical challenge. Real photographs contain paper edges, shadows, grid lines, handwriting, nearby objects, and sometimes several characters. Children also draw bodies in many different ways, so one fixed skeleton cannot work for every drawing. A single image does not show the back of a character either. I had to combine segmentation, pose estimation, learned topology, depth reconstruction, and a human review step instead of pretending every result would always be perfect. I also worried about whether WallAlive would be genuinely useful or only an interesting hackathon demo. I kept asking myself whether it solved a real problem and whether it was truly a good fit for WebMCP. Testing it with my daughter helped me find the answer that the value is not simply converting an image into 3D. It is helping a child continue creating, storytelling, collaborating, and learning from something they made themselves. Another challenge was using WebMCP meaningfully. At first, the app exposed too many tools and expected technical inputs. I changed it so the agent sees only the tools relevant to the child’s current activity and accepts natural requests such as “make a short wizard story” or “paint it with blue spray.” shop webmcp Accomplishments that we're proud of The moment I am most proud of was watching my daughter become curious about a character made from her own drawing. It was no longer just another game chosen for her. It began with something she created. I am also proud that WallAlive creates a complete journey that draw, check, build, paint, play, collaborate, and with adult approval prepare the artwork as a real Shopify product draft. Most importantly, the agent supports the child’s imagination without taking control of it. What we learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when the person and the agent have different roles. The agent can inspect information, organize a story, recommend the next activity, and handle complicated preparation. The child should still draw, paint, choose, and play. An adult should remain responsible for publishing or selling anything. I also learned that art and technology do not need to compete. Technology can give a physical drawing another life while keeping the child’s original work at the center. What's next for Wall alive Next, I want to improve character reconstruction with more varied children’s drawings, stronger multi-character segmentation, and better movable rigs. I also want to add richer collaborative stories, more interactive worlds, classroom activities, teacher-created challenges, and safer parent controls. The longer-term goal is for children to build shared 3D exhibitions, stories, and small creator shops from artwork they made themselves not from premade characters someone else gave them. title: C2C — Cancellation to Compensation
pitch: An AI agent that uses WebMCP to take passengers from flight cancellation to compensation.
about_excerpt:
An AI agent that uses WebMCP to take passengers from flight cancellation to compensation.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 C2C Agent 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 C2C Agent 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 C2C Agent 
 
 1 2 



 
 C2C (Cancellation to Compensation) is a durable agent for airline disruption compensation claims. 

 Everything outside the agent is synthetic — no real airline is contacted, no real claim is submitted, and every legal-looking artifact is stamped SYNTHETIC DEMO — NOT FOR SUBMISSION — NOT LEGAL ADVICE. 

 Repo: https://github.com/yablokolabs/c2c-agent 

 The problem
A passenger whose flight was cancelled is probably owed money and has a job. 

 Deciding whether a claim is worth anything takes a competent person ~15 minutes. Everything after that is where claims die: submit, then wait 4–8 weeks; read a rejection that contradicts the airline's own operations log; challenge it; wait another 4 weeks; escalate — but only when the escalation is ripe. 

 The work is small. The calendar is enormous. That's the persistence gap: whether you get what the policy says you're owed depends less on the merits than on whether you have the knowledge, time and stubbornness to keep coming back for three months. 

 The thesis
The hard part of agentic AI isn't making an agent reason once. It's making it reliably stay with a real-world problem until the problem is actually resolved. 

 Agents reason. Workflows remember. 

 A stateless caseworker (4 tools, 10-step loop) and an independent verifier do the thinking; a Restate workflow owns the case. The agent forgets everything when it returns; the workflow survives kill -9, waits days for a human, and cannot execute a consequential action twice. 

 That split is why NanoClaw was evaluated and rejected — its persistent sessions would have competed with the workflow for owning case memory. 

 Tools, not an oracle. No tool returns a verdict. A check_eligibility() backed by a rules engine would have made the benchmark a test of whether the agent can call one function. 

 Independent verification. The verifier sees the case and the policy but not the caseworker's working — a second opinion, not a reviewer inheriting a wrong turn. It can reject; a rejection citing no clause is downgraded to a pass. 

 Human approval that is enforced, not requested. Every consequential action blocks on a durable promise, and the rejection branch returns before any outbound call is reachable. 

 Results — two suites
Suite A · reasoning · 28 synthetic cases. 

 Primary metric is Case Resolution Accuracy: a case counts only when the next action, the compensation figure and the other entitlements are all correct at once. 

 System CRA Model calls Cost
Baseline — one direct prompt, no tools, no verifier 0.82 28 $1.37
Full agent — tools, loop, independent verifier 0.93 102 $3.77
Same model, same policy, same cases, same schema, same grader, same endpoint. 

 The best possible constant answer on this suite is 0.25. Read +0.11 as directional, not significant — it is three cases, and this project has no valid variance estimate; the one it had was withdrawn in FAILURES.md F-008. 

 Suite B · durability · 6 failure-injection scenarios. 

 6/6 passed (6/6 again inside Docker), workflow completion 1.00, failure recovery 1.00, state preserved after kill -9 1.00, and 0 duplicate consequential actions. 

 The load-bearing one is D06: SIGKILL the worker inside the submission window — the carrier received 2 submission attempts and 1 claim landed, because the idempotency key is generated inside a durable step and is stable across replay. 

 In D05, when the human refuses, the carrier is called zero times, not once and then reversed. 

 The baseline scores nothing here, and that is not reported as a win. 

 The biggest improvement
On the reasoning axis, the independent verifier — not the tools. 

 The agent made 1.4 tool calls per case and called calculate three times in 28 cases. The verifier is isolated by case R16, a partial settlement that fails under the baseline and under tools-only and passes only with verification. 

 It costs 3.6× the model calls for +0.11. 

 But the improvement that mattered wasn't a component. It was answering where does the case remember itself? and being strict about it — which is why there is no database, why FastAPI holds no case state, and why a crash produces two attempts and one claim instead of two claims. 

 The main failure mode we did not fix
The agent asserts money it never computed. 

 Both remaining wrong cases fail on duty-of-care arithmetic; calculate was available on both and called on neither, despite a bolded prompt instruction with an example. 

 It does the sums in its head because it is capable of doing them in its head and confident about it. 

 That is invisible in an aggregate score and it is the one that reaches the passenger: a confident, well-cited, correctly-formatted claim letter with the wrong number in it. 

 Corrective experiment EXP-005 is specified and recorded as unrun. 

 Hot take
When a control moves and you did not touch the control, stop theorising about the treatment. 

 Three times this project reported infrastructure as capability: a required schema field zeroed a well-formed verdict; six cases were never sent to the model and were scored as six wrong answers, standing as the headline comparison for two days; a gateway served a different model while every result file recorded the one that was requested. 

 All three looked exactly like reasoning results. What caught all three was the baseline moving when nothing about the baseline had changed. 

 A missing answer is not a wrong answer. If your grader can't tell them apart, it will report your infrastructure as your agent's reasoning. 

 The model field is not provenance. The endpoint is. 

 Re-run your control, not just your treatment. 

 And the thing I got wrong at the start: I assumed the reasoning would be hard and durability would be plumbing. 

 A single prompt already handles most of these cases. What a single prompt cannot do is still be holding the case in week six. 

 Reproducing it
git clone https://github.com/yablokolabs/c2c-agent.git && cd c2c-agent 

 make setup 

 make test — 165 tests, no model calls, no services 

 make reproduce — baseline + agent + comparison 

 The headline result needs no Restate server, no Docker and no Telegram. 

 For the durability half: 

 make up && make failure-tests && make down

Deliverable Location
01 · Code + improvement changelog the repo · IMPROVEMENT_CHANGELOG.md
02 · Reproduction guide REPRODUCTION_GUIDE.md
03 · Solution video script in docs/DEMO_SCRIPT.md, submitted separately
04 · Agent trajectories trajectories/README.md
Failure journal: FAILURES.md 

 Experiments including removed ones: experiments/ 

 Raw results: evaluation/results/ 

 Raw results are never overwritten, each carrying its commit, model, backend and prompt digests.

A human-first automotive showroom where people and AI agents search, compare, estimate trade-ins, and prepare a test-drive request together.

 Inspiration 

 Buying a car rarely begins with a perfect form. It begins with a thought: “I need an automatic SUV, I have a trade-in, and I do not know where to start.” The Dealer's Desk turns that thought into structured, inspectable progress without hiding the human decision at the end. 

 What it does 

 The experience combines a natural-language agent brief with a clear showroom UI. An agent can call four page-level WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_inventory finds matches in a synthetic Emilia-Romagna dealer inventory. 
 compare_vehicles returns a contextual comparison, not just a list of fields. 
 evaluate_trade_in prepares an indicative range with explicit assumptions. 
 draft_test_drive_request prepares a request for human review. 
 

 The interface shows the same work to the person: the active brief, the shortlist, the comparison board, the trade-in context, and the final handoff. Search and comparison calls update that visible state directly, so the agent and the person stay in the same showroom context. Every action in the demo is draft-only: no message is sent, no appointment is booked, and no real lead is created. 

 How we built it 

 The public repository is a small Next.js application with a typed synthetic inventory, client-side WebMCP feature detection, and four structured tools registered through document.modelContext . The UI is intentionally usable without an agent, while capable browsers can discover the same actions as tools. 

 Why WebMCP matters here 

 WebMCP lets a website expose capabilities instead of forcing an agent to guess through clicks and visual labels. The Dealer's Desk uses that capability to make the first steps of a dealership journey more useful while keeping scope visible and human-controlled.

title: BuildBrief Studio
pitch: A shared WebMCP decision workspace where people and agents turn a rough structure idea into a transparent, reviewable project brief.
about_excerpt:
A shared WebMCP decision workspace where people and agents turn a rough structure idea into a transparent, reviewable project brief.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Planning a workshop or vehicle shelter starts with ordinary language but quickly becomes structured: use case, footprint, height, roof, openings, material, anchoring, budget, and unresolved site constraints. A normal chat can suggest an answer, but the reasoning often disappears into prose and the page on screen drifts out of sync. 

 BuildBrief Studio makes WebMCP the product interface between those two modes. The visual worksheet and six imperative Website Tools share one validated configuration. An agent can discover catalog options, compare two or three candidates, apply a partial recommendation, read the result back, review constraints, and create a preliminary brief. Write tools update the visible UI before returning and leave exact field-level receipts. If the person changes a value afterward, the revision advances and the old brief is visibly marked stale. 

 The demo is deliberately safe and easy to judge: no login, no personal information, no external API, and no production system. Every dollar value comes from a bundled synthetic catalog and a deterministic formula. Strict schemas and runtime validation reject extra fields and incompatible choices. Read-only annotations match behavior. Permit, access, anchoring, snow-load, and site conditions remain explicit human work rather than being hand-waved by automation. 

 The result is a small but complete example of what WebMCP enables: not an agent operating beside a website, but a person and agent collaborating through one observable decision surface. 

 How WebMCP is used 

 
 search_catalog discovers relevant structures from natural-language needs. 
 get_build_state grounds the agent in the person’s latest visible choices. 
 compare_builds evaluates two or three validated alternatives in one call. 
 apply_build performs a partial visible update and returns exact before/after changes. 
 check_constraints separates catalog fit from human verification. 
 create_build_brief renders a deterministic handoff artifact on the page. 
 

 All tools are registered imperatively from the top-level page through document.modelContext.registerTool . They use strict JSON Schema, truthful read/write annotations, concise structured output, and an AbortSignal lifecycle. 

 Quick judge path 

 Open the live demo in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, wait for “6 Website Tools ready,” and send the demo prompt shown on the page. Verify that the agent searches, compares against the $15,000 illustrative budget, applies an enclosed 20 × 24 workshop with a roll-up door, surfaces human checks, and creates the visible project brief. No credentials are required.

Like Comment Story Updates instructions transcript tool calls and state log Flow Control - Web-Native Supervision for Operational Agents Trying to delegate real-world work to black-box agents using brittle scrapers or custom wrappers is a mess. We need a shared workspace where humans and agents operate on the exact same live state, keeping real authority when things go sideways. Flow Control turns the web app itself into that control plane using WebMCP. By moving typed tooling directly to the endpoint, content creators stay in control instead of leaving the world to guess how to scrape an interface. The app registers authority-aware tools that dynamically shift based on what the human picks—whether it's "Observe," "Assist Me," or "Take the Sector." The agent handles routine traffic using strict, state-version-checked tool calls, but the moment things get exceptional—like a runway blockage—it stops, stages a recovery plan, and pings the supervisor for approval. Both human and agent actions flow through the same engine, logging everything for later audit or review. While I built this demo around a fictional air traffic control simulation, the architecture isn't locked to ATC. Swap aircraft for warehouse robots, drones, or delivery fleets, and the core pattern stays identical. Flow Control is an illustrative simulation, not an operational air traffic control product.  Inspiration 

 CrisisRoom AI was inspired by the need to make AI-assisted incident response safer and more practical. The project explores how an AI agent can investigate a security incident, analyze evidence, and prepare a containment action while keeping a human in control of the final decision. 

 What I built 

 CrisisRoom AI is a fictional incident-response dashboard connected to WebMCP. It exposes structured tools that an AI agent can use to retrieve incident information, inspect affected assets, analyze the situation, create an action draft, and generate an incident report. 

 Human-in-the-loop 

 The key design principle is that the AI can investigate and prepare an action, but it cannot execute containment on its own. The proposed action remains pending until a human explicitly approves or rejects it. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can connect AI agents directly to useful web application capabilities instead of relying only on UI interaction. I also learned how important clear tool definitions, application state, and human approval are when building AI-assisted security workflows. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing a realistic workflow while keeping the application fictional and safe. I focused on demonstrating the interaction between the agent, WebMCP tools, the incident state, and the human approval interface.

title: BlockSmith
pitch: AI builds websites fast and generic. BlockSmith captures a design system from any site in seconds, hands the rules to the AI, checks its work, and tells it no when it breaks them.
about_excerpt: AI builds websites fast and generic. BlockSmith captures a design system from any site in seconds, hands the rules to the AI, checks its work, and tells it no when it breaks them. Like Comment Story Updates BlockSmith + Chatgpt generated the Moda design wiki in under a minute BlockSmith captured the Moda website to create a design wiki, then used it to generate this custom landing page Wiki is Interactive itself, you can visualize the design system within the wiki Snapshot of interactive wiki component playground generated within few minutes. Snapshot of a custom landing page built from the Moda design wiki Snapshot of a Chart Page built from the Different design wiki Blocksmith strict design governance Snapshot of a custom dashboard interface page built from the Different design wiki Snapshot of a custom landing page built from the Different design wiki Inspiration Anyone can ship a website now. You describe it, an AI writes it, it's live the same afternoon, and the web is filling up with work that is fast, competent, and completely interchangeable. The same gradient. The same drop shadow. The same rounded card. In short, website now are full of AI slops. It is tempting to call that a taste problem. It isn't. Nobody ever gave the agent a standard. Real companies usually have one: the exact colours, the exact spacing, the things you never do, but it lives in a Figma file, a Notion page, or Confluences. The agent is looking at a rendered web page, and none of it is in a web page. So it does the average thing, and the average of the whole internet is what we have all been looking at, which we all know is a disaster! Gradient borders, wrong spacing.... Halfway through building this, Vercel published how their agents build on-brand pages with a design.md , and it turned out to be the best argument for what I was making. They wrote the rules down, published them at a public URL, and measured the result: 57% fewer brand failures. And then the honest part: "every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping." A file is passive. The agent has to be told to fetch it, has to interpret it, their words: "every model reading it interpreted that description differently" , and has to not be working from a copy that went stale. Reading the rules and being told no are different things. WebMCP is what closes that gap. The page stops being a document the agent reads and becomes an authority it can ask. What does BlockSmith even do? Every big company has rules about how its product looks: the exact colours, the exact spacing, the things you never do. Almost nobody else does. If you are one developer shipping something this weekend, you have no design system, no time to write one, and no way to make an AI follow it. BlockSmith gives you one either way and makes it usable by people and by AI at the same time. If your team already has a design system, this is where it lives: point BlockSmith at your codebase or your Figma file and it becomes a documentation site anyone can read and edit. If you don't have one, point it at any website you admire (vercel, openai , any website you like) and you have one in about few seconds instead of months! From there it is the same product for both. It hands those rules to any AI working in your browser, checks what that AI builds, and tells it no quoting the rule a designer actually wrote, so the AI learns the rule instead of just deleting a line. When the AI wants to change a rule, it cannot: it has to ask you, and you approve or reject it. Every version is kept, so you can see what changed and undo it. And the same rules follow the work out of the browser into your code editor, into an installable package, and into a check that stops a commit before it breaks anything. Imagine you now have a jenkins pipeline for each ui component :v How do you get in? From How A live website Reads what a page actually paints: colours ranked by how much of the screen they cover, type and spacing scales, radii, and the repeated components it can find Your codebase Scans a local workspace or a GitHub repo: every React component, its props and variants, every CSS custom property Figma Imports variables and published components, and reconciles them against code: "Figma says X, shipped code says Y" , with renames and near-misses told apart from real drift A document Paste or upload the design system you already wrote with this, blockSmith turns your design system into a documentation site. You get pages for colours, typography, spacing, components, and usage rules. There is also a playground where you can test values and see which tokens the system allows. Everything can be edited from the page. Human edits and approved AI suggestions go through the same review process. If a component does not have a usage rule yet, BlockSmith can draft one for you to edit. You can also preview the whole documentation site using the colours and typography from the design system you captured. It gives the rules to AI BlockSmith turns the design system into tools AI can use: 16 tools on the design system page, 4 for any website through the bookmarklet or Chrome extension, and 16 for coding agents like Cursor and Claude Code. Agents can also discover all available tools through /.well-known/webmcp.json. It catches design system violations When AI creates something, BlockSmith checks it against the design system. If something breaks a rule, it tells the AI exactly what went wrong and can auto-fix simple issues, but if a real design decision is needed, it stops and asks instead of guessing. It keeps track of versions With a connected code repository, BlockSmith manages design system changes like software releases: changes can stay in draft until approved, and a lockfile keeps AI and CI on the same approved version. You can also roll back changes, view release history, and track approved exceptions. Systems that are only pasted, uploaded, or captured stay in preview mode until connected to a repository. The same rules work outside BlockSmith You can use the design system in other tools too. Export it as a file for a coding agent Connect it to Cursor or Claude Code Generate an npm package with tokens and components Add a pre-commit check that blocks code that breaks the rules It works for teams Teams can invite people by email, create API keys, see the history of changes to each component, and publish the design system to a public link. Why WebMCP Most agent tools help AI do more. BlockSmith does something different: it tells AI what it should not do . For example, a design system might use red on the page but still have a rule saying, "Don't use this red for buttons or interactive elements." An AI looking at the screenshot or DOM can see the color, but it can't see that rule. The same goes for components. BlockSmith can tell AI not to build things like a tooltip, carousel, modal, accordion, or hero banner, and tell it what to use instead. You can't scrape something that doesn't exist. BlockSmith gives AI those missing rules so it doesn't just guess or invent them. How it creates a better user experience The agent stops guessing, Before an agent writes a line it calls get_governance_rules and gets this system's palette, scales, motion timing and authored rules. When it is wrong, the verdict is specific enough to act on in the same turn: REJECTED: 4 violation(s) in Portfolio. - Line 1 `banned-shadow`: `shadow-lg`. Shadows are not allowed in this design system. Rule: "Do not add drop shadows to cards or buttons. Separation comes from the Rule (#e2e4ea) hairline and from space, not elevation." - Line 1 `off-token-utility`: `bg-blue-500` is a stock Tailwind color, not a design token. - Line 1 `off-scale-utility`: `p-5` resolves to 20px, not on the spacing scale. Use `p-4` (16px) instead. Then fix_violations repairs what is mechanical and hands back what isn't : Applied 5 fix(es): p-5 → p-4, rounded-lg → rounded-md, text-sm → text-[13px] … 5 need a decision from you: - `bg-blue-500`: no token matches this colour; pick one from the palette - `shadow-lg`: removing this changes the design, not just a value That is intentional. womp womp done by me. :v If AI is asked to use a color that is not allowed, BlockSmith should not quietly replace it with something else. Instead, it knows when to stop and ask. The goal is not just to make AI do more, but to make sure it does not make design decisions it was never allowed to make. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An agent can be told no by the product itself, and then be told what changed. The loop, in one conversation: You ask for a launch banner in #7c3aed . The agent calls propose_component . The system answers: "Nothing in Cohere is close to this color; the nearest is Accent (#4c6ee6), which is a different hue. Adding a new color is a design decision for the user, not a substitution to make silently." The agent cannot add the colour . I

title: AI Boardroom
pitch: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide.
about_excerpt: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide. Like Comment Story Updates One COO and 6 Ai Assistant Agents Inspiration Founders often need to make consequential decisions with incomplete evidence, changing constraints and too many disconnected conversations. AI Boardroom puts a founder and a browser assistant in one shared decision room where specialist perspectives, evidence and trade-offs remain visible. What it does AI Boardroom gives one browser AI six specialist perspectives: Product, Evidence, Commercial, Operations, Technology and Chair. WebMCP lets the assistant read the live brief, request named roles, post evidence-linked contributions, respond when constraints change, and retrieve the exact decision record. The central interaction is deliberately human-controlled. A fictional launch budget changes from R20,000 to R8,000; the previous recommendation becomes stale, the assistant reads the new revision, and a new recommendation can be prepared without rewriting the earlier record. The founder reviews alternatives and reservations, then approves, rejects or requests revision in the visible page form. This is stateful collaboration rather than a detached chatbot transcript. The app does not run six independent AI workers or call a model API. One browser assistant adopts the roles and the human retains the final decision. How we built it The app is built with the OpenAI Sites React and TypeScript scaffold, Vinext and D1. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes seven WebMCP tools: start_session, get_boardroom_context, update_agenda, request_perspective, add_contribution, prepare_recommendation and get_decision_record. UI actions and WebMCP tools share the same API and persistence logic. Mutation inputs use expectedRevision for optimistic concurrency and operationId for safe retries. Evidence is stored with the relevant contribution and rendered as untrusted text. The visible review channel is a workflow boundary, not proof of human identity. Challenges The design challenge was making an AI council useful without pretending that six hidden agents or automatic consensus exist. We made the roles explicit, preserved disagreement, invalidated recommendations when the brief changed, and kept approval out of the WebMCP tool surface. A second challenge was handling uncertain browser or network outcomes without duplicating or overwriting decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the agent can operate on the same visible, stateful interface as the human. Structured tools make the collaboration legible, while revision checks, evidence snapshots and a human review stop make the limits legible too. What's next Production use would require stronger identity and access controls, consent design, privacy and retention rules, abuse and rate-limit controls, independent security review, and integrations governed by explicit human approval. Disclosure All briefs, budgets, evidence and decisions in this project are fictional. The app does not make purchases, send messages, or change external systems. Browser-generated council text is created at runtime and is not preseeded consensus.  Inspiration 

 Imagine searching for a remote job. You look up React Native roles, open a few listings, and find three worth considering.
Then come the simple questions: Which pays the most? Which am I actually eligible for from India? Which needs the least experience? How do their tech stacks differ? Which company has better benefits? What was that seventh listing again, and how does it compare to the first?
None of this is hard. It's just tedious. Multiple tabs, scattered details, manual comparison, and it only gets worse as the number of listings grows into the hundreds or thousands. 

 The Problem 

 There's a mismatch between how much useful information exists and how much a person can realistically explore. Comparing job listings by hand, salary, eligibility, experience, tech stack, benefits, is annoying even with three jobs and basically impossible at scale. 

 Why AI Agents Alone Don't Fix It 

 Agents seem like the obvious answer. You should be able to just say "compare the top three" or "which pays more but needs less experience?" and get an answer.
But most websites are built for humans, not agents. That means an agent has to reverse-engineer meaning from a visual interface, cards, buttons, clicks, rather than working with clean, structured data. 

 The Fix: WebMCP 

 Instead of forcing agents to scrape and interpret the interface, WebMCP lets a website expose its data and actions directly as structured tools: search_jobs, get_job_details, compare_jobs, save_job, unsave_job, get_saved_jobs, and get_filter_options.
The agent can just ask the site directly. No guessing required. 

 What We Built: TrueRemoteJobs 

 TrueRemoteJobs is a job board prototype with 200 fictional listings. It works normally for humans browsing the site, and it exposes WebMCP tools for agents working alongside them.
A typical flow looks like this: "Find React Native jobs open to India, paying $60K+" returns nine results. Then: "show me the first," "compare the first and seventh," "save the first and third." 

 Interfaces Can't Anticipate Every Question
You simply can't build a button for every possible query, like comparing jobs one, seven, and twelve on compensation, location, React Native experience, and benefits alone.
With structured data, the agent can combine and filter information however the user actually wants, without anyone needing to pre-design every possible screen. 

 A Real Bug That Proved the Point 

 During testing, the agent misidentified "the first result" because it was inferring meaning from whatever happened to be on screen rather than from real structure.
The fix was straightforward: every result now carries a stable jobId and an explicit resultNumber, so references like "the seventh one" are unambiguous.
The lesson stuck with us: giving an agent access to a webpage is not the same as giving it access to the actual information. 

 Humans and Agents Coexist 

 This isn't about replacing the website. It's the same underlying data and the same actions, just two ways of reaching them.
Browse visually when you want to. Delegate deep comparison and research to an agent when you don't. And the two stay in sync, if the agent saves a job, it's saved in the real app too. 

 Takeaway 

 Websites already hold rich information, and agents already have the reasoning ability to make sense of it. WebMCP is the structured bridge between the two, letting anyone, human or agent, dig as deep into a site's data as they want, rather than only as deep as the UI happened to be designed for.

title: NOVNA
pitch: NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision—so agents can inspect, challenge, and act without taking the decision away from the human.
about_excerpt: NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision—so agents can inspect, challenge, and act without taking the decision away from the human. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can already recommend products, compare options, and answer shopping questions. We wanted to explore a different question: what happens when an AI agent can participate directly in a decision that is already happening inside a website? Traditional shopping experiences separate the decision from the AI conversation. The user may have already created a shortlist, rejected products, compared options, and formed preferences, but an AI agent usually does not have access to that live context unless the user manually explains it again. NOVNA was built around a third model: the human keeps the decision, while the agent participates in it. What it does NOVNA is a decision-first shopping workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live decision. A user can define a goal, budget, urgency, priorities, shortlist products, reject options, compare products, and build a decision over time. Through WebMCP, an external AI agent can then interact with that existing decision context. The agent can: Inspect the current decision and user goal Understand the existing shortlist and comparisons Search and compare products Challenge the current choice Find better-fit alternatives Surface an alternative directly into NOVNA Update the decision through exposed tools The human remains in control throughout the process. The agent participates in the decision rather than replacing the decision-maker. How we built it NOVNA is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP . The application maintains a structured decision state containing the user's goal, budget, priorities, considered and rejected products, comparisons, insights, and decision history. We built a transparent decision engine that evaluates products against the user's actual requirements rather than relying on an unexplained universal score. The WebMCP layer exposes decision-specific tools through the browser's document.modelContext API. These tools allow an external agent to inspect and act on NOVNA's live decision state. The implementation includes tools for retrieving decision context, searching products, comparing products, finding alternatives, evaluating whether to wait or buy, challenging decisions, surfacing products, and updating user goals. We also built an agent activity surface and decision timeline so the human can see how the decision evolves and what actions were taken. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what WebMCP should actually enable. It was easy to build a product-search demo where an agent simply calls a search tool. We wanted something more meaningful: a workflow where the agent needs the context already accumulated inside the website. Another challenge was preserving human control. Agent actions needed to be useful without turning NOVNA into an autonomous shopping system. This led us toward explicit decision state, visible agent activity, and a decision timeline. We also had to work with a real product catalog and manufacturer-sourced specifications while keeping the architecture flexible enough for the catalog to grow. Finally, testing WebMCP required working with browser environments that expose the emerging API, which made the agent-to-website interaction an important part of our development process. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that NOVNA goes beyond demonstrating that a website can expose a WebMCP tool. The agent can enter an existing human decision , understand its context, challenge the current choice, find an alternative, and surface that alternative back into the same workspace. That creates a genuine human-agent loop: [ \text{Human Decision} \rightarrow \text{Agent Inspection} \rightarrow \text{Challenge} \rightarrow \text{Alternative} \rightarrow \text{Human Review} ] We are also proud of building the decision itself as a first-class product state rather than treating the website as a collection of isolated product pages. The result is a working end-to-end experience where the human and agent operate on the same decision context. What we learned We learned that the most interesting WebMCP use cases are not necessarily about giving an agent more information. They are about giving an agent access to the right context and actions at the right moment . We also learned that AI recommendations are already a mature interaction pattern. The opportunity we found was different: reducing the friction between an agent and the web application where a user's actual workflow and state already exist. Building NOVNA also taught us that human control becomes more important, not less, when agents gain the ability to act. Making agent actions visible and understandable is therefore part of the product, not just a debugging feature. What's next for NOVNA NOVNA currently focuses on laptop purchasing as a concrete demonstration of the decision-first model. The next step is to generalize the decision architecture beyond laptops and support more categories where decisions involve changing requirements, multiple options, trade-offs, and accumulated context. We also want to expand the decision timeline, make agent interventions more explainable, and explore richer collaboration between multiple agents and the human decision-maker. The long-term idea is simple: Websites should not just contain information for agents to read. They can become spaces where humans and agents work together on real decisions. NOVNA is an exploration of what that future could look like.
