title: Cogsmith
pitch: CogSmith helps gearheads turn old bikes into modern single-speeds. Making cool bikes for everyone!
about_excerpt: CogSmith helps gearheads turn old bikes into modern single-speeds. Making cool bikes for everyone! Like 8 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I started CogSmith because I needed a calculator to do some garage math for me. In my downtime I’ve started converting older MTBs into cool single-speed bikes, I find the tinkering in my garage really relaxing. The challenge is I'm constantly trial-and-erroring to figure out good combinations of gears to use, and I don't have a million gears to select from. I only have what the bike came with. There is math to help with this, but after crunching these numbers manually one too many times, I built a tool to handle it. I ended up fully fleshing out CogSmith because the calculator worked incredibly well for my own projects, and I was looking for a practical excuse to learn about vibe coding. What it does A rider enters information about their project bike, including wheel size, chainstay length, available chainrings and rear cogs, desired gearing, and dropout adjustment range. CogSmith then evaluates the possible combinations and calculates the Goldilocks combination for the rider. Instead of only calculating a gear ratio, CogSmith tries to answer the more useful question: "Can I actually build this combination on my bike?" CogSmith also supports WebMCP, allowing AI assistants to interact directly with the calculator. This is great as sometimes in the garage, your hands are filthy and the AI assistant can do lookups for you. How I built it I have a background in DevOps and infrastructure type scripting, so I wanted to use this as a chance to learn some vibe coding. For tools I wanted to do this as cheaply as possible so the best fit was to build this on GitHub, for its CI/CD pipelines and its static page hosting. It also integrated well with workflows I had used in the past AND worked well with GPT Work and Codex. CogSmith was built as a static web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It slowly grew from an all-in-one HTML file into something broken out into components, ultimately getting to a point where resources were broken up into testable pieces and I started using GitHub releases. As the project matured so did its architecture. It focuses on two areas now. A tool for humans and a tool for robots. Human interface → CogSmith calculation engine and AI through WebMCP → CogSmith calculation engine Both paths use the same underlying logic, so an AI recommendation is based on the same calculations that appear in the browser. CogSmith exposes WebMCP tools that allow an AI to read the current bike configuration, calculate possible gearing combinations, and display a selected setup back in the user interface. One of the core measurements CogSmith uses is gear inches: G = D × (T_f / T_r) where: G is gear inches D is wheel diameter T_f is the number of teeth on the front chainring T_r is the number of teeth on the rear cog CogSmith then combines that gearing calculation with chain-length and axle-position calculations to determine whether the setup will physically fit within the available dropout range. We also added automated tests and CI validation around the calculator and WebMCP interfaces so changes can be tested before being deployed. Challenges I ran into Honestly most of the infrastructure and pieces of the website were well understood and commonly used, however I started to face challenges with understanding how MCP worked and pivoting to how WebMCP works. WebMCP isn't well documented yet and honestly the test frameworks aren't great for it right now. That was the hard part, learning MCP :) Accomplishments that I'm proud of I love everything about CogSmith, I've used it for 3 different bikes so far and it saves me from fiddling around with gears. I'm most amazed and proud of learning about WebMCP. I'd been familiar with taking a function and exposing it as an API, but I never knew you could do something similar like taking a math formula and passing it to an AI. I think that's cool. It's like APIs for LLMs :D What I learned I had already learned that the voice assistant was useful in the garage, like "tell me the wheel lug nut torque rating for a 2018 GMC 1500 truck" or "I need 50:1 fuel mix for my outboard motor, I have 5L of gas, how much oil do I add" , but I never knew I could build a tool and plumb it into GPT. I had always thought GPT needed to search the internet to find this knowledge. What's next for CogSmith CogSmith is gonna simmer for a bit, it's Fall soon and I have some bike projects to finish. Other than that, I think I might do some repo cleanup, create some linting (I love linting) for the repo, and probably patch things as they need it. title: Fasting Tracker
pitch: A real iPhone-first fasting tracker with 17 app-defined WebMCP capabilities for agents.
about_excerpt: A real iPhone-first fasting tracker with 17 app-defined WebMCP capabilities for agents. Like Comment Story Updates The agent calls create_history_view; the tracker renders its own 90-day duration chart from source records. Saved changes stop at an app-owned approval gate. Nothing changes until the person approves. One real app for people, with safe, explicit capabilities for agents. Fasting Tracker is a real, iPhone-first timer and journal I built for myself and still use. A person can start a fast, check the countdown, correct an active start time, review history, compare periods, and track a goal without ever using a chatbot. WebMCP adds a second control surface to that same app. A compatible browser agent gets 17 named capabilities that the tracker defines and limits. The agent can read the current timer, build one of six history views, compare periods, highlight the records behind an explanation, preview several timing options, switch the open tab to a different layout or visual mode, and request a small set of saved changes. The important part is where control stays. The app validates every input, renders every result, and decides which actions exist. Reversible view changes can happen immediately in the open tab. Any action that changes fasting or experiment data stops at an app-owned approval dialog. The person sees the exact request and can approve or cancel it. A confirmed request still has to pass the Worker’s session, same-origin, CSRF, validation, idempotency, and audit checks. That creates a better experience than screen scraping. The agent does not guess which button to click or receive broad access to an account. It calls a capability with domain meaning, such as create_history_view , highlight_history_records , preview_fasting_decision , or start_fast . The tracker then responds through its normal interface, where the person can understand and verify the result. The public demo is credential-free and contains only synthetic data. It has an isolated Worker and D1 database, hides production admin and remote MCP routes, and includes a reset control that restores the same 11-record starting state for every judge. Why this is a strong WebMCP use case People should not have to choose between a well-designed app and an agent. Fasting Tracker shows how both can use the same product safely: The person gets a focused mobile interface for the everyday job. The agent gets explicit capabilities for questions and multi-step work. The app owns the allowed actions, validation, presentation, and safety rules. Read results stay connected to visible source records. Saved changes stop for human approval and produce audit evidence. This pattern applies far beyond fasting. Any established web app can keep its human interface while exposing a smaller, safer contract for agents. What people and agents can do together A person can ask, “Show my last 90 days as a duration trend.” The agent calls create_history_view , and the tracker renders its own chart from its own records. They can ask, “Highlight the records behind my longest fast.” The agent calls highlight_history_records , and the app points to the source entry instead of returning an unsupported answer. They can ask, “Compare 16, 18, and 20-hour options without starting a fast.” The agent calls preview_fasting_decision , and the app shows end times and history context without changing data or giving medical advice. They can ask to start an 18-hour fast. The app opens a clear approval dialog. Nothing is saved until the person chooses Start fast . What changed during the Challenge I first built the original app on Replit around January 2025 and kept using and improving it. I moved it to a newer Cloudflare Workers and D1 version in early August 2026. During the final week, after the Submission Period opened, I added the agent-facing API and action layer, the MCP and browser WebMCP integration, 17 agent capabilities, and the new history, visualization, workspace, experiment, confirmation, audit, and demo features. The public repository includes a dated provenance document that separates this work from the earlier tracker. How WebMCP was implemented The React page detects document.modelContext and registers 17 tools with JSON input schemas, descriptions, read-only annotations, and bounded execute functions. Read tools use the same Cloudflare Worker routes as the visible app. View tools update React state so results appear inside the tracker. Mutation tools wait on an app-owned approval controller before sending a protected request to the Worker. The Worker stores demo records in Cloudflare D1. It enforces origin and content-type checks, CSRF protection, strict validation, idempotency keys, and append-only audit events. Production and demo share source code but use separate Workers, databases, sessions, and secrets. title: Observatory
pitch: A local-first fantasy map builder where people and browser agents create together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A local-first fantasy map builder where people and browser agents create together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Fantasy maps help writers and game designers think, but creators often have to choose between complex graphics software and flattened AI images that are difficult to revise. Browser agents face a related problem: canvas interactions are hard to infer and fragile to automate visually. Observatory gives people and agents a shared, semantic mapmaking workspace. What it does Observatory is a local-first fantasy map builder where writers paint terrain, compose rooms, draw walls, place objects and labels, manage layers, undo changes, and export finished maps. Through WebMCP, a compatible browser agent can inspect and modify that same map using bounded, structured tools. A request such as “Build a map of a lone tower in a dense forest” becomes editable terrain strokes, structures, objects, and text—not a flattened image. Human and agent actions use the same state, persistence, revision, and undo paths. Destructive semantic changes require visible, single-use approval. How we built it Observatory uses Vue 3, Pinia, PixiJS/WebGL, IndexedDB, and Vite. Terrain remains editable vector data and is rendered through adaptive cached chunks. Structures, objects, labels, and layers retain stable semantic IDs. The WebMCP adapter registers library and project tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Strict JSON schemas, bounded responses, optimistic revision checks, idempotent operation IDs, abort handling, compact result envelopes, and approval tokens keep agent operations predictable and safe. IndexedDB is the durable boundary. Logical mutations increment a project revision and persist changed stores transactionally. Failed saves roll visible state and history back, while BroadcastChannel notifications prevent stale cross-tab writes. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping agent operations and human editing genuinely unified. Routing every action through the same application stores and transaction boundary required careful rollback and revision semantics. Terrain rendering also required balancing painterly materials, deterministic output, responsive previews, and large-map performance. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human map editor that remains useful without an agent. Structured WebMCP operations for discovery, inspection, terrain, geometry, objects, labels, layers, history, removal, and export. Agent changes that remain manually editable and undoable. Revision guards, idempotency, bounded payloads, and approval-gated removal. Local-first operation with no account, backend, telemetry, or runtime model API. Automated lint, type-check, locale, coverage, unit, browser, build, and dependency-security gates. What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes the product's actual domain model instead of mirroring UI clicks. Stable IDs, revisions, and approvals make collaboration faster and more reliable while preserving human control. What's next for Observatory Future work could add restorable project archive import, richer templates, and optional collaboration while preserving the local-first core. Testing Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser, create a blank map, and ask: “Build a map of a lone tower in a dense forest.” Inspect and manually edit created elements, use undo and redo, request a refinement by element ID, test approval-gated removal, and export as PNG. No account or credentials are required. Maps remain in browser IndexedDB.  ScAInce Draw 

 As a physics student, I've learned that the right diagram can often make a difficult problem immediately understandable. While sketching a figure on paper takes only a few seconds, creating the same diagram digitally is surprisingly time-consuming. Unlike mathematical equations, which are straightforward to typeset (thank goodness we have LaTeX), diagrams are a completely different story. I've spent dozens (maybe hundreds) of hours tweaking figures just to make it look right. 

 With the rise of AI, I became curious whether it could automate this process. The results were initially disappointing. At first there was no even harness for generating diagrams, and even when equipped with general-purpose coding tools, AI struggled to produce accurate diagrams -even for simple block diagrams, let alone figures describing physics problems. 

 This led me to an important observation: diagram creation is an ideal human-in-the-loop task . AI can dramatically accelerate the drafting process, but the final validation should remain with the human, who ultimately decides whether the figure correctly represents the intended concept. 

 This idea became ScAInce Draw . 

 What is ScAInce Draw? 

 ScAInce Draw is a graphical application for creating mathematical and physics diagrams, which covers geometry, mechanics, optics, circuits. 

 The application is equipped with WebMCP , exposing a rich set of tools that allow AI agents to construct diagrams programmatically while performing numerous validations. These validations help prevent common issues such as overlapping elements, inconsistent layouts, and incorrect object placement. 

 Beyond the WebMCP itself, ScAInce Draw also includes a dedicated Skill . As demonstrated throughout this year, MCPs are significantly more effective when paired with a skill. 

 Human–AI Workflow 

 ScAInce Draw supports two complementary workflows: 

 
 Human → AI 

 
 The user quickly sketches the diagram. 
 The AI refines it into a clean, pixel-perfect figure. 
 
 AI → Human 

 
 The AI generates the initial diagram from a natural-language description. 
 The user validates the result and applies the final adjustments. 
 
 

 Current Status 

 ScAInce Draw is still an early-stage prototype, but it already demonstrates the potential of combining WebMCP with a domain-specific graphical application. 

 The application is still relatively simple, but it already contains a substantial amount of validation logic. In my testing, it consistently generates accurate diagrams from well-crafted prompts (e.g. from elementary mechanics problem statements). 

 There is still considerable room for improvement, particularly in refining the generated layouts and validations. However, my experiments consistently show that integrating WebMCP significantly improves both the quality and the speed of AI-generated scientific diagrams (as an alternative to simply asking ChatGPT to click around the browser and figure out what it can do) 

 Ultimately, ScAInce Draw demonstrates that meaningful diagram generation is not simply a drawing problem - it is a collaborative workflow where AI accelerates creation while humans provide the final validation and scientific judgment.

title: Recall Response Workbench — Recall the Right Items
pitch: Find the right 37, protect the other 8,383, and put the irreversible decision behind a visible review control.
about_excerpt: Find the right 37, protect the other 8,383, and put the irreversible decision behind a visible review control. Like Comment Story Updates Overview: trace one exact supplier lot across 8,420 synthetic orders. Staged review: 37 exact matches, 213 lookalikes excluded, zero simulated commits before confirmation. Visible confirmation gate: review 10 quarantines, 9 intercepts, and 18 outreach drafts before committing. Confirmed rehearsal receipt: synthetic actions recorded in memory; no real messages or operational changes. Why is this a strong fit for WebMCP? Product recalls are ideal structured-agent work: many precise, auditable steps happen inside a UI, but the final operational decision should remain with an accountable person. WebMCP lets the page expose exact business operations instead of asking an agent to scrape tables or guess which controls to click. The tool set follows the recall lifecycle—read, trace, resolve, classify, preview, and stage—while the visible page stays synchronized after every call. The demo makes WebMCP’s value concrete. It searches 8,420 generated orders, returns exactly 37 orders for lot L24-091 , and explicitly proves that 213 orders from the confusable L24-019 lot were excluded. How is the user experience better? The user receives a reviewable answer, not an opaque automation result. Exact-match evidence, fulfillment states, action classifications, staging status, and activity history are visible in one responsive workbench. Agents can do the repetitive reconciliation, while final commit occurs through a visible normal page control. The complete atomic tool set is registered once, and domain preconditions reject out-of-order actions with corrective errors. The product also works immediately in demos: a clearly labeled deterministic rehearsal invokes the same domain service when WebMCP is unavailable and still stops at the visible review gate. What can humans and agents now do together? An agent can read the selected recall, trace an exact supplier lot, find affected fulfillments, classify a response for every match, preview the scope, and stage 10 warehouse quarantines, 9 carrier intercept requests, and 18 customer outreach drafts. Classifications remain mutually exclusive: each in-transit order is an intercept, while its response package also includes a customer notice. A reviewer can inspect the evidence, verify the 37 exact recipients and 213 exclusions, cancel drafts, or activate the visible final control. Ordinary browser or Codex actuation may also reach that control. Any host or browser safety policies apply independently; the app’s safety claim is specifically that no consequential WebMCP tool exists. After confirmation, the agent can read—never create through WebMCP—the current rehearsal receipt. How was it implemented? The submission is a static Vite + React + TypeScript app with plain CSS and deterministic in-memory data. Imperative WebMCP tools are registered atomically in the top-level document through document.modelContext , with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback. All registrations are initiated together; when any failure is observed, the lifecycle rolls back its successfully registered tools and aborts pending work. An AbortController manages registration lifetime; callbacks accept optional execution options for older previews and polyfills, validate input in code, and define the synchronous domain transition as the mutation commit point before paint synchronization. Read-only and mutation annotations are accurate. Mutating tools commit through a synchronous React flushSync boundary and do not yield to paint hooks after state mutation. The app does not expose a confirm, commit, release, or send WebMCP tool. Vitest covers exact counts, carrier/customer staging, ephemeral receipt reset, confusable-lot rejection, one-time registration, asynchronous cleanup, duplicate protection, and synchronous visible mutation. Impact This prototype demonstrates how explicit browser tools can reduce brittle UI automation and make a high-consequence workflow easier to audit. It does not claim measured production savings or regulatory approval. Its grounded claim is narrower: for the included deterministic scenario, every one of 8,420 orders is evaluated, all 37 affected orders are identified, all 213 confusable-lot orders are excluded, and zero durable actions occur before review confirmation. AI and Codex usage Built with OpenAI Codex using the WebMCP skill from webmaxru/web-ai-agent-skills. An external AI client interprets the operator's request and invokes the page's structured WebMCP tools. The app itself has no embedded LLM backend: matching, classification, staging, and receipts are deterministic TypeScript operations. The project was tested using GPT-5.6 Sol in Codex with the in-app browser and Site Tools. The documented demo discovers the tools, performs the seven staging steps, pauses for the visible review control, and reads the receipt afterward. Known limitations This is a deterministic prototype using synthetic data. No real warehouse quarantine, carrier intercept, or customer message occurs, even after confirmation. All state, including the confirmed receipt and the UI's simulated commit counter, is held in memory and resets on reload. The demo checksum is not cryptographic or a durable audit record. The visible control is not an enforced human-only authorization boundary: ordinary browser actuation may reach it. WebMCP availability depends on the client, and the guided rehearsal is not a substitute for testing agent discovery and invocation. Hackathon scope This is a new project for the challenge. The recall domain model, UI, WebMCP surface, tests, and documentation are the hackathon work. title: African Market OS WebMCP Decision Readiness Lab
pitch: A browser-agent lab that turns high-context market decisions into evidence gaps, safe next steps, and human-controlled activation.
about_excerpt: A browser-agent lab that turns high-context market decisions into evidence gaps, safe next steps, and human-controlled activation. Like Comment Story Updates Live WebMCP first-call returns a bounded, gap-first response and maximum-safe next action. The agent converts missing evidence into observable requests before any consequential decision. Exactly five page-defined WebMCP tools are discoverable in the browser agent. Inspiration High-context market decisions often fail before execution because founders, investors, and advisers mistake a persuasive narrative for sufficient evidence. A browser agent can read a conventional page, but it still has to infer which fields matter, what sequence to follow, and when to stop. In market-entry, partnership, investment, and scale decisions, that guesswork can turn thin evidence into false confidence. We built the African Market OS WebMCP Decision Readiness Lab to explore a better interaction: the human supplies context and intent, the website supplies authoritative tools and boundaries, and the browser agent helps turn uncertainty into a practical evidence plan. What it does The live page supports both people and WebMCP-capable browser agents. A user scopes a non-confidential decision with an entity, country, local market or corridor, sector, decision type, timeframe, and evidence note. The page registers exactly five WebMCP tools: amos_scope_market_decision strictly validates and structures the decision context. amos_run_public_first_call calls African Market OS's live, keyless MVR first-call preflight for the active scope. amos_extract_evidence_gap_plan turns returned evidence gaps into observable requests only after a bound preflight exists. amos_prepare_human_next_step validates and prepares a bounded route for a human to choose. amos_get_webmcp_demo_script provides a repeatable state-aware reviewer sequence. The result is deliberately not an approval or readiness verdict. It identifies what is known, what evidence is absent, what must not be claimed, and the maximum-safe action available now. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent must scrape labels, guess UI state, and improvise the workflow. With WebMCP, the page exposes named tools, descriptions, JSON input schemas, execution logic, and explicit authority boundaries in the same context the person is viewing. The agent can invoke the intended operation and receive a structured response consistent with the human-facing experience. This creates a better experience through shared context, lower ambiguity, and safer activation. The workflow distinguishes evidence support from commercial, legal, credit, investment, procurement, or regulatory authorization. What people and agents can do together A person decides which real-world decision to examine and controls every consequential or commercial next step. The browser agent can structure the input, call the live preflight, summarize the evidence gaps, and prepare a focused plan. The visible buttons call the same functions, so browsers without WebMCP retain the full human workflow. How we built it The demo is a self-contained HTML, CSS, and JavaScript application deployed on African Market OS through Cloudflare. It uses the imperative WebMCP API, document.modelContext.registerTool() , to register five page-specific tools. Schemas describe the contract, but every handler also validates independently. Required fields, allowed values, lengths, unexpected properties, and sensitive-data indicators are rejected rather than silently repaired. A deterministic scope_id binds the visible decision to the first call, and the returned preflight_id binds every downstream action. Changing the scope invalidates the old preflight. Same-key retries reuse the active workflow unless an agent explicitly requests a new one. The default agent_compact profile returns one canonical page-level next action. An opt-in debug_full profile preserves deeper inspection without burdening normal agent context. If the upstream MVR response recommends a capability that is not one of the page's five tools, the response labels it as a separate remote-MCP continuation instead of pretending it is locally callable. Protected MVR scoring and private calibration assets are never exposed. The public result states when live scoring did not run and carries a clear not_a_verdict boundary. Challenges The hardest part was not registering a browser tool. It was making schema declarations, handler behavior, visible page state, retries, and downstream handoffs tell the same truth. We had to prevent sample fallbacks from masking invalid agent input, stop stale preflights from surviving a changed form, make retries idempotent, and keep remote MCP capabilities distinct from page-defined tools. Accomplishments Exactly five page-defined WebMCP tools are discoverable. Empty, malformed, over-limit, unexpected, and stale-state inputs fail explicitly. A valid first call returns HTTP 200, a compact gap-first response, and one bound next action. Same-key retries reuse the exact preflight rather than creating duplicate workflows. Human and agent paths share one implementation, while payment and consequential action remain human-controlled. A post-build adversarial review was converted into regression coverage: the production Worker suite passes 153 of 153 tests, the public repository includes a passing dependency-free contract test, and a 30-case Agent Experience regression records the post-fix evidence and caveats. The production /mcp/ and canonical /mcp/preflight surfaces remain separate and unchanged. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it carries semantics, not just clicks. Schema declaration alone is not enough; handlers must defend the same contract. Every multi-tool handoff needs explicit state identity. For evidence-sensitive decisions, a well-designed stop condition is a feature: helping an agent say collect this proof next can be more useful than producing another confident answer. What's next We plan to test the workflow with founders, programme operators, investors, and advisers; measure where agents stop in the handoff sequence; improve accessibility of structured results; and evaluate how evidence plans change real decisions over time. Consequential judgments, credentials, contracting, and payment will remain human-controlled. title: Tendero — WebMCP for a Colombian corner store
pitch: WebMCP commerce tools assume a US checkout. Tendero hands an AI agent the eleven tools a Colombian sale needs — DIAN, VAT-by-destination, freight, Wompi — and closes only after a human's click.
about_excerpt: WebMCP commerce tools assume a US checkout. Tendero hands an AI agent the eleven tools a Colombian sale needs — DIAN, VAT-by-destination, freight, Wompi — and closes only after a human's click. Like Comment Story Updates Tendero is a working WebMCP storefront for a Colombian corner store — Surtitienda La Milagrosa , Manrique, Medellín. It hands an AI agent the eleven tools a Colombian sale actually needs via document.modelContext.registerTool , and it closes the sale only in Wompi sandbox and only after a human's one-click authorization the agent structurally cannot bypass. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The default commerce tool set ( search_products / add_to_cart / checkout ) quietly exports US assumptions — a prepaid card, a street address, a self-serve checkout. A Colombian sale is none of those, and the correct action depends on local rules the agent cannot infer and only the page knows: Cash on delivery is the dominant rail — with a collection ceiling, partial carrier coverage, and towns no carrier will reach. VAT depends on the destination department — the same basket is VAT-excluded in Amazonas and San Andrés. Colombia has four VAT treatments plus consumption tax; exento and excluido differ in law. A statutory 5-business-day right of withdrawal , against the real holiday calendar. An e-invoice is rejected by DIAN without a valid document type and a correct NIT check digit. How it creates a better UX The surface matches what's possible: an agent on a clean page sees 4 tools, not 11, and grows the surface 4 → 7 → 11 as the cart fills and a destination is set. Tools rewrite their own descriptions from page state — cash on delivery becomes "unavailable: Leticia has only air access" — firing toolchange so the agent re-reads the rules. Refusals are recovery-shaped (the NIT check digit that should have been 8). Every execute() calls the same render the human buttons call, so the person sees the machine work . What people and agents can do together The agent assembles the order and the page supplies the law — VAT treatment per line, cash-on-delivery reachability, the withdrawal deadline, whether the buyer's document survives e-invoicing. Then the split that makes it collaboration, not automation: a human's one-click authorization seals the sale; only then can the agent open the Wompi checkout and confirm the payment (sandbox — no real money). The human authorizes; the agent executes. How we built it (WebMCP implementation) 11 tools , each document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) with full JSON Schema. Progressive disclosure in three rungs , gated on page state; descriptions computed from state so a change forces genuine re-registration and a real toolchange event. MCP-shaped responses ( content[0].text + structuredContent ); discriminate annotations ( readOnlyHint , idempotentHint , destructiveHint , untrustedContentHint ); host-portable teardown. No backend at runtime — static files; the Colombian rule engine runs in the page , with a Python reference implementation pinned by parity tests. CI: ruff, mypy --strict , pytest ( 99% coverage ), and a headless harness that drives the real page with a mock modelContext and asserts an agent can grow the surface and close the sale by itself. Verified live 4 → 7 → 11 tools · cheapest freight to Leticia $86,435 · total $110,835 with VAT $0 (Amazonas excluded) · NIT 900123456-0 → invalid, check digit should be 8 · payment closes APROBADA in sandbox · zero console errors. What's next Colombia is the instance, not the point — swap the rule module for Brazil (NF-e), Mexico (CFDI), or India (GSTIN). MIT-licensed; adoption is one static file and a <script> tag. title: Can an Agent Fly a Plane?
pitch: I built a flight simulator, then used WebMCP to see if an AI agent could fly the thing, handle an emergency it didn’t know was coming, and somehow land.
about_excerpt: I built a flight simulator, then used WebMCP to see if an AI agent could fly the thing, handle an emergency it didn’t know was coming, and somehow land. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I've been watching a lot of pilot content lately, and I've always been interested in planes. An agent-driven flight evaluation sounded cool, and using STL, where I'm from, felt obvious. What it does This project is a real-time WebMCP evaluation for model developers and evaluation researchers. Your agent has to take off from STL on a flight to MDW in Chicago, handle a sealed emergency, coordinate a diversion with simulated ATC (air traffic control), and land safely back in St. Louis. ATC defines the route and checkpoints, but the agent decides how to fly them. It chooses the flight targets, aircraft configuration, and activation conditions. The simulator applies those targets continuously using 60 Hz physics at a fixed 2x time scale. It never pauses or changes that rate while the agent thinks, and the emergency decision window and mission deadline still use real elapsed time. Completing the flight requires hitting the route checkpoints and configuring the aircraft correctly. The score deducts points for slow emergency decisions, exceeding the mission window, high G-force, abrupt motion, hard or off-center landings, and crashes. The page registers six WebMCP tools for reading the manual, starting the flight, programming commands, coordinating with ATC, and waiting for events. WebMCP gives the agent structured state and validated actions instead of making it guess at visual controls. A person can fly the same aircraft manually, or start an agent evaluation and watch it go. The exported trajectory records every WebMCP call, action, result, latency, before-and-after state, score change, and simulator event. How I built it I used Codex to build and test each version. My first Cesium.js scene used a real route from STL to Chicago, but it hurt performance and was very buggy. I switched to Three.js and built a simplified but representative wide-body twinjet flight envelope. The simulation runs outside React render state at 60 Hz. The WebMCP layer uses document.modelContext.registerTool to expose the six tools, but the simulator still works manually without WebMCP if you want to fly it yourself. I went through probably 15 to 20 iterations of the world itself, adding audio and the minimap along the way. The hard part was deciding what the agent should actually control. We revised the tools until the agent was calling the shots instead of taking credit for decisions buried in the simulator. Challenges I ran into The V1 version was kind of cool, but it was too easy. The agent was basically on autopilot. The deterministic simulator controlled pitch, bank, and power while the agent only decided whether to return or continue. I set a /goal challenging Codex to make a fresh subagent complete the flight using the actual flight model. The results were pretty interesting. After 13 hours and 73 attempts, it finally got three runs to land with scores around 90, but of course it cheated. Somewhere along the way it decided the easiest way to fly a plane was to stop time whenever it needed to think. That obviously defeated the entire point. That exposed the most interesting part. As soon as the agent has to think, time becomes part of the problem. Even Terra at low reasoning could take long enough that the aircraft crashed or flew too far away. The solution was to meet in the middle. Simulated ATC supplies the route, but the agent writes the flight program before takeoff and replaces it after the emergency. The simulator tracks its targets at 60 Hz without pausing or deciding what comes next. I tested that version with ten agents in cold threads, and all ten failed. I decided they needed a “manual” explaining the aircraft and command interface. I really didn't want to do this, but they needed enough context to land without moving the decisions back into the simulator. The manual publishes rotation speed, climb and landing configuration, approach speed, flare limits, and the go-around sequence. It does not reveal the emergency, choose the diversion, or provide a program. The agent still has to fly. The resulting architecture completed three fresh blind runs in a row without pausing, changing the fixed simulation rate, or revealing the emergency early. Every WebMCP interaction was captured in the browser-side trajectory export. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that I didn't stop at “this works because the agent said it does” (which happens every single time lmao). I grilled Codex on how the simulation worked and kept pushing until the agent, rather than a hidden policy, owned the decisions. Thinking still hurts performance here, but I believe that is useful signal rather than something to hide. Models should be able to judge when deeper reasoning is worth the time. What I learned I learned a lot about building with WebMCP and understanding the agent experience. It isn't as simple as “give the agent all the information and let it do the thing.” I had to run fresh agents repeatedly and fix ambiguous tools without taking decisions away from them. The manual is part of the interface, not an answer key. The same applies to human UX. If people and agents get stuck at the same point, the interface probably is not communicating clearly enough. What's next? This could become an evaluation environment for model developers and researchers testing decisions under time pressure. Most evaluations I've seen analyze time after the run. Here, time changes the environment. A longer response means the aircraft has traveled farther, burned more fuel, and moved closer to failure. The sealed scenario and exported trajectory make that measurable. The idea also does not have to stop at flying a plane. The same setup could test an agent acting as ATC, coordinating a ground crew, or handling another system where the world keeps moving while the model thinks. The bigger question is whether models can learn when to reason deeply and when they need to act now. title: Waypoint — plan trips with your agent, beside you
pitch: A trip planner where your AI agent works INSIDE the page with you — visible, constrained by your 🔒 locks, and corrected by the app's own math
about_excerpt: A trip planner where your AI agent works INSIDE the page with you — visible, constrained by your 🔒 locks, and corrected by the app's own math Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Trip planners are single-player, and AI travel agents that book through a backend leave your screen behind — the agent works on a hidden copy of your data while you stare at a chat window. We wanted the third model: an AI agent that works INSIDE the page, beside you — visible, correctable, and constrained by your decisions. WebMCP made that possible, so we built Waypoint for The WebMCP Challenge. What it does Waypoint is a trip itinerary planner where you plan in the UI and an AI agent (ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser) works on the same board through 8 tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() : The agent reads the itinerary, adds/updates/removes activities, re-orders days, audits conflicts and budget. You keep hard control: activities you 🔒-lock are enforced in the tool contract — reorder_day refuses to move them and explains why. The agent literally cannot touch your locked lunch. The app does the math, the agent does the judgment: overlap detection and budget totals are computed deterministically and returned as JSON from every mutation, so the agent verifies its own changes in one turn. A shared activity feed logs every human and agent action — you watch your agent work beside you. In the demo video, the human resets the board mid-session, the conflict reappears, and the agent catches it and fixes it live on screen — leaving the locked lunch untouched. How we built it React 18 + TypeScript + Vite 6 + Tailwind v4 — a static site with zero backend and zero API keys : the browsing agent is the AI. src/webmcp.ts registers all 8 tools per the WebMCP spec , with JSON-Schema inputs and agent-oriented JSON returns (post-change schedule + new conflicts + budget deltas + actionable hints). Both WebMCP APIs in one app: set_trip_budget is also a real HTML <form> carrying the spec's proposed declarative attributes ( toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription / toolautosubmit ). Flag-enabled Chrome auto-registers the form as a tool — we watched it happen ("Duplicate tool name" was the happy error). An in-app agent simulator executes the identical tool implementations, so visitors without a WebMCP browser still experience the collaboration. State lives in a pure reducer + localStorage; tool mutations apply synchronously so a tool's return value always reflects its own change. Deployed on GitHub Pages; the Devpost video's voiceover is Deepgram TTS and the edit was scripted with ffmpeg. Challenges we ran into Chrome 152 expired the #enable-webmcp-testing flag — "Enabled" was a silent no-op until we also enabled the "Temporarily unexpire M150/M151 flags". Then "modelContext" in document returned true and all 8 tools registered. ChatGPT's regular chat only "searches" pages — Site tools attach only in the desktop app's built-in browser with Codex/Work (on GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra). Finding that flow took real debugging. A sneaky HTML5 validation bug: the budget form had step=5 + min=1 , silently rejecting round numbers like 150 — caught only because we functionally tested every form before recording. Hosting hurdles: a leftover CNAME in a GitHub user-pages repo was redirecting all our Pages URLs, and Git Bash mangled Vite's --base=/WebPoint/ into Program Files/Git/WebPoint/ on the first deploy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full human + agent loop works end-to-end in the judges' environment: green "WebMCP live" chip, agent fixing conflicts live on screen, lock refusals, budget checks — verified, not mocked. The collaboration contract (human locks as tool-enforced constraints, app-returned math) is implemented exactly as designed. What we learned WebMCP flips the integration model: instead of the agent bypassing your UI, your UI becomes the agent's API — and that makes human control a schema-level feature , not a hope. Returning rich post-state from mutating tools lets agents self-correct in one round trip. Test the boring paths (HTML forms!) as hard as the shiny ones. What's next Multi-trip support and shared trips (multiple humans + agents on one board). A lock-approval flow: agent proposes, human accepts — one click at a time. Shipping a small "site tools" badge pattern other sites can copy. title: VoiceGuard
pitch: A browser agent spots risk while the human keeps the controls.
about_excerpt: A browser agent spots risk while the human keeps the controls. Like Comment Story Updates Native Chrome WebMCP inspector showing audit_guardrails structured output. Demo video contact sheet: shared cockpit, tool calls and human review. VoiceGuard hero: the agent finds the signal, the human owns the action. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for VoiceGuard Inspiration Voice AI can listen, reason and respond in real time, but consequential calls still need accountable human judgment. Conventional browser automation forces an agent to infer meaning from buttons and dashboards, while a hidden backend tool can remove the shared context that helps a person supervise safely. We wanted the agent and operator to work from the same visible page without giving the agent invisible authority. What it does VoiceGuard is a synthetic voice-operations cockpit with four WebMCP site tools. An agent can inspect the current call state, audit visible guardrails, draft short operator guidance, or stage a pause request. The first two tools are read-only. The latter two change only visible draft or request state. A trusted human click is required before guidance can be applied or the synthetic call can be paused. The public demo deliberately exposes no tool for dialing, sending guidance, speaking, listing contacts, starting campaigns, transferring or hanging up. Every call, person, transcript and metric on the page is fictional. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Supervision depends on live shared context: phase, latency, transcript, policy signals and pending actions. WebMCP lets the browser agent discover narrow, schema-defined actions directly on that same page instead of scraping the DOM or calling a detached backend. Tool calls update a visible activity trace, so the operator can see what the agent read or prepared. This makes the experience faster and less ambiguous while preserving the human-first interface. The agent finds the signal. The human owns the action. How we implemented WebMCP The static top-level page registers four imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema, bounded text inputs and explicit read-only or untrusted-content annotations. The two draft-only tools return structured proof that no call action was executed. Human review buttons require trusted click events. The optional ?inspector=1 view is a transparent native test client. It uses document.modelContext.getTools() and executeTool() to show the exact JSON returned by Chrome's WebMCP implementation. The app has no backend and makes no network request after loading. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was designing useful agent actions without quietly creating an unsafe control plane. We removed every direct call action and separated drafting from execution. We also treated transcript text as untrusted page content, bounded all inputs, made tool activity visible, and built native Chrome tests that prove the page remains live until a human confirms a pause. Accomplishments Four working top-level WebMCP tools with native Chrome discovery and execution tests. A polished responsive shared workspace rather than a hidden JSON-only demo. Visible synthetic-data and autonomy boundaries throughout the product. A clean-room public repository with no production dependency or credential. Automated static, browser, responsive, safety and public-deployment checks. What we learned The most interesting WebMCP design question is not how many actions an agent can take. It is which actions should remain deliberately unavailable. Narrow tools, shared state and visible confirmation can make an agent more useful without making it less accountable. What's next Next we would connect the same interface contract to an authenticated pilot, add role-based tool availability, retain privacy-safe audit events, and test the workflow with real operators under explicit consent and legal review. None of those future production capabilities are represented as part of this synthetic contest demo. title: Break WebMCP consent, then fix it with a mandate
pitch: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests.
about_excerpt: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Shown, ran, refused: one attack caught by the mandate Devpost submission — ROAST (WebMCP Challenge, filled 30 Aug 2026) Name: ROAST · break WebMCP consent, then fix it with a mandate Pitch: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests. Thumbnail: data/webmcp-challenge/roast-devpost-thumb.png Demo: https://crowley.nl/webmcp-challenge/ Essay: https://crowley.nl/blog/webmcp-consent-theater.html Built with: javascript, webmcp, mcp, html5, css3, elevenlabs, github-actions, security Project Story (pasted into "About the project") Inspiration I first heard about WebMCP on Greg Isenberg's YouTube channel, where the conversation was all possibility: agents driving websites through your own browser, no scraping, no brittle automation. I love MCP, so I started reading the proposal properly. What struck me was the gap: the security story was thin. WebMCP's best trick is that the agent inherits your logged-in session - and that same trick is the loaded gun. So I asked the obvious questions. How does consent actually work here? What could go wrong? And when it goes wrong, what would stop it going wrong again? What it does ROAST is a fake coffee shop an AI agent can drive through WebMCP - and misuse. It plays four acts: No consent - the agent acts silently on your session Naive consent - a dialogue shows the tool's friendly description; feels safe Poisoned consent - the same dialogue, with three real attacks underneath: label mismatch, tool substitution, and a hidden-instruction manifest. You approve a coffee; your shipping address changes, your account closes The mandate - the proposal. You grant bounded authority up front: two coffees, $30, never my address, ask before paying. Every call is checked against the executed tool and the hidden chain, before any dialogue renders The model is Intent → Authority → Effect . Inside the mandate the agent just works - no prompt fatigue. Outside it, the call is refused before a dialogue exists to be fooled. At the boundary (paying), it escalates to the human. Once. A built-in test rig asserts all nine cases - three attacks, six legitimate paths - live on the page. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, no framework, one funnel: every tool call (simulated or real) resolves through request → resolvePlan → mandate check → consent gate → execute → log . The attacks are pure functions that warp the mapping between what is shown and what runs - which makes them honest test cases, not theatre. Tools register for real via navigator.modelContext where the browser supports it; a deterministic sim harness plays the same pipeline everywhere else. The instrumentation panel shows intent, consent, and effect side by side - the technical truth lives "below the waterline" of the UI. Challenges we ran into The honest one: the mandate check runs inside the page, and the page is the attacker. We state this in the UI rather than hide it. In a real deployment the mandate belongs in the browser or the agent - the layer a site cannot rewrite. ROAST prototypes it in the page because the page is what a demo controls. That is the proposal to the spec, not a shipped fix. The other challenge was UX density: showing an attack, a refusal, and the raw call log without drowning the visitor - solved with plain-English verdicts above the waterline and the technical log beneath it. What we learned The consent moment is the whole human-agent interface, and a dialogue that renders a human-authored description is a dialogue that can lie. Better warnings do not fix this; bounded authority does. Checking the executed call against a standing mandate defeats all three attacks with one invariant: an effect may only execute when it matches both the declared tool and the human's current mandate. What's next for ROAST Take the mandate out of the page: a browser-level or agent-level authority layer for WebMCP, mandates expressed in the user's own words and parsed to scopes, and fingerprinted tool manifests so substitution is detectable across the boundary. The write-up and the argument live at crowley.nl/webmcp-challenge/ . The security argument, the interaction design, and the video are mine. title: Givens
pitch: Stuck on a sudoku? Point an agent to help you with it.
about_excerpt: Stuck on a sudoku? Point an agent to help you with it. Like Comment Story Updates Screenshot of the 'Givens' website featuring a sudoku grid and other sections like shared logs and tools so your agent can help you with it The story of Givens Givens is a Sudoku studio where a person and an agent share one live grid. The agent names the next technique and highlights the cells. You decide whether to fill, lock, or take one safe step. What inspired this I am an avid sudoku solver and have had countless moments where I make good progress on the puzzle itself but then I've gotten stuck on some step. Now, there are online resources and guides and communties that can help out here, but I thought WebMCP was an interesting solution to this problem. A complete solution is a string of 81 digits. If the agent dumps it in chat, the page was pointless. If it clicks around the DOM, it will mis-click. The product I wanted is the thing in between: collaborative deduction. What I learned WebMCP is not MCP in the browser. MCP can live on a server with no page open. WebMCP tools exist only while a visible, origin-isolated document is connected. ChatGPT’s in-app browser also implements a subset: Imperative document.modelContext.registerTool works. Declarative HTML form tools do not show up as site tools. Tools inside iframes are invisible, even same-origin. So registration has to happen on the top-level page, after the board mounts, with feature detection: if (typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool === "function") { await document.modelContext.registerTool({ /* ... */ }); } I also learned that Codex can solve Sudoku in its head. If the only write tool is set_cell , it will skip the tutor and emit 81 answers. Tool descriptions and every read_board snapshot have to say: do not dump the grid; change it only through tools; trust the snapshot, not memory. On the puzzle side, computed candidates are not enough for pairs. A naked pair does not fill a cell; it removes digits elsewhere. That elimination has to be stored, or the next hint never sees it. Bundled puzzles have to be uniquely solvable. One “evening” grid I wrote by hand had two solutions. The brute-force solver is a backtracking search over the cell with the fewest candidates; we keep going until we have 0, 1, or >1 completions, and we only ship grids with exactly one. title: MarketPane
pitch: Bring your AI agent along to explore financial products and test your screener ideas.
about_excerpt: Bring your AI agent along to explore financial products and test your screener ideas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 This is our design goal for a grid and widget based editable UX Inspiration MarketPane, is an AI assisted research workbench for doing stock price analysis. Our goal is to build a tool that removes the barriers between an AI and the research canvas, so that a user can spend more time developing their hypothesis, and less time copying charts data back and forth. By putting the tools directly into the hands of an AI, we are basically shortening the iteration loop, allowing you to get to your goal faster. What it does MarketPane is a WebMCP-powered stock screener and research workbench shared between a human and an agent. Either one can define a screener over a universe of instruments (asset class, exchanges, sectors), build a filter tree of typed conditions, set a ranking, and run it to get a pinned, stable set of results. Results land in a panel grid: a results table the agent or the human can inspect, and — via drag-and-drop or a tool call — individual rows become live price charts on the same canvas. Every panel, chart, and result the agent creates is visible and rearrangeable by the human in real time, and vice versa. How we built it The frontend is SvelteKit 5 (SPA) with a browser-side panel/grid system and a workspace document that both the UI and the WebMCP tool layer read and write. WebMCP tools ( define_screener , run_screener , get_screener_results , create_panel , resolve_ticker , search_catalog , get_canvas_state ) operate on that same document, so an agent's actions show up as first-class panel changes instead of hidden side effects. The backend is a FastAPI service (Python, pandas) that evaluates screeners against an OHLCV panel of real market data (EODHD-sourced, object-store backed) and exposes a stateless /api/screener/run endpoint. A typed catalog of fields, operators, and universes keeps every filter condition validated rather than arbitrary code — the agent composes screeners out of known building blocks, it doesn't write expressions the backend has to trust blindly. Challenges we ran into There was a series of challenges that we ran into along the way. Firstly, we ran out of coffee half way through development and had to make an emergency trip to Costco. There were also a number of WebMCP specific challenges that we resolved: The browser was not aware of any WebMCP tools being available and kept trying to use UI elements. The agent has to query a document schema to know that the tools exist, and if it does not suspect them to be there it does not do this. We had to add specific UI elements to notify the agent. The browser did not support the number of tools that we initially created, and blocked them entirely. We had to minimize our implementation. It was very difficult to debug issues with the tools, especially in prod where we don't have all the BE logs handy. This is because issues are not just "bugs" in the app code, but problems with the sequence of actions that the agents take over time. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got a late start on the hackathon and had to build everything very quickly. Our AI enabled development platform has allowed us to achieve the capacity necessary to deliver a POC in time. We managed to add some not-so-simple features, and will continue to expand the feature palette. What we learned Building agentic tools is more than just developing the right workflow and backend scalability. It is also very much about giving the agent the proper awareness and context for the tools that you build. Without clean, self-explainable interfaces, agents will spend extra tokens going on detours or producing errors. What's next for MarketPane Next, we want to widen the live tool surface back toward the fuller design we already built and tested: similarity search ("find setups like this one"), chart annotation and capture, computed fields and custom studies, watchlists, alerts, and backtesting are all implemented behind feature flags today and just need to be wired back into the live composition root. We also want richer chart controls (timeframes, overlays, multi-ticker comparison) and stronger measurement tools so a user can move from spotting a pattern to testing it across cohorts, outcomes, and market regimes. title: Ensemble
pitch: Your look does not come from one store. Ensemble composes a purchasable outfit across Shopify stores through the tools the stores themselves publish: try it on your photo, mix catalogs, and checkout
about_excerpt: Your look does not come from one store. Ensemble composes a purchasable outfit across Shopify stores through the tools the stores themselves publish: try it on your photo, mix catalogs, and checkout Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Shopify storefronts already register native WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . It is on by default on Liquid storefronts, no store opt-in: catalog search, product lookup, and cart updates, published by the page itself as a contract any agent may use. The contract is live. The agent side is what has been missing. Meanwhile the actual shopping problem has not moved. An outfit rarely comes from one store. Putting one together means tabs, screenshots, and re-finding everything at checkout, and the try-on tools that exist paste a product image onto a photo without knowing what the item is, what it costs, or whether your size is in stock. Ensemble puts the two together. Shopping across stores is the shape WebMCP was made for: the page itself declares what an agent may do here, search this catalog, add this variant, and the agent composes those grants across origins into one task. No scraping, no guessing at themes, just the surface the store maintains for itself. What it does Ensemble is a Chrome extension. Browse any Shopify store and its catalog loads into a side panel automatically; every store you visit becomes a chip, and one look spans all of them with a running total. Hover a product tile on the store's own grid and two buttons appear: Render on me shows that item on your photo without leaving the page, and Suggest matches proposes pieces from the store's live inventory that complete the outfit. On a product page, a compact pill offers the same controls and picks up the exact variant you selected, so US 2 on the page is US 2 in the cart. When the look is right, one click fills every store's cart with exactly those variants. Checkout stays native per store: Ensemble fills the carts, you finish each one in the store's own checkout, where trust and payment already live. Every item in a look is a specific, in-stock variant with a live price. A look in Ensemble is purchasable, not a moodboard. The division of labor is the point. The person makes the taste decisions: which jeans, which size, whether the jacket earns its place. The agent does the cross-store bookkeeping: searching the catalogs you have browsed, resolving each choice to an in-stock variant with a real price, filling carts on multiple origins in one action. And the storefront draws the boundary, because its registered tools define exactly what the agent may touch. None of that was reliably possible when acting on a store meant scraping its theme. How we built it The WebMCP layer is a MAIN-world content script injected at document_start . When the browser exposes the WebMCP API (Chrome with the WebMCP feature enabled), it wraps modelContext.registerTool and captures every tool object the storefront registers. On stock Chrome, where no native API exists yet, it plants a minimal modelContext shim first; Shopify's storefront script feature-detects it and registers its ten native tools into the shim unchanged. Either way the extension ends up holding the store's own tool objects and serves listTools and callTool to the extension's isolated world over a postMessage bridge. Product lookups and cart adds go through the store's registered tools first: get_product for variant data, update_cart with variant GIDs (Shopify's global IDs), get_cart to confirm what actually landed. Storefronts that register nothing fall back to the public /products.json and /cart/add.js endpoints, so the same flows work everywhere and the supported surface is preferred wherever it exists. The overlay UI lives in an open shadow root so store CSS cannot touch it, and finds product cards by climbing from the hover target to the smallest container holding exactly one product handle, which survives themes that cover their tiles with overlay layers. Try-on renders and style suggestions run on Gemini with the user's own key. There is no server: the photo and the key stay in local extension storage. Challenges we ran into The tool-call contract has sharp edges the examples do not show. executeTool at the API boundary takes a JSON string and rejects a tool name in place of the registered tool object, but a captured tool's execute callback takes parsed arguments, because the native layer parses before invoking. Passing the wrong shape does not error loudly; Shopify answers with a polite "No line_items provided" and your cart stays empty. We also learned that update_cart 's top-level id addresses existing cart lines only; adds must nest the variant GID under item . On a product page, the store's own get_product returns only the currently selected variant, a single-element array. To honor the size a shopper picked we resolve variants catalog-first and match requested IDs in both GID and numeric forms, verified live by watching a stored look flip from the default US 0 to the selected US 2. Repeat adds taught us that Shopify dedupes them, returning updated: false with no item count, so cart confirmation falls back to get_cart rather than trusting the add response. And real storefront themes fight overlays: one of the live demo storefronts covers its product tiles with layers that swallow hover targets, which is what forced the container-climbing card detection. Accomplishments we are proud of The full loop runs against live storefronts: catalog in, look built, render on the shopper's photo, and both stores' carts filled with the exact variants, a dress from one catalog and wool runners from another under one total. The native tool path works on stock Chrome today through the shim capture, so the WebMCP story does not wait for a browser flag. And variant fidelity is proven end to end, the size picked on the page to the line in the cart. What we learned WebMCP's design carries real weight in practice: because the page defines the tools, an agent can act on a store it has never seen without guessing at DOM structure, and the same contract that serves a chat agent serves a product UI like ours. The gap between a demo and a product is exactly the sharp edges above, and the supported surface made them tractable to debug. What's next Tighter checkout is the obvious V2, exploring how far per-store checkout can collapse toward one action. Beyond that, the look itself wants to become a page: a shareable board that registers its own WebMCP tools, so your agent can discuss, edit, and price a look you were sent. At that point Ensemble both consumes the open web's tools and contributes surface back to it. Try it Open https://ensemble-dhf.pages.dev and download ensemble.zip (or clone github.com/sneg55/ensemble). chrome://extensions, Developer mode, Load unpacked, pick the folder. Paste a free Gemini API key in the extension options (aistudio.google.com/apikey). Visit any Shopify store, click the toolbar icon or just hover a product tile. Optional, for the native API path: run Chrome with --enable-features=WebMCP. Without the flag the shim capture keeps every feature working. title: Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap
pitch: Human and an AI agent can draw on the same mind map at the same time — no copy-pasting, no separate windows. It's built on WebMCP, so the agent uses real page tools instead of faking clicks.
about_excerpt: Human and an AI agent can draw on the same mind map at the same time — no copy-pasting, no separate windows. It's built on WebMCP, so the agent uses real page tools instead of faking clicks. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Vertical Structure of Architecture Diagram Export (JSON, SVG, MARKDOWN, PNG, JPEG, PDF) Export as PNG Agent has completed colouring the components via script Import (JSON, SVG, Markdown) Agent has completed the import and drafted on the canvas via script Select all tool Vetical Architecture using the straight line connector Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap Inspiration Every AI tool I'd used fell into one of two buckets: either the agent takes over completely and you just watch it work (and hope it doesn't do something you didn't want), or it's a chatbot bolted onto the side of an app, completely disconnected from what's actually on screen — you describe what you want in a text box, and the app has no idea an agent is even involved. Neither felt right for something as personal as a mind map. A mind map is your thinking laid out — I didn't want an agent replacing that, I wanted one that could sit down next to me and actually draw on the same page. When I found WebMCP — a way for a web page to expose its own real functions as tools an agent can call directly, in the browser, no backend required — that was the whole idea in one API. So I built the thing I actually wanted: one canvas, one undo history, a human and an agent both reaching for the same nodes. What it does Canvas Co-Pilot is a mind-mapping canvas that a person and an AI agent can edit at the same time , live, in the same browser tab. Add nodes, branch out ideas, drag things around, color-code by hand — and an agent can do all of that too, through 20 real tools registered via document.modelContext (add a branch, restyle a node, connect two ideas, reorganize the whole layout, export to SVG/PNG/Markdown/Mermaid, import any of those back in). Every change either of us makes lands in one shared undo history, so nothing an agent does is ever outside a person's ability to take back. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no framework, on purpose, so the whole render/state pipeline stays easy to reason about. Dagre handles auto-layout, the canvas itself is hand-rolled SVG with full round-trip fidelity (export a diagram, re-import it, get back exactly what you started with, including every color and shape override). For WebMCP itself, the app checks for native document.modelContext support first and only falls back to the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill when it's not there — the header badge tells you honestly which mode you're in, native or polyfilled, rather than pretending it's always native. It's deployed on both Netlify and Vercel. Challenges we ran into Most of the real work wasn't the happy path — it was the bugs that only show up once you actually try to break the thing. A user pasted a Mermaid-style edge list ( root --> human ) into Import, and it silently created 39 broken, half-named nodes instead of failing loudly. The importer's "is this quick-outline shorthand" check was matching on any > character — which also matches an arrow. Fixed with a negative-lookbehind regex that tells an arrow apart from actual shorthand syntax, and now a bad paste tells you it didn't understand instead of quietly corrupting your canvas. "Select all connectors" would silently reset back to nothing the moment you clicked anywhere on the empty canvas — even just panning to look at something. If every connector already had its own color (which they do once you've styled a diagram), the next color change would then land on the invisible graph-wide default instead, and visibly do nothing at all . Took real reproduction work to catch, since it only shows up with an incidental click in between two actions that each look correct on their own. I tried making multiple connectors landing on the same node spread out instead of converging on one point — and it technically worked, with proper diamond/ellipse-aware geometry and everything. But it just looked wrong. "Multiple octopus hands" was the exact feedback, and it was right — I reverted the whole thing. Good reminder that a fix being technically correct doesn't mean it's the right call. Two of the 20 tools had names close enough to trip up an agent, not a human: combine_nodes and connect_nodes sound almost identical but do very different things (one creates a brand-new node, the other just links two that already exist). Caught it by checking the tool descriptions against Chrome's own published guidance for testing WebMCP tools — and fixed it with one clarifying sentence in each description. Accomplishments that we're proud of Getting a second AI vendor to prove the point without any custom integration work: I handed ChatGPT nothing but the live tool schema and a canvas snapshot, and it wrote genuinely correct document.modelContext calling code — right API shape, right pattern — with only two small gaps (a missing await , a guessed return shape) that came from never having seen a live response, not from misunderstanding the standard. That's the whole promise of WebMCP working, not just Claude working. I'm also proud of how much of this session was bug-hunting rather than feature-building. Reproducing the connector-selection bug took building the exact failure chain step by step before I even knew what was wrong — not just patching the first thing that looked broken. What we learned The most validating thing I found wasn't something I built — it was rereading WebMCP's own spec and seeing my own instincts already written into its stated goals: "enable human-in-the-loop workflows," explicitly not "fully autonomous agents operating without human oversight." I hadn't copied that language, I'd just built toward the same idea independently, which is a nice signal I was pointed the right way from the start. I also learned that small stuff in a tool's description matters far more than it looks like it should. Two similar-sounding tool names, or three tools that could all plausibly answer "make it red" — those are exactly the kind of ambiguity that trips up a model even when every individual tool works perfectly in isolation. What's next for Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap Native support: Chrome 149 and Edge 150 both have live Origin Trials for real (non-polyfilled) document.modelContext — worth registering for so the badge can honestly say "Native" for more visitors, not just the polyfill. Dynamic tools: right now all 20 tools are registered once at load. The spec supports tools that appear only when relevant (e.g. a delete_node tool that only shows up once something's actually selected) — that's a more honest surface for an agent to reason about than one static list. Multiplayer: right now it's one human, one agent. Extending the same shared-state model to multiple people on the same canvas is the natural next step.
