This was my first real project working with WebMCP specifically, and figuring out how an agent actually behaves against real tool descriptions (not just what looks right on paper) took a lot of live testing and bug-hunting I didn't expect going in. Debugging issues that only showed up when an agent used the tools a certain way was the most intimidating part, but also where I learned the most. sathiya prasad A Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates sathiya prasad A started this project — Sep 04, 2026 04:36 AM EDT

title: ShrineKeep + WebMCP
pitch: A versatile collection manager for devoted collectors and hobbyists from any space, now with agent-automated onboarding and monetary analytics, making reasoned decisions even for niches.
about_excerpt: A versatile collection manager for devoted collectors and hobbyists from any space, now with agent-automated onboarding and monetary analytics, making reasoned decisions even for niches. Like Comment Story Updates Agent asked to set up data for a collection of the user's choice All edits are staged and require approval Staged edits that are not yet accepted are put in the review inbox Example output Activity of each tool use is recorded for technical users to debug Tool descriptions are also provided so technical users can be more productive and write more complex prompts Agent making decisions gives effective and reasonable automation of item valuation ShrineKeep + WebMCP project story Inspiration Collectors can end up hoarding rather than collecting, leaving them with questions. What do I already own? How much have I spent? What is all of this worth now? A lot of people have to manually make use of notes or spreadsheets, if they track them at all. That is the problem I made ShrineKeep to solve. It can organize collections in nested boxes and give you useful analytics, but there was an awkward catch: first, you had to manually add everything. Names, dates, purchase prices, current values, wishlist prices, and so on. The more useful I made the app, the more data it asked the user to enter. I've wanted to use agents for this for a while. An agent can research a niche product line, tell similar editions apart, find price references, and do in minutes what would be a very boring evening of data entry. But running those agents for every user would be expensive. Locking the feature behind a subscription would solve my problem by creating a new one for users. WebMCP and it solved my problems well! The user can bring an agent they already have, and ShrineKeep can give it the right context and a safe way to help. The agent does the research and reasoning; ShrineKeep knows what box is open, what the user owns, and what is actually allowed to change. I don't have to run an AI service or pass that cost on to the user. What it does On the dashboard or wishlist, a user can now talk to a compatible browser agent and ask it to work with the collection that is already in front of them. It can: research and initialize a new collection box; compare a complete set with the current box and stage only the missing items; estimate current values or likely acquisition prices for owned items; research expected prices for wishlist items; edit item names and descriptions through the same review flow; work only with the items explicitly selected in the interface; and optionally find a thumbnail for each newly approved item. The agent gets small, structured pieces of context instead of trying to scrape the screen. It can read the open box, include its child boxes when that is actually needed, look at the relevant wishlist, or ask for only the cards the user selected. There are seven tools on the dashboard and three on the wishlist page, each limited to what makes sense there. Tools are written in accordance to Chrome's WebMCP Best Practices The important part is that none of those tools silently changes the collection. Anything the agent wants to add or edit goes into a staging inbox. ShrineKeep shows the user the proposed names, prices, Owned/Wishlist choices, before-and-after values, reasons, sources, and possible duplicates. Every row can be edited, unchecked, approved, or thrown away. Only approved rows reach the real write APIs. I also built a new tutorial around these agent features. WebMCP will undoubtedly be unfamilar to most users, and I feel it is an essential UX requirement to introduce users to a newly adopted technology. It asks what the user collects, gives them a prompt to take to their agent, and walks them through confirming the researched set, reviewing the new cards, opening the created box, and trying a valuation. They learn the app by setting up something they already collect. They can skip individual steps, leave the tutorial, or use sample data instead. If WebMCP isn't available, ShrineKeep still works normally. How we built it ShrineKeep is built with Next.js 16, React, and TypeScript, with Supabase handling authentication, Postgres, row-level security, and image storage. The collection manager existed before the hackathon. During the submission period, I added the WebMCP tools, their staging and approval flow, and the new agent-based tutorial directly to the existing app. A reusable React hook checks for document.modelContext and registers the right tools for the page the user is on. Registrations are cleaned up with an AbortController when that scope changes. The same hook records calls as they happen, which let me show a status panel without pretending that “the browser accepted a registration” means “an agent is connected and understands everything.” The read tools use small authenticated routes that check ownership and return only the fields needed for the job, with pagination so a large collection doesn't become one giant prompt. Selection is even smaller: get_selected_items reads the current React selection state directly. I generalized the edit tools to accept just the fields being changed, so the same operation can fix a name, update a description, or suggest prices without a separate tool for each field. Shared tool copy lives in one module so those contracts stay consistent. Tools that can lead to a write only build typed suggestion batches. A shared client-side provider keeps those batches around while the user moves between the dashboard and wishlist. When the user finally applies one, the server authenticates them again, checks ownership and price fields, catches stale records through updated_at , and then reuses ShrineKeep's normal item and box operations. That also means value updates still appear in the existing value history. Optional thumbnail lookup reuses the regular image search and is allowed to fail without blocking the batch. The tutorial runs as a state machine inside the existing agent panel. It listens for the relevant tool calls, successful approvals, and box navigation. Tutorial progress is saved for the session, while completion or dismissal is saved to the account. The state also needs to handle someone skipping creation, opening a different box, or coming back after navigating away. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was deciding where the agent should stop. Niche product research is messy, and secondhand prices are even messier. I wanted the agent to save real time without letting a confident mistake rewrite someone's collection. The model I kept coming back to was a code review: let the agent prepare a useful diff, then let the person who owns the data decide what lands. The tutorial became a major challenge of its own. Exposing the tools didn't explain to a new user what to ask for, or why they were moving between an agent chat and ShrineKeep. I had to build a walkthrough that taught both sides of that interaction while helping them make a real collection. There also had to be a useful way through for someone without a compatible agent, or someone who just wanted to skip ahead. Another early mistake was treating “set up this collection” and “complete the collection in this box” as the same operation. They sound close, but one should create a new box and the other should reconcile against what is already there. Using the first flow for both produced duplicate cards and unnecessary child boxes. I split them into separate tools, and the completion flow now checks both owned and wishlist cards before proposing only what is missing. Choosing how many tools to expose was another balancing act. I didn't want a separate tool for every small task, with more schemas and descriptions for the agent to read. But making one tool do everything would bring back the scope confusion. I kept separate operations where the destination or approval flow really differs, and generalized edits within those boundaries. Furthermore, I directly acknowledge that destructive, relocation, and exploration actions should not be accessible to the agent, as these can destroy data, confuse users, and waste tokens, respectively. It was not worth it to implement this when users already have fast batch deletions and movement options. Pricing caused a different kind of ambiguity. Original retail, a current listing, a secondhand asking price, and a recent sold price are all valid approaches to price an item. I experimented with defaults, but collections from different spaces just aren't compatible with it and often lead to lots of time and tokens wasted looking at obviously wrong decisions. I ended up with just asking the agent to suggest a research approach for each requested field, wait for user approval on all of them, then research. The review still keeps the explanation and links next to the number. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this became a complete bring-your-own-agent loop rather than a chat demo. title: TREMOR — Agentic Blast Radius Cockpit (WebMCP)
pitch: See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does.
about_excerpt:
See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 TREMOR: Agentic Blast Radius & Regression Prevention Cockpit 

 
 See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does. 

 An interactive, browser-native blast-radius cockpit and trust layer built on the official W3C WebMCP standard ( @mcp-b/global ). 

 Live Cockpit: https://tremor-cockpit.vercel.app 
 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ABHIGH15/TREMOR 
 (Note: TREMOR is an independent project built for the WebMCP Challenge 2026 and is not affiliated with the @tremor/react UI library or tremor-runtime.) 
 

 

 1. Inspiration: The Emergence of "AI-CFR" 

 In 2026, engineering organizations are formally tracking "AI-Specific Change Failure Rate" (AI-CFR) as a core engineering KPI. While autonomous coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) generate pull requests four times faster, they operate under a fundamental limitation: Architectural Myopia . 

 When an agent refactors an isolated file (such as auth-service/session.ts ), it reads 200 lines of local code, completely blind to the downstream microservices that depend on that token schema. A two-line cache TTL refactor passes local unit tests, but under peak production traffic triggers a catastrophic Redis cache stampede that knocks out the checkout pipeline. 

 TREMOR was built to solve this problem: forcing autonomous coding agents to simulate systemic blast radius, review regression history, and obtain human sign-off inside an interactive cockpit before any change reaches production. 

 

 2. Why WebMCP? (And Why Backend MCP Cannot Solve This) 

 Multiple backend MCP servers exist to analyze codebase dependencies (e.g., code-impact-mcp , code-review-graph , Port.io ). However, every existing implementation suffers from the same architectural limitation: they run silently inside a terminal CLI, returning raw text back to an LLM. 

 To a supervising staff engineer, terminal text provides zero real-time situational awareness, no shared visual truth, and no enforceable guardrails. 

 WebMCP transforms this paradigm: 

 
 Zero-Install, In-Browser Runtime: Tools are registered directly onto document.modelContext via the official @mcp-b/global standard polyfill. There are no local sockets, daemons, or machine configurations required. 
 Shared Visual Reality: When an agent queries simulate_change_impact , the browser's 2D canvas dynamically illuminates the blast zone at 60 frames per second. Both the human engineer and the AI agent look at the exact same live visual impact graph in the same tab. 
 Enforceable Browser Gates: High-risk operations are locked behind real UI event handlers that the agent cannot programmatically bypass. 
 Ecosystem Extensibility: Platforms like Vercel or Netlify could expose their own deploy-preview dependency graphs through WebMCP built this way, catching systemic breaks before code even reaches staging. 
 

 
 "Backend MCP tools already hand agents blast-radius data as text in a terminal. TREMOR is browser-native — a human and their agent look at the same live impact graph in the same tab, and nothing risky ships without a human clicking Confirm." 
 

 

 3. The Dual-Engine Architecture 

 TREMOR ships with a dual-engine architecture designed for both deep enterprise scenario modeling and arbitrary real-world codebase ingestion: 

 Mode 1: Enterprise Demo Scenario (Default) 

 A curated 18-microservice topology featuring the complex auth-service to redis-session-cluster P1 outage scenario, flaky test suites, dynamic tool lifecycle unregistration, and a human confirmation gate with counterfactual replay. 

 Mode 2: Live GitHub Repository Ingestion 

 Allows an evaluator or engineer to input any public GitHub repository (e.g., ABHIGH15/TREMOR ). 

 
 Fetches the repository file tree in a single API call. 
 Retrieves source code via CDN with zero GitHub REST API rate-limit cost. 
 Client-side regex extracts genuine import ... from and require(...) statements to construct real file-to-file dependency edges. 
 Dynamically computes in-degree graph centrality risk scores (e.g., identifying src/types/dataset.ts as highest-risk at 0.95 with 12 dependents). 
 Dynamically re-binds WebMCP tools so connected AI agents immediately inspect the live repository topology. 
 

 

 4. The 6-Tool Canonical WebMCP Suite 

 TREMOR registers six standardized tools directly on document.modelContext : 

 
 get_system_snapshot : Returns full topology snapshot (18 nodes, 28 edges), top risk bottlenecks ( auth-service 0.88 , jwt-security-core 0.82 ), incident index, and test suite health summary. 
 get_blast_radius : Multi-root transitive BFS graph traversal mapping downstream callers and flaky tests. 
 check_regression_history : Incident pattern matcher surfacing past outage root causes and post-mortem precedents. 
 get_change_provenance : Live GitHub API commit telemetry combined with AI vs. Human authorship auditing. 
 simulate_change_impact : Centerpiece simulator computing composite predicted risk (0.0 to 1.0) and driving real-time canvas particle acceleration. 
 flag_for_review : Non-self-approving Trust Layer gate generating pending review cards in the UI. 
 

 

 5. The Trust Layer: Why AI Cannot Self-Approve 

 When an agent simulates a change resulting in Critical Risk (score ≥ 0.70): 

 
 Dynamic Tool Lifecycle: The runtime dynamically unregisters simulate_change_impact via AbortController , dropping active tools from 6 to 5. The agent's simulation capability is revoked. 
 Non-Self-Approving Gate: flag_for_review sets can_tool_self_approve: false . The agent has no programmatic tool to approve its own flag. 
 Human Sign-Off: An authorized engineer inspects the risk justification in the cockpit and clicks Confirm / Approve . 
 Counterfactual Replay: The human approval restores tools back to 6, permanent audit logs are written, and an animated banner replays the exact historical outage that the human review just averted. 
 

 

 6. Live Native ChatGPT Verification 

 Verified live inside the official native ChatGPT desktop and mobile applications: 

 
 ChatGPT connected to https://tremor-cockpit.vercel.app via its in-app browser. 
 Discovered all six WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . 
 Autonomously analyzed src/types/dataset.ts in our open-source repository, accurately identifying the 0.95 Risk Score, 0.72 Critical Composite Blast Risk, and the exact 11 downstream dependent files. 
 

 

 7. Implementation & Technology Stack 

 
 WebMCP Standard: Built on official @mcp-b/global@5.1.0 polyfill by Alex Nahas (W3C contributor). 
 Frontend & Physics: React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and react-force-graph-2d for 60fps HTML5 canvas physics. 
 Accessibility: Fully compliant with WCAG 2.1 AA standards (high-contrast focus rings, keyboard shortcuts: H for Hero, S for Simulate, R for Reset, ? for Help). 
 Deployment: Vercel Global Edge CDN with zero backend server dependencies. 
 

 

 8. Challenges We Faced & Solutions 

 
 Strict Read-Only Properties in ChatGPT Host Context: In ChatGPT's native in-app browser, document.modelContext is defined with writable: false . Direct property assignments threw runtime TypeErrors . We resolved this by keeping all tool registrations strictly compliant with W3C registerTool({...}) protocols. 
 Multi-Root Transitive BFS Traversal: Simulating changes touching multiple services simultaneously required deduplicating cyclic dependencies and aggregating risk metrics without blocking the 60fps canvas thread. Built an asynchronous BFS graph engine in TypeScript that computes downstream reach in sub-millisecond time. 
 

 

 9. Known Limitations & Roadmap 

 
 Static Analysis Depth: Current live repository ingestion uses client-side regex-based import extraction for zero-install execution. The roadmap includes compiling Tree-sitter to WebAssembly in the browser thread for compiler-grade AST parsing. 
 Runtime Telemetry: Dependency maps currently reflect static source code imports; integrating OpenTelemetry distributed trace spans will enable weighting edges by real-time production RPC traffic volume. 
 GitHub PR Webhook Integration: Automatically triggering TREMOR blast simulations on incoming agent-created pull requests.

title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: PaperSpace
pitch: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI tools treat a research paper as a file to summarize or a block of text to retrieve from. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What becomes possible when a person and an agent share a paper's text and its spatial reading environment inside the browser? Reading a paper is rarely linear. A reader moves between related work, methods, equations, figures, experiments, and appendices while building a mental map of where each idea lives. Conventional PDF viewers collapse that map into one page at a time. Chat interfaces collapse it even further into excerpts detached from their visual source. PaperSpace preserves that spatial memory. Every page of every imported PDF is unfolded onto a borderless two-dimensional desk. Pages remain live, selectable PDF surfaces, but they can also be moved, grouped, searched, compared, and revisited as part of a persistent visual workspace. The browser is essential to this interaction. It owns the PDFs the person explicitly selected, the rendered pages, the local text index, the page geometry, the current camera, and the workspace the person is looking at. WebMCP gives an agent direct access to that authorized, browser-local state, keeping the person and the agent aligned on one live workspace. We built PaperSpace for the WebMCP Challenge as a focused, open-source, single-person tool centered on reading, understanding, and presenting research papers. PaperSpace is a shared spatial instrument where the person controls the source material and the agent helps organize attention inside the same visible world. What it does PaperSpace is a local-first spatial desk for research papers. When a person imports a PDF, PaperSpace unfolds every page from left to right and top to bottom using each page's real aspect ratio. Every page becomes an independently movable and resizable live sheet with selectable text. The complete paper stays visible as a spatial place with its reading order intact. PaperSpace extracts text and normalized page geometry locally with PDF.js. Each page becomes searchable as soon as its index is ready. A reusable inspect_workspace briefing reports exact coverage and compact sampled page excerpts, so an agent can prepare once and then read the broadest useful contiguous range in one call, including the whole paper when full context matters. Through WebMCP, the agent can search the available corpus, batch-read paper text, locate an exact passage, and guide the shared camera to that region. The camera first pulls back to establish spatial context, travels across the desk, and then lands with the source itself centered in a calm view with generous breathing room. The app exposes nine WebMCP tools: inspect_workspace returns reusable readiness, compact paper briefs, every page's world geometry, visual artifacts, sequences, and camera state. search_papers progressively searches indexed pages and returns page-level matches with normalized source regions plus exact coverage. read_paper_pages reads one contiguous range or a whole indexed paper in one call, with optional block geometry and an explicit caller-selected character cap. focus_region guides the camera to a search match or an explicit PDF region. arrange_papers reflows pages into reading-order grids and arranges complete paper groups. snapshot_paper_region places a source-linked raster crop from an exact PDF region. place_plot creates a safe declarative line plot from finite numeric data. place_image validates and places PNG, JPEG, and WebP visuals. present_sequence creates a captioned sequence of semantic paper regions and visual artifacts. PaperSpace also gives the agent an explicit delivery contract. When PaperSpace is available, substantive introductions, explanations, reviews, comparisons, and answers grounded across multiple paper regions are delivered through present_sequence . Chat provides concise supporting context, while a single grounded passage can use focus_region and simple localized Q&A remains lightweight. The sequence interaction is the heart of the product. Suppose one experiment is explained across related work, methods, and results on three distant pages. The agent can build a three-frame sequence with a caption for each view. When presentation begins, PaperSpace temporarily draws those original pages together beside their paper in first-appearance order. Quiet numbered source slots preserve the paper's topology throughout the presentation. The same original page can support several region frames through one staged page. Visual artifacts stay in their existing world positions. Exiting the sequence restores every moved page—including its position, size, and layer—and returns the camera to its exact entry state. Keeping a sequence saves its semantic frames; replaying it organizes pages again from their current positions and restores them again afterward. This enables requests such as: “Find where this experiment is motivated, defined, and evaluated, then organize those pages for me.” “Focus on the ablation equation and keep the surrounding paragraph in view.” “Read the method and results, plot the reported trend, and place it beside the source page.” “Present the three views in sequence and explain what changes between them.” Everything happens on the same desk the person can inspect and manipulate. Agent actions produce visible feedback, and temporary organization is transactionally isolated from the person's saved layout. Spatial mutation tools perform an atomic visual preflight inside the app. Standard calls place plots, images, source crops, and arrangements in clear areas. An agent can use force: true for an intentional dense layout, while media, schema, source-target, and security validation remain active. How we built it PaperSpace is a pure frontend SvelteKit and TypeScript application compiled as a static site for Cloudflare Pages. Browser storage and browser-authorized files provide the complete runtime state. The application is organized around four client-side layers: Svelte components render the infinite desk, unfolded PDF sheets, artifacts, search interface, frame editor, and presentation chrome. A single reactive workspace model owns paper metadata, per-page geometry, the camera, artifacts, semantic sequences, and all person- and agent-triggered state transitions. PDF.js renders pages and extracts text plus normalized block geometry in a same-origin Web Worker. IndexedDB stores validated workspace metadata, browser-authorized PDF copies, raster images, and saved semantic frames. The workspace schema stores a stable paper identity and page number for every PDF page, while position, size, and layer remain mutable world properties. PDF inspection records each page's true dimensions. A deterministic row-major layout uses a bounded column count to keep long papers spatially legible, and complete paper bounds are used to prevent different imports from overlapping. Every page has a DOM sheet so its identity remains stable in the world. PaperSpace activates detailed PDF canvas and text rendering near the viewport and above a useful zoom threshold, keeping long unfolded papers responsive. PDF rasterization uses a two-tier residency system. Every successfully rendered page retains a 288-pixel-wide aspect-preserving preview, while an LRU applies a 48-million-pixel budget to unpinned high-resolution page canvases. Pages in the strict viewport, the current focus target, and the active sequence frame are pinned and may temporarily exceed that budget. A compact preview preserves visual continuity as high-resolution canvases move through the working set. Raster canvases and selectable text layers have independent lifecycles, and a double-canvas pipeline swaps each completed bitmap into view atomically. Region targeting uses top-left normalized coordinates. The same semantic region can therefore be mapped through a page's current world geometry after the page has been moved or resized. Camera motion is handled by a cancellable controller with pull-back, travel, and landing keyframes, smooth center interpolation, logarithmic zoom interpolation, distance-aware timing, responsive caption-safe insets, and an immediate path for prefers-reduced-motion . Presentation staging is transactional. PaperSpace validates every frame before changing state, deduplicates source pages by first appearance, snapshots their exact geometry and the entry camera, stages the original pages, and exposes their source slots. Presentation mode pauses page manipulation, while persistence serializes the source geometry and entry camera to keep the durable desk unchanged. WebMCP is registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP adapter is intentionally thin: every tool calls the same workspace
video_transcript_excerpt: This is PaperSpace, a browser-native research workspace that exposes its live reading desk to AI agents through WebMCP. The paper is our test. Can an agent turn one request into visible, grounded interaction? The user asks Codex, "Introduce this paper using PaperSpace." PaperSpace is open beside the conversation in the built-in browser. WebMCP lets that page expose its own capabilities to the agent. So, the answer appears as visible interaction on the shared desk with chat providing concise guidance. When the page opens, Codex discovers the tools declared by the site. It calls inspect workspace once for a compact desk briefing, reads the index paper in one broad request, then calls present sequence with semantic page regions and captions. The browser-local workspace connects the agent directly to the active reading context. PaperSpace keeps every PDF page live on a borderless two-dimensional desk. Page identity and order remain visible while positions can change. Browser authorization keeps the PDF, extracted text, layout, and saved sequences together in local workspace storage. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Here, Codex moves from the paper's motivation to its method, to the evidence with every explanation anchored to the original pages. If the user asks about a precise figure or equation, focus region targets normalized coordinates on the live page. The camera pulls back, travels across the desk, and lands with the requested region centered in a readable view. The person can redirect the motion at any time. Every command participates in one shared reversible state. The person sees each change in the browser, can move pages or stop a flight, and can keep or exit a sequence. On exit, Paper space restores the exact page geometry and the previous camera. That is the Web MCP loop. Codex understands the request, the browser exposes the tools, and Paper space becomes the shared interface. It is a pure SvelteKit front end, persisted in IndexDB, and deployable to Cloudflare Pages. The browser itself is the integration layer.

title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: Mini Paint WebMCP Extension
pitch: A real image editor where you and ChatGPT edit the same document. The agent sees the edits you just made by hand; you undo its edits with Ctrl+Z. One shared undo stack, 27 WebMCP tools, no backend.
about_excerpt: A real image editor where you and ChatGPT edit the same document. The agent sees the edits you just made by hand; you undo its edits with Ctrl+Z. One shared undo stack, 27 WebMCP tools, no backend. Like Comment Story Updates Create a Black Friday Banner Inspiration Most AI integrations hand the agent a copy of your document and give you a result back. You are not editing together, you are taking turns. And undo belongs to whoever touched it last. I wanted the opposite. One document, two editors. A real image editor where the person and the agent work on the same canvas, each can see what the other just did, and the same Ctrl+Z undoes either of them. That only works if the page itself says what it can do, which is what WebMCP is for. What it does Mini Paint WebMCP is a browser image editor with 27 WebMCP tools registered, so ChatGPT can drive it directly. It is build ontop the famous https://viliusle.github.io/miniPaint/ project. Four of them read: the document, the layers, the selection, and an export. Seven work on layers, covering text, moving, resizing, duplicating, deleting, selecting and opacity. Three change the document itself through canvas resize, crop and rotation. Three are adjustments for brightness, contrast and saturation. One sits a level higher: create_social_variant reshapes the document into an Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X or YouTube format and carries the existing layout across. Then undo and redo, which work on the same history a human uses. The sequence that shows the point is short. You drop in a photo and drag it where you want it. ChatGPT inspects the document and tells you what you just did. Ask for a square Instagram version and the canvas reshapes with your layout scaled into it. Ask for a headline, then nudge it by hand into a better spot. Ask for a portrait version and the agent starts from your position, not the one it picked earlier. Press Ctrl+Z and its variant disappears in a single step. How we built it Adobe App Builder hosts the whole thing as a static SPA on Adobe's CDN. Nothing in the agent path touches a server. Every tool runs in the browser. Deploys are headless from credentials in .env, so they never depend on somebody being logged in. miniPaint 4.14.3, MIT licensed, is the editor, vendored as its prebuilt bundle. The layering matters more than it looks: ChatGPT -> document.modelContext -> WebMcpAdapter -> ToolRegistry | EditorCommands | miniPaint Every transport goes through the same ToolRegistry.invoke(). WebMCP, the debug panel inside the app, and the test suite all take that one path. No tool logic is duplicated anywhere, so a tool that passes a test is the same code the agent runs. Challenges we ran into miniPaint cannot be embedded as a library. Its maintainer says so directly in issue 169. The bundle initialises itself on window load, styles the page from body down, and needs its own HTML skeleton, so a same origin iframe is the only supported way in. The catch is that ChatGPT does not discover tools registered inside an iframe. So the tools are registered by the top level page and the handlers reach into the frame. Getting both of those true at once was the central design problem. Then undo. miniPaint never exposes window.app, so its own action classes are unreachable from outside. What rescued it is that State.do_action() does no instanceof check. It only wants an object with action_id, action_description, do(), undo() and free(). So I define command objects in the host page and push them onto miniPaint's real history. No fork, no second history, and a human Ctrl+Z reverses an agent edit because it genuinely is the same stack. The WebMCP API also moved under me while I worked. Chrome 149 and 150 expose navigator.modelContext, 151 and later expose document.modelContext. registerTool returns a promise from 151 but throws synchronously before that. executeTool takes a JSON string in Chromium and an object in the draft IDL. RegisteredTool.inputSchema is a string through Chrome 153 and an object from 154. The adapter handles all of it, and it is the only file in the project that knows WebMCP exists. Three smaller things cost real time. Only ten of miniPaint's effects implement the filter render hooks, and passing any other name to add_filter throws inside the render loop and kills it permanently, so adjustments go through an allowlist. Dynamic text layers get measured during a requestAnimationFrame tick, which a background tab throttles, so an agent could read width: null and have nothing to position against; measurement is forced synchronously now. And on Adobe's CDN the cache header key has to be lowercase cache-control, otherwise it lands in S3 object metadata and never reaches the browser, which cost 30 seconds of load time until I found it. Accomplishments that we're proud of 191 automated tests, and not one of them needs an LLM. 87 unit tests, 104 Playwright tests, and the Playwright suite runs unchanged against localhost and against the deployed Adobe URL. 104 of 104 on both. The assertions check miniPaint's own internal state rather than what a tool claims it did, so a tool that lies still fails. That harness is why I trust the tool layer at all. It caught a spurious REVISION_MISMATCH that would have rejected the agent's own writes, and the throttled measurement bug above, before either reached anyone. documentRevision came out of the same thinking. A write can carry an optional expectedRevision, and if the human edited in between, the write is refused instead of quietly overwriting their work. What we learned Designing tools for an agent is API design, not UI automation. Explicit units, explicit coordinate spaces, additionalProperties set to false so a typo produces a clear error instead of a silently ignored argument, and errors that carry structured detail. LAYER_NOT_FOUND ships the ids that do exist rather than a sentence about it. The shared state idea only survives if you resist building your own history. Give the agent its own undo stack and it stops being one document and becomes two programs arguing over a file. What's next for Mini Paint WebMCP Selection aware tools, so "brighten just the sky" works. A load_image tool so the agent can bring in assets itself. And the orchestration this architecture was built for: applying one layout to six social formats as a single composed operation with a single undo. title: Open Dots
pitch: A pixel-art storybook for families to create, read, and share with an AI co-creator.
about_excerpt: A pixel-art storybook for families to create, read, and share with an AI co-creator. Like Comment Story Updates An editor to create pixel art story book with AI A gallery of pixel art storybooks Open Dots Open Dots is an agent-native pixel-art storybook for children and families. Together, they turn story ideas into illustrated pages with an AI co-creator, then read, revise, and share the artwork. The problem Families want creative screen time that they can do together: a child imagines a character or scene, an adult helps shape the story, and both can see and change the result. But making a picture book takes drawing confidence, time, and specialized tools. Many pixel-art products are either one-off image generators or professional editors. A generated image can be impressive, but it is often a paid, opaque endpoint: it does not teach a child how a scene is built, preserve reusable pieces, or make it easy for a family to revise a character across the next page. Traditional editors expose the craft, but can be intimidating for beginners. People who already have access to an AI client such as ChatGPT need a more approachable middle ground: a shared canvas where they can learn by making, keep creative control, and ask an agent for help without handing the whole story to a black box. The solution Open Dots pairs a tactile pixel-storybook editor with a structured WebMCP surface. A family turns an idea into a sequence of illustrated pages, adds pixel text and shapes, reviews and revises each scene, and reads the finished book page by page. Individual pages can be exported as PNGs to share. The in-browser agent reads the storybook state, creates reusable sprites, paints them in deliberate passes, stamps them into layered scenes, and inspects PNG feedback before the next pass. This is collaborative storymaking, not a prompt-to-image handoff: the family directs the narrative and art direction; the agent performs precise, inspectable canvas work through document.modelContext . How WebMCP is used WebMCP is the product capability, not an add-on. Open Dots treats its 15 tools as an agent-quality harness, not a thin UI automation layer. The agent loads a pixel-art guide, sets a named palette, creates small assets, refines them in outline/fill/shade/highlight passes, compares inline PNG feedback, stamps assets back-to-front, and inspects the composed page. This harness exists because an unconstrained agent is poor at pixel art: it may paint whole pages flatly, make oversized props, skip shading, or continue without looking at what it just made. Open Dots gives it the constraints and feedback that a careful pixel artist uses: reusable small sprites, palette tiers, bulk drawing primitives, inline visual inspection, and scene-quality hints. Mutating asset operations return inline PNG feedback and the required next comparison pass, preventing blind multi-step drawing. Read tools expose the storybook, asset images, and page images; write tools create pages, assets, palettes, pixels, text, and placements. The tools use typed schemas, intent-rich descriptions, structured errors, and read/write annotations. Deterministic evals test the tool surface, input validation, error handling, and journey coverage; the live browser flow tests whether an agent can use that harness to make a coherent scene. Considerable iteration went into scoring agent output and turning recurring failure modes into guide, feedback, and composition checks. How it was built Codex assisted with implementation, debugging, visual editor iteration, WebMCP registration, and verification. The repository documents browser checks, deterministic WebMCP checks, TypeScript checks, linting, and production builds. Try it Open the live site in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Ask the agent to create a picture-book scene in Open Dots: it should load the pixel-art guide, wait for readiness, define a palette, create and refine small assets with PNG feedback, then stamp them into a story page. title: Approval Desk
pitch: The agent does the work. The human holds the pen.
about_excerpt:
The agent does the work. The human holds the pen.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 What it is 

 Approval Desk is a WebMCP powered approval surface for agentic work that should not be allowed to complete itself. 

 The core idea is simple: an agent can do useful work, propose revisions, draft engagement letters, estimate scope, check availability, and prepare decisions. But when the work reaches a trust boundary, such as approval, booking, pricing, or publication, the human has to act. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 This is a strong fit for WebMCP because the tool surface changes with the work. The page registers 12 baseline tools through document.modelContext. When a human approval gate is pending, a 13th tool appears. When that gate closes, the extra tool disappears. 

 The tools are not just a fixed manifest. They reflect the live state of the work. 

 Better experience 

 For the human, the page reduces decision fatigue. Instead of hunting through drafts, calendars, pricing notes, and approval threads, the person sees what is waiting, what changed, why the agent proposed it, and the exact decision needed. 

 For the agent, the page removes guesswork. It can call structured tools for pending approvals, deliverable review, revision proposals, variant queues, scope, quotes, availability, and staged engagement letters without scraping the layout or pretending that a click equals judgment. 

 The human and agent boundary 

 The demo's Judge mode shows the central proof: a scripted approval click is refused. The gate only closes on a trusted human gesture. 

 That is the memorable point of the project. WebMCP is not only about making websites easier for agents to use. It can also make websites safer by giving agents useful tools while preserving human authority. 

 Implementation 

 Approval Desk is a fully static app hosted on Cloudflare Pages. It registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, uses typed input schemas and tool annotations, listens for toolchange, and reads back the active tool registry with document.modelContext.getTools. 

 The approval flow uses an abortable human gate. The agent can ask for approval and can withdraw its own pending request. It cannot approve, publish, book, or send on a person's behalf. 

 All engagements shown in the demo are invented sample data. No real client work appears in the project.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 Content creation is one of the biggest opportunities today, so we imagined a tool where humans and AI could work together from the first idea to the final video. By combining AI with WebMCP, we created a collaborative workflow for scripting, recording, and editing -> covering the whole content creator workflow 

 What it does 

 Deskmate is an AI powered content creation studio where both the user and AI can edit together. 

 It allows you to: 

 Write and refine video scripts collaboratively 

 Record videos with an on screen teleprompter that follows your script 

 Edit videos alongside AI using WebMCP 

 Add transitions, animations, captions, and audio through natural language 

 How we built it 

 We built Deskmate using Vite, React, JS, Chatgpt, and Claude. 

 The core idea was giving the AI direct access to a browser based editing environment through WebMCP, allowing it to make real edits while the user stays in control. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was balancing AI autonomy with user control. Early versions allowed the AI to overwrite changes that users wanted to keep, so we introduced an approval system where edits must be accepted before being applied. 

 Also getting ai to make motion graphics, write script the way you want it. Our solution was allow users to make use of the abundant ai skills available online and to be able to import them to our app and use it 

 As the project grew, the codebase became difficult to maintain. We eventually rebuilt the UI from scratch, creating a cleaner foundation before re integrating the features. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're especially proud of the collaborative video editor. Seeing ChatGPT successfully add motion graphics, animations, transitions, captions, and audio through WebMCP felt like a glimpse into the future of creative software. Something we used to spend hours building, literally was made in the blink of an eye 

 What we learned 

 This project taught us a huge amount about WebMCP, how AI interacts with browser applications, and the practical differences between traditional MCP servers and WebMCP. We also learned how important human approval is when building collaborative AI tools. 

 What's next for Deskmate 

 We're going to continue using Deskmate for our own content creation while expanding its features. Namely focus on adding sfx integration, more transitions and being able to generate complex transitions between clips 

 Our goal is to make it an open source platform for AI assisted scripting, recording, and video editing.

title: GitWand Agent
pitch: A WebMCP-powered Git Merge Room where agents resolve deterministic conflicts and humans decide the ambiguous ones.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered Git Merge Room where agents resolve deterministic conflicts and humans decide the ambiguous ones.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Agents are useful when they can act directly on Git problems, but they become fragile when they have to guess through a UI or pretend every conflict is machine-solvable. GitWand started from a boundary-first idea: resolve what is objectively deterministic, surface what is ambiguous, and keep the human in control of the decision. 

 What it does 

 GitWand Agent turns a Git conflict into a shared Merge Room for humans and agents. The page exposes three WebMCP tools: resolve_conflict , parse_git_error , and list_cases . Deterministic hunks are settled automatically; genuinely ambiguous ones are filed for the human to choose; and the agent can read the room back to resume work once a decision is made. 

 How we built it 

 We registered the tools directly on the page and wired the UI around live case state. The same browser tab that the agent sees also shows the Merge Room, so the result is visible in real time. The implementation keeps the resolution logic narrow and explicit: no guessing, no hidden side effects, and no tool that can silently pick a side for you. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was resisting the temptation to make the agent do too much. Git conflicts often mix deterministic edits with real intent decisions, so the product had to make that boundary obvious. Another challenge was designing list_cases so the agent can return after a human decision and continue without losing context. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native software works best when it is precise about what the machine can and cannot decide. WebMCP is a good fit because it lets a website define exactly how an agent should interact with it, instead of forcing the agent to infer the UI. 

 What's next 

 More conflict patterns, richer case history, and tighter integration with real repository workflows.

title: WebMCP-QCG: Quantum Call Gate
pitch: A browser-native HITL gate that inspects a Q# request, recommends the next safe action, and records evidence before quantum execution.
about_excerpt: A browser-native HITL gate that inspects a Q# request, recommends the next safe action, and records evidence before quantum execution. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Quantum developers already have capable frameworks, simulators and hardware services. The risky moment often comes before execution: an AI agent can prepare a technically valid-looking call before the human has verified the artifact, target evidence, limits, scientific intent or authority to spend. I built WebMCP-QCG to make that moment inspectable. Its promise is simple: review before you run. What it does WebMCP-QCG is a browser-native, human-in-the-loop quantum preflight workbench. A human imports a local Q# artifact. QCG keeps the source in session memory, computes a SHA-256 digest over the exact bytes, compiles it locally with the pinned Q# WebAssembly runtime and freezes a dated target-profile snapshot. Its deterministic policy returns exactly one recommendation: reuse_result reject recompile simulate_first ready_for_external_execution The agent can use four progressive WebMCP tools: inspect_quantum_experiment evaluate_quantum_call run_bounded_qsharp_simulation export_quantum_evidence_report The first two appear only after a human-loaded artifact is ready. A bounded simulation tool appears only after a valid simulate_first recommendation and visible human acceptance. Its one-use consent is consumed after invocation. QCG exports a JSON or Markdown evidence receipt binding the artifact, target snapshot, recommendation, human choice and measured effects. The MVP never submits a provider job, uses a provider credential or calls a QPU. Its QPU counter remains zero. Live application: https://qcg.securedme.ca/ Source and reproducible evidence: https://github.com/SeCuReDmE-main-dev/webmcp-hackathon-2026 How I built it The application uses React, TypeScript and Vite. Strict Zod contracts reject unknown properties and bound artifact size, shots, qubits and timeouts. qsharp-lang@1.31.0 runs inside a Web Worker so compilation and the published Bell simulation remain local and cancellable. Raw Q# stays out of WebMCP responses and IndexedDB; only evidence receipts persist locally. All human buttons and WebMCP tools call the same service layer. Tools are registered through document.modelContext with AbortSignal cleanup. The retained HTTPS origin serves the required WebMCP and security headers, the Worker and the pinned WebAssembly asset. Challenges I ran into The hardest design problem was separating three different things: an agent recommendation, a human authorization and an actual effect. Treating them as one state would make a convenient demo and a weak control system. The first live smoke run also exposed a real browser race: the inspection tool could be discovered before the initial WASM analysis finished. I changed the registration lifecycle so artifact tools stay absent until the manifest exists, then repeated the full test on the public origin. A second challenge was restraint. A multi-provider quantum router is an attractive future direction, but the hackathon proof needed one narrow, falsifiable vertical slice. Accomplishments I am proud of A real Q# file produces a byte-exact manifest and zero-diagnostic compiler evidence. Five falsifiable requests exercise all five decisions. The human can accept, defer or override with visible provenance. One accepted Bell simulation returned 64 correlated shots with the Bell invariant passing. The simulation tool disappeared after its one-use consent was consumed. The evidence export contained no raw Q#, local path, secret or provider error. Vitest passes 17/17 tests, including exact-versus-near reuse and false-ready regressions. Official WebMCP smoke evaluation passes 2/2 on the retained HTTPS origin. The live trace records one local simulation and zero QPU submissions. What I learned WebMCP adds value when the agent needs a compact capability that is absent from the visible DOM and shares the same state transitions as the human interface. Progressive registration is part of the product contract, not decorative plumbing. I also learned that a refusal, reuse decision or request for better evidence can be a useful outcome. Quantum tooling does not become safer by executing more calls; it becomes clearer when every proposed call has a reason, an authority boundary and a receipt. What's next I will test the frozen cases with quantum developers, measure false-ready decisions, refresh target-profile evidence and refine the visual workbench. Future adapters may normalize evidence from additional ecosystems while preserving their native semantics. Provider submission and paid execution remain outside this MVP and would require a separate authorization design. Built With indexeddb q# react typescript vite web-workers webassembly webmcp zod Try it out qcg.securedme.ca github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I originated WebMCP-QCG and serve as its solo architect, researcher, developer, and technical writer. I defined the problem, compared the candidate directions, designed the four-tool quantum preflight contract, audited the relevant quantum ecosystems, implemented and verified the QDK WebAssembly spike, and maintain the public evidence journal. Codex supports this work as my research partner for mapping, source comparison, quality assurance, and deliverable preparation; I retain authorship, technical judgment, and responsibility for every project decision. title: NUDE Private Fitting Room
pitch: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice.
about_excerpt: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice. Like Comment Story Updates 01-result 02-thesis 03-the-brief 04-the-workflow 05-consent-gate 06-real-tryon 07-the-correction 08-three-looks 09-webmcp-workflow 10-prepared 11-why-each-piece 12-not-confirmed 13-handoff 14-data-boundary 15-closing About the project Most virtual try-on tools are designed to help people check out faster. We wanted to build something different: a private lingerie fitting room that a person's own agent can prepare for them, without taking the final decision away from the person . Lingerie shopping is unusually personal. Fit, comfort, color, recovery needs, body confidence, and privacy can matter as much as product specs. An agent can do a lot of useful work — research products, compare options, remember constraints, and prepare a shortlist — but there is a point where automation should stop. That became our core principle: Your agent prepares the fitting room. You make the final choice. What we built NUDE Private Lingerie Fitting Room combines a real virtual try-on experience with a WebMCP layer that lets a user's own agent operate the shopping workflow. Through WebMCP, the agent can: Research available pieces. Inspect structured product details. Read the current fitting-room state. Request a virtual try-on after the user gives consent. Verify that the correct product asset was delivered. Prepare a fitting room with recommended pieces and reasons for the user to review. The final choice is deliberately left to the person. In our demo, the user is six weeks into shoulder rehabilitation and wants options that are easier to manage while recovering. Her agent researches the collection, proposes pieces, asks for consent before initiating virtual try-on, and prepares three completed looks. The agent initially chooses the wrong color. The user simply says: “i need the beige one” The agent corrects itself and continues. That moment matters to us. The goal is not an agent that pretends to be infallible. It is an agent that can do useful shopping work, accept human correction, and hand the decision back gracefully. The agent corrects. The person decides. How WebMCP fits The fitting-room product existed before this challenge, including the NUDE shopping experience and Perfect Corp virtual try-on. During the submission period, we added the WebMCP layer that makes the workflow operable by a user's own agent. We expose five real tools: nude.list_pieces nude.get_piece nude.get_fitting_room_state nude.try_on nude.prepare_fitting_room This turns a normal website interaction into a structured agent workflow: Research → Inspect → Try on → Verify → Prepare → Human handoff For us, the interesting part of WebMCP is not reducing the number of clicks. It is allowing an agent to do meaningful preparatory work while the website remains the place where the person sees the result and makes the final judgment. Privacy and the data boundary Privacy was especially important because this is a lingerie fitting experience. The user's photo is sent to Perfect Corp when virtual try-on is requested. However, no photo of the person and no try-on result is returned through the WebMCP tools . The agent works with structured information such as product data, the user's brief, fitting-room state, completion status, and verified product delivery. This also means our recommendation reasoning is intentionally grounded in the user's brief and structured product information , not in pretending that the agent visually inspected the person's try-on image. The rendered result is there for the person. Challenges we faced The hardest part was deciding what the agent should not do . It would have been easy to make the demo look more magical by implying that the agent could see everything, judge the person's body, or make the final selection automatically. We chose not to. Instead, we had to design clear boundaries between: what the agent knows, what the try-on service renders, what WebMCP returns, and what only the person should judge. We also had to make the workflow robust enough for correction. If the agent prepares the wrong color or misunderstands a preference, the product cannot collapse. The user must be able to correct it naturally and continue. Finally, we learned that agent UX is not simply normal UI with an API added. The agent needs structured state, clear tool semantics, verifiable completion, and an explicit handoff back to the human. What we learned The biggest lesson was that good agentic commerce is not maximum automation . An agent can remove a lot of shopping work without removing human agency. WebMCP gave us a way to separate those two things cleanly: the agent can research, operate tools, verify state, and prepare the experience, while the person remains responsible for the subjective decision that actually matters. For a category as intimate as lingerie, that balance feels more useful than an autonomous checkout button. We think the future of shopping agents is not: “The AI chose for me.” It is: “Everything is ready when I'm ready to choose.” What people and agents can now do together We gave the same brief — ‘’ six weeks into shoulder rehab, can't reach behind her back, needs something invisible under white office shirts ‘’ — to an agent with no site tools, and to the same brief through WebMCP. Without tools, the agent produced a warm, well-organised consultation. It recommended a specific piece, described its cup as "seamless" — that is a different product in the catalogue; this one is two-panel seamed and push-up — asserted the nude colourway would be "completely invisible" under a white shirt, then asked her to simulate the fitting in her mind and to run the white-shirt test herself, on a bra she does not own. Through WebMCP, the same brief produces three real Perfect Corp try-ons on her own photo, a per-piece reason the agent had to supply before the fitting room would accept it, and this caveat: "VTO cannot prove white-shirt invisibility or all-day comfort; confirm permitted movements with the rehab clinician." The tool-less answer reads better. It is warmer, more confident, better structured. That is the problem. Fluency is not verification, and this decision lands on a body — someone in week six of rehab, deciding what she can physically put on. WebMCP is what lets the page hand the agent the things it can actually check, and refuse the things it cannot.
