title: ArchitectureLab
pitch: ArchitectureLab is a WebMCP-native architecture studio where engineers and their agent co-design a system, run it against traffic and failures, and turn the result into an explainable architecture.
about_excerpt: ArchitectureLab is a WebMCP-native architecture studio where engineers and their agent co-design a system, run it against traffic and failures, and turn the result into an explainable architecture. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Thumbnail Main Page Use case Inspiration Architecture diagrams in software engineering are usually static, dead pictures—boxes and lines on a whiteboard that capture none of the underlying physics: no capacity limits, no queueing behavior, and no failure modes. When engineers ask an AI assistant for architecture review, the agent is forced to guess what the user is looking at from a screenshot, prose, or brittle DOM scraping. It has no semantic context, no knowledge of the active flow, and no ability to test hypotheses. We built Executable ArchitectureLab to turn system design diagrams into a live, executable, shared workbench between a human engineer and an in-browser AI agent using WebMCP . Instead of treating the agent as a disconnected chatbot, WebMCP enables the browser page to expose the exact scope, revision, and constraints the engineer is currently focusing on—allowing human and agent to simulate incidents, uncover bottlenecks, and co-design mitigations together. What it does Executable ArchitectureLab is a WebMCP-native architecture studio where a person and an AI agent collaborate on the same live system model: Context Follows Human Attention: Three global read-only tools are available at load ( get_architecture_summary , list_simulation_scenarios , get_component_catalog ). When the user selects a specific request flow (e.g., Checkout → Redis → Product DB ), three scoped tools dynamically register; the moment the selection clears, they are immediately revoked. The agent’s capabilities literally follow the human’s focus. Deterministic Failure Simulation: The agent (or the human) can run simulated load and failure scenarios (such as a 10× traffic surge combined with a Redis cache outage). The simulator models queueing delays, load shedding, and retry amplification to pinpoint the exact bottleneck (e.g., database connection saturation) and generates an ordered causal event chain presented across structured KPI metric cards. Draft-Only Patch Proposals with Revision Binding: When asked for a mitigation, the agent uses propose_architecture_patch to draft a concrete change (e.g., adding a read replica or increasing capacity) alongside expected trade-offs. The proposal is bound to the current graph revision ( baseRevision ). If the human modifies the graph in the meantime, stale proposals are automatically disabled and rejected. Strict Human-in-the-Loop Safety: The agent cannot apply changes or delete components. There is no destructive tool registered in the system. The proposal sits in the review queue as a diff until the human clicks Apply , which is the only operation that mutates the architecture graph and increments the revision. Prompt Injection Resilience: Component notes can contain untrusted user content (including our seeded prompt injection test in Redis). The tools flag this data with untrustedContentHint and fence it as data, ensuring that even if an instruction attempts to hijack the agent, there are no destructive tools available for it to misuse. How we built it We implemented the project using React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and custom SVG styling, strictly adhering to the latest WebMCP imperative API specification: WebMCP Adapter ( src/webmcp/adapter.ts ): Encapsulates all interactions with document.modelContext . Manages dynamic tool lifecycles using AbortController (since unregisterTool() is absent from the spec), serializes JSON schemas safely, shields runtime errors, and emits real-time activity logs for on-screen visibility. Smart Output Budgeting ( src/webmcp/tools.ts ): Enforces Chrome’s recommended 1.5K character output budget. Instead of naively truncating from the end (which would silently cut off critical modelling assumptions and disclaimers), our assemble() engine dynamically drops non-essential sections while preserving crucial headers, causal events, and assumptions. Port & Controls Seam ( src/contracts/ ): A strict architectural boundary separating the read-only WebMCP tool surface ( ArchLabPort ) from the mutation surface ( ArchLabControls ). A static AST test asserts that src/webmcp/ never imports controls . Deterministic Simulation Engine ( src/contracts/fixture/ ): Models the FlashCart e-commerce architecture with synchronous paths (CDN, Gateway, Checkout, Redis, DBs) and asynchronous tails (Order Queue, Invoice Worker, Email), calculating realistic queue penalties and dependency interactions. Automated Verification Harness ( scripts/verify-live.mjs & Vitest): A 31-test Vitest suite covering revision safety, patch validation, and causal models, coupled with a Playwright harness that launches installed Google Chrome with WebMCP flags enabled ( WebMCPSupport , WebMCPTesting ) to validate 23 live contract assertions against the deployed production origin. Challenges we ran into Adapting to Evolving WebMCP Specifications: The standard moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext , and APIs like provideContext() , clearContext() , and unregisterTool() were removed. We built strict guardrail tests to ensure no deprecated or removed APIs leaked into the codebase. Race Conditions in Dynamic Registration: In WebMCP, duplicate tool names throw errors if a re-registration races a pending abort. Furthermore, React 19's StrictMode double-invokes effects on mount. We solved this in adapter.ts by serializing registrations on per-tool promise chains and tracking abort signals cleanly. Avoiding Dangerous Output Truncation: Simply cutting strings at 1,500 characters dropped the disclaimer "Every number is synthetic and directional" from the most detailed replies—the exact answers judges and users are most likely to believe. We engineered section-based assembly to drop optional metrics first and keep disclaimers intact. Deployment & Origin Isolation Requirements: WebMCP requires origin isolation ( window.originAgentCluster === true ). Configuring vercel.json with Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , ensuring /debug rewrites functioned without 404s, and managing cross-origin headers required thorough end-to-end verification. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero-Destructive Architectural Guarantee: Proved that human-in-the-loop safety can be enforced structurally through interface isolation and static scanning tests rather than relying on LLM prompt compliance. Dynamic, Context-Aware Capability Surface: Achieved seamless registration and revocation of WebMCP tools that mirror user selection in real time without flickering or race conditions. Interactive Zero-Dependency Canvas: Crafted a lightweight, responsive SVG canvas featuring animated packet traces, zoom controls, clear architectural lanes, and live bottleneck heatmaps without bloated external canvas libraries. 31 Vitest & 23 Live Browser Verification Checks: Built comprehensive regression coverage and an automated Playwright harness validating production deployment in real Chrome. Transparent Agent Activity: Every tool call, duration, payload, and output preview is streamed live to the UI and the /debug dashboard, making agent reasoning inspectable and demo-ready. What we learned WebMCP transforms web apps from static viewports into structured, bidirectional workspaces where human and AI capabilities complement each other seamlessly. Gating tool availability via the registration lifecycle ( registerTool + AbortSignal ) is far more reliable than writing prompt-based flow control instructions ("call tool A before tool B"), which models often misunderstand or ignore. Designing with character budgets, schema validation, and origin isolation from day one is essential when building robust WebMCP applications. What's next for ArchitectureLab Freeform Drag-and-Drop Topology: Expanding the canvas from structured architectural lanes into a full freeform drag-and-drop editor allowing custom node creation and connection routing. Custom Architecture Modeling: Allowing engineers to define and import their own distributed systems, microservices, and queue topologies via JSON or OpenAPI specs. Export to Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC): Enabling the agent to translate human-approved architecture revisions directly into Terraform, Pulumi, or Docker Compose manifests. Advanced Multi-Region Simulation: Expanding the simulation engine to model multi-region failover, consensus algorithms (Raft/Paxos), and partition tolerance (CAP theorem scenarios). title: Move Board
pitch: An agent's property research dies with the chat. Move Board turns it into a board the agent fills and you keep - searching 15.79M UK sold prices, right in your browser.
about_excerpt: An agent's property research dies with the chat. Move Board turns it into a board the agent fills and you keep - searching 15.79M UK sold prices, right in your browser. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Hero Nine tools Board Code About the project Inspiration Deciding where to live in the UK means holding a dozen things in your head at once: what a street actually sold for, whether an area is rising or flattening, what your current place is worth, how far it is from work. The data exists. It is scattered across a dozen tabs and comparable only in a spreadsheet. An AI agent can do that research today and then hands you back a wall of prose. You cannot sort it, cannot pin two candidates side by side, cannot come back to it tomorrow. The research dies with the conversation. What it does Move Board gives an agent nine tools, and they split into two kinds. That split is the whole idea. Four tools look things up in rielty's public property corpus is 15.79M UK sold-price records and 1.96M commute journey times: search_properties , property_details , area_report , estimate_value . Five tools edit the board itself , and have no server behind them at all: add_to_board , remove_from_board , get_board , compare_on_board , annotate_card . A conventional MCP server could serve the first four. Only WebMCP can serve the other five , because they act on a surface the person is looking at, in their browser, in their session. There is nothing to authenticate and no state to sync. Ask, inside ChatGPT's in-app browser: "I'm moving to Yorkshire on a £400k budget, 3 beds minimum - research it and keep the three best on the board, with a note on each." Findings appear as it searches. Cards land on the board only when it decides they are worth keeping. Notes get written onto them explaining why. When it finishes you will have a board and you can drop the one you never liked, and the agent sees your edit next time it calls get_board . How we built it Deliberately boring. No framework, no build step, no dependencies: index.html , styles.css , app.js and one serverless function. Tools are declared as data and registered in one loop: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "add_to_board", description: "Pin a finding to the board so it survives the conversation…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { … }, required: ["card_id"] }, execute: async (input) => { /* mutate the board, re-render, reply */ } }); Every execute() mutates state and re-renders before it resolves, so the human sees the result at the same moment the agent receives it. No polling, no websocket. readOnlyHint is declared per tool rather than inferred from the name - search_properties is not read-only, because it changes what is on screen even though it writes no data. Challenges we ran into The browser cannot call an MCP server directly. We assumed a static page could talk to rielty.co.uk/mcp/v1 and found otherwise: it sends no CORS headers, answers OPTIONS with a 405, and does not expose the mcp-session-id header its own handshake depends on. Hence one serverless function that speaks MCP server-side - initialize , notifications/initialized , tools/call . It allows only the four tools rielty publishes, so it cannot be used as an open relay. A page full of tools looks broken. Our first deploy was correct and felt dead: open it in Safari, or Chrome without the flag, and you get two empty boxes and nothing to click, because there is no agent present. Correct behaviour, indistinguishable from a bug and judges would open it exactly that way. So we added Watch it work and ?demo=1 , which run the same nine tools in the order an agent calls them. Nothing is faked; every card is live data. Saying where the agent actually is. Our copy read "ask your agent something like…" beside a page with no input box. The agent is not in the page - it is whatever is browsing it. That sentence had to be rewritten to teach the model, not just describe the feature. API details that are easy to get wrong. The spec says document.modelContext ; some write-ups say navigator . Chrome 152 has it on document , so we feature-detect both. And executeTool takes the tool object from getTools() plus a JSON string - passing a name throws not of type 'RegisteredTool' , passing an object throws Failed to parse input arguments . Accomplishments that we're proud of The honesty survives the trip to the agent. rielty's corpus is predominantly sold history, not homes for sale, so every card is labelled "Sold record", and estimate_value returns no figure at all where there are too few local sales. The tool descriptions tell the agent to check listing_type before calling anything available. It would have been easy to ship something that quietly implies 15.79M homes are for sale. What we learned WebMCP changes what a page is for. We started thinking of it as a second transport for an API we already had, and finished thinking of the page as a shared workspace - the agent's tools and the human's hands acting on the same DOM. The moment that clicked was writing get_board : an agent has to be able to ask what the person changed, because they are editing the same thing. What's next The same nine tools are already built into rielty's own Phoenix/LiveView app and verified in Chrome, where search_properties runs the page's real typed-search path - so the map pans and the result list repaints as the agent works. That branch is not deployed yet. Beyond it: outbound tools (price alerts, enquiring with an agent) behind an explicit human confirmation step, since an agent reading a property description is reading attacker-controllable text. title: RiffSmith
pitch: Write riffs with an agent: the whole editor is 15 WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Write riffs with an agent: the whole editor is 15 WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Tools: the 15 tools with their real descriptions, styled like the app. Import modal: a messy hand-written tab pasted in, with the section headers, chug runs, 5h7, dead notes and slides. Mountain King in E standard mid-playback with the rig open, model showing RiffSmith Distorted. Imported result: that tab as a song with sections, repeat marks, a 3/4 bar, and the amp selected. Showcase: the Guitar Showcase's 16th-note riff section with the playhead on it. Inspiration I play guitar in a metal band, and like every guitarist I have a folder of half-finished riffs living in text files. Tab editors make those playable, but writing metal in one is slow, mechanical work: sixteenth-note chug runs, odd meters, repeats, and sections you have to loop a dozen times to know if they're any good. That's exactly the kind of structured, iterative writing an AI agent is good at, and yet an agent looking at a tab editor sees a grid of identical cells it can only click one at a time, with no idea what a cell means, whether a write landed, or what any of it sounds like. WebMCP was the missing piece. Instead of teaching an agent to screen-read a grid, give it the editor's own verbs. RiffSmith is the tab editor where every feature is a tool, and the human and the agent write in the same document at the same time. What it does RiffSmith is a browser tab editor for guitar and bass, tuned for metal. It imports and exports ASCII tab, including messy hand-written tabs with dense chug runs, section headers, and repeat marks. It handles per-bar time signatures from 2/4 to 12/8, grids from quarters to 16th triplets, and loops any section while you keep editing. Playback runs through a sampled guitar engine with persistent per-string voices: palm-muted chugs, hammer-ons, pull-offs, taps, slides, bends, vibrato, tremolo picking, pinch harmonics, dead notes, and chord strums, built from real direct-input recordings with open licenses. The signal goes through a real Neural Amp Modeler capture running as WebAssembly inside an AudioWorklet (the bundled one is a capture I trained on my own rig), or a built-in amp chain. A performance layer adds what a hand does: tension glide on every pick, pick position, one-sided fretting-hand vibrato, finger-shaped bends, pick scrape, wound-string slide squeak, fret clank, and micro-timing. Bass tunings get a real bass and their own amp. Every one of those capabilities is exposed to agents as one of 15 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : songs, bars, notation, imports, the rig, and playback. An agent can create a song, write a four-bar riff in one atomic call, set the amp tighter with all downstrokes and double tracking, play it, and read back the tab to verify its own work, while the human watches it land in the grid and edits any note it wrote. How I built it Next.js App Router, TypeScript, and the Web Audio API, deployed as a static site on Vercel. There is no backend; songs live in localStorage and sample banks and amp captures in IndexedDB. The WebMCP layer follows one rule, parity: every tool runs through the same state operations the UI uses, so there's no agent-only document or hidden mode. Tool returns are built for verification, with write_notes echoing the affected bars back as ASCII tab and get_song returning the full rendering. Notation is validated before any write, and a rejected token comes back with the complete notation guide so the agent can self-correct. Writes take a batch that is validated in full and applied atomically. Calls go through a serialized queue and mutations wait for React to commit before the next call runs, which gives read-after-write consistency for chains like create-then-read. Tools register at module evaluation, before React mounts, so an agent's first page snapshot already has the complete set, and a console shim at window.__webmcp is always available for testing. The audio engine is a lookahead scheduler placing events on the audio clock, driving a sampler with continuous per-string voices, plus an experimental physical string model written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly (no bindgen, about 21 KB) that runs in its own AudioWorklet. Sound comes from the Guitar-TECHS dataset (CC BY 4.0), FreePats (CC0), and Karoryfer's bass (CC0), chosen string-aware so a note plays from the string it's tabbed on. Every sound decision was measured before it shipped: offline renders through the real engine, pitch tracking, banded spectra, transient detectors, and level profiles around transitions. The pure scheduling and import layers have 31 unit tests. Challenges I ran into Pitch shifting is time stretching. Web Audio's detune folds into playback rate, so every pitched sample also stretches its pick transient. That was the source of a lot of "synthy". The fix was a set of real-recording handovers: held bends, slides, hammer-ons and pull-offs crossfade into a recording of the target pitch, energy-matched and decay-matched. The "pick" in every hammer-on. Legato kept sounding picked no matter what we did to the crossfade. The real bug was that the envelope was being re-read about 130 ms early and reset upward on every legato event. Tracking the envelope analytically from our own schedule fixed it in one afternoon after days of chasing filters. A dead string in the dataset. The low E string of the Guitar-TECHS guitar had almost no upper partials, about 28 dB below the same pitches on the A string, and that's the string every metal riff lives on. We regenerated its partials from the recorded fundamentals, fitted to the A string's spectrum. The first pass came out 145 cents flat because the files are 48 kHz and the script assumed 44.1. A pitch check caught it. Licensing. The best-sounding amp capture we found is not redistributable, and the rules require the submission to be fully open. The answer was to train a capture of my own rig and ship it with the repo under MIT, so the hosted demo and the repository are identical. Bare tools aren't usable tools. The first version of the tools worked and agents still failed with them: silent write errors, snapshot pipelines that missed late-registered tools, create-then-read races. Most of the WebMCP work was making the tools honest and verifiable, not making them exist. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A human and an agent editing the same riff at the same time, audibly, with no export step and no agent mode. The agent writes a riff, I click a cell it wrote and change one note while the loop keeps running, and it builds a variation on my edit. That was the whole point and it works. The engine went from a sampler to something a guitarist listens to and says "that's pretty great": real-recording legato landings, one-sided vibrato, finger-shaped bends, a fully synthesized pinch harmonic that screams through the amp, a bass with its own amp, a slide squeak that follows the speed of the slide, and a physical string model in Rust running in the browser. Every tool is verifiable by the agent that called it, and the whole thing runs as a static page with no server. What I learned Agents need feedback loops more than they need features. The tools that mattered most were the ones that echo the result of a write back as tab, return the notation guide with a rejection, and guarantee that a read after a write sees the write. Registering tools before the framework mounts matters because snapshot pipelines are unforgiving about timing. On the audio side, measure before you listen. Almost every "it sounds synthy" turned out to have a specific, measurable cause (input level into the capture, a compressor that shouldn't have been there, a stretched transient, an envelope step) rather than a vibe, and an offline render harness found each of them faster than ears could. And a real guitarist's ear is the final test. Several things that measured fine still got sent back. What's next for RiffSmith Chord and multi-string helpers in write_notes so agents can write power chords and octaves in fewer lines. Drum and bass companion tracks on the same scheduler. Render-to-WAV. MIDI and Guitar Pro export. A clean-channel capture and a bass capture to sit next to the distorted one. A wider low-tuned sample bank recorded on my own guitar, since no open dataset covers Drop B. And publishing the WebMCP bridge pattern (serialized queue, commit waiting, early registration, console shim) as a small standalone package so other editors can adopt it. title: Agentic Self-Service: Website Compliance and Discoverability
pitch: A WebMCP page where a person and an in-browser agent share a website audit, then check that the fix landed.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP page where a person and an in-browser agent share a website audit, then check that the fix landed. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agentic Self-Service Website Compliance and Discoverability About the project A public API is not enough when a person and an agent have to work on the same page. Scraping the DOM is brittle. Handing the agent an unchecked POST is worse: it can spend budget, kick off work, or touch production with nobody in the loop. anc.dev audits a site for the interfaces both sides actually use: machine-readable docs, OpenAPI, MCP discovery and protocol behavior, auth metadata, and browser-side WebMCP tools. The page renders a scorecard a human can read. The same markup is also a worksheet the in-page agent can query. The agent can fill the target URL and leave a short plan. I click Audit and complete Turnstile. After the result is on screen, the agent can read that scorecard and pull remediation prompts. It cannot start a second audit, skip the challenge, switch targets, or submit the form. Why WebMCP I wanted the agent on the same page I was looking at, with tools that match what that page is for. On /web-audit , WebMCP tools prepare the form: fill_audit_url , set_plan , and a few other helpers scoped to that page. They do not submit it. On a result page, four read-only tools turn the visible scorecard into a repair queue: get_worksheet lists findings as JSON rows ( id , keyword , status , evidence , remediable ). Filter by RFC 2119 keyword and status; omit status, and you get the remediable set that was actually observed. Each page is a JSON envelope with cached , scored_at , refresh_after , and next_offset . get_fix_prompt returns the stored remediation prompt for one check id, or remediable: false with a reason. get_fix_prompts returns prompts for many checks at once, with the same filters and pagination. get_audit_summary returns site and global scores, per-status counts, freshness, and the paged issue list. The tools read the DOM I am looking at. They do not call a backend and dress the response up as a browser tool. Output is capped, and a row that cannot be auto-fixed says so. The two-pass loop The demo target is Sounding , a public Worker I shipped in an incomplete state so there would be something real to fix. A browser agent prepares an audit of Sounding. A person authorizes it. On the result page, the agent asks get_worksheet for MUST findings and pulls get_fix_prompt for each remediable row. Those fixes land in Sounding, get deployed, and we audit again. The second scorecard shows the new evidence. Same page, different results. Inspect, fix, audit again. The agent helps turn the report into a small patch set I can review. I still own the audit click and the deploy. How I built it This is a production Cloudflare Workers site. A client bundle registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser supports WebMCP. Which tools appear depends on the pathname: the form page can prepare an audit, a result page can expose the worksheet, and the scoring route registers nothing. The result renderer stamps stable metadata on every visible finding. The WebMCP tools read that metadata back, so status and remediation eligibility match what is on screen. Responses are sized for the browser-tool cap. The engine checks discovery documents, OpenAPI, MCP protocol behavior, auth metadata, markdown availability, bot reachability, and whether the page exposes WebMCP. The running stack is Workers, KV and R2 for audit data, Turnstile, and a public TypeScript repo. What I learned In this use case, WebMCP became more useful when I started removing capabilities. Filling a form from a tool is easy. What I actually needed was a hard line between "prepare this" and "spend this audit," plus tool output that does not hide state from the person looking at the page. The result-page webmcp tools are read-only and make no network requests. They cannot skip Turnstile. They return complete JSON items, include cache freshness next to the findings, mark which rows are fixable, and link out to the full remediation doc when a prompt is too long for the browser-tool budget. I checked this in a real browser: captured the tools registered on rendered audit pages, ran the result tools against the DOM, compared their schemas to the published docs, and confirmed none of them can hit the audit endpoint. The live site is meant to open in ChatGPT's in-app browser or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. title: AOZU：
pitch: Image models can draw a character. AOZU lets an AI agent turn that drawing into a consistent, editable, reusable character pack — through WebMCP, in the same browser a human reviews.
about_excerpt: Image models can draw a character. AOZU lets an AI agent turn that drawing into a consistent, editable, reusable character pack — through WebMCP, in the same browser a human reviews. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Generating one beautiful character image is easy; producing a coherent set of expressions, outfits, and props is not. Separate generations drift in pose, scale, alignment, transparency, and identity. We wanted a workflow where a person can simply describe a companion while an agent handles the mechanical work without taking control away from the creator. Why the name AOZU? AOZU combines Aotter with two fictional digital worlds that inspired us: OZ from the Japanese animated film Summer Wars and U from Belle . The name also sounds like the Taiwanese expression A-tsóo (阿祖) , meaning a great-grandparent, elder ancestor, or keeper of inherited memories. This reflects our vision for AOZU: a WebMCP-powered gateway where people create lasting companions or avatars, build their identities and memories, and explore an ever-expanding digital world together. What it does AOZU turns the browser into a shared character forge for a human and an AI agent. A creator starts or imports a character, asks the agent to inspect the current workspace, and works through body, expression, outfit, and prop layers. AOZU validates every submitted asset, protects pixels that must not change, checks revisions and source hashes, normalizes supported inputs, stitches layers deterministically, and renders the result for human review. The creator can adjust alignment, undo or redo changes, duplicate a character, and export a portable character pack containing editable sources and a lossless WebP texture atlas. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent must infer application state from screenshots, guess which controls to click, and hope that generated assets satisfy invisible technical constraints. AOZU exposes the exact state and contract instead. The agent can discover what is missing, read the correct reference image and editable-region mask, submit a candidate against a specific revision and SHA-256 source hash, apply a measured transform, and navigate the creator directly to the result. The website remains the source of truth while the human remains the final reviewer. This makes the experience faster and more reliable, but also enables something that was previously difficult: probabilistic image generation inside a deterministic, reversible production pipeline shared by a person and an agent. How we implemented WebMCP AOZU registers nine public tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : inspect_workspace navigate_character inspect_character_contract update_character_profile replace_character_asset repair_character_asset set_character_variant_transform undo_character_change redo_character_change The public tools are projected from the same Mantle application contracts used by the React UI. IndexedDB stores browser-local character workspaces and image blobs. Candidate submission checks dimensions, RGBA transparency, visible bounds, canvas overflow, revision freshness, and source hashes. PixiJS renders the same compiled atlas that is included in the exported character ZIP. What people and agents can do together A person describes a coherent character instead of manually preparing every production asset. The agent reads machine-readable visual constraints instead of guessing from the UI. AOZU rejects unsafe or stale changes and preserves protected pixels. The person reviews each result in context and can adjust, undo, redo, duplicate, or export it. The finished pack can leave AOZU and be imported again without an account or server-side state. Challenges The hardest problem was defining a safe boundary between creative generation and deterministic editing. AOZU deliberately does not hide uncertainty: the agent creates the pixels, while the application owns validation, normalization, protected regions, revision control, stitching, persistence, and export. Building one contract that could serve both the human UI and WebMCP tools prevented the two workflows from drifting apart. Accomplishments A non-trivial nine-tool WebMCP workflow rather than button automation Revision- and SHA-256-bound asset mutations Protected-region character editing and deterministic layer stitching Local-first persistence, undo/redo, duplication, import, and export A lossless WebP texture atlas shared by preview and exported packs Responsive AOZU parchment UI with nine languages What is next The competition build intentionally closes one loop: create, repair, review, and export a companion. The same portable character contract can later power AOZU adventures, memories, skills, rewards, and task-specific companion cards without weakening the character pipeline demonstrated here.  Inspiration 

 Contract review is where AI chat fails hardest: the model pastes a wall of suggested language into the sidebar while you’re staring at a different paragraph. The risk isn’t “bad writing” — it’s silent apply . 

 WebMCP lets the page expose review actions on the live document. Redline was built so ChatGPT can propose edits and flag risks as hunks you can see, while accept/reject stays a human gate. Propose ≠ commit. 

 What it does

pitch: Get help. Hire a Tasker. Or let an agent book the same site.
about_excerpt:
Get help. Hire a Tasker. Or let an agent book the same site.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Websites are still built as if only humans will use them: click, search, filter, compare, book. Agents can already drive that UI, but they do it by guessing at buttons. WebMCP flips that. A page can expose the same capabilities as tools — document.modelContext.registerTool , getTools , executeTool — so an agent uses the site the way a developer would use an API, while a person still uses the normal interface. 

 TaskRabbit is the perfect test of that idea. A move-in is never one listing. It is furniture assembly, cleaning, and TV mounting, coordinated under a budget, with a human still in the loop before anything is booked. We wanted a marketplace that looks like a real service site and behaves like an MCP server in the browser. 

 What it does 

 TaskFlow is a dual-use TaskRabbit-style marketplace. 

 For people: browse services, compare Taskers, and book from a profile — search, listings, hourly rates, availability, confirm. 

 For agents: the same pages register WebMCP tools ( searchServices , findTaskers , getTaskerAvailability , getTaskerPricing , createTaskRequest , scheduleTask , …). An in-page agent dock takes an outcome like “I just moved in. Make my home ready tonight. I have a $250 budget.” It discovers those tools, builds a plan (Marcus $85, Sarah $95, David $60 = $240), and waits for approval before it schedules. 

 Both paths write to the same booking store. My Tasks shows You booked next to Booked by agent . One website, two clients, one set of capabilities. 

 How we built it 

 
 Next.js App Router , TypeScript, Tailwind, and shadcn/ui — no backend, no real payments, no live TaskRabbit API. 
 A shared marketplace layer ( search , findTaskers , pricing, create/schedule). Human buttons call those functions. WebMCP execute callbacks wrap the same functions. 
 A spec-faithful document.modelContext polyfill so the demo runs in current browsers, using the official WebMCP shape if the native API exists. 
 A deterministic planner (no LLM) so the killer demo is reliable, with staged delays so the tool activity is visible. 
 A TaskRabbit-like light marketplace plus a dark agent dock that keeps Show WebMCP on screen for judges. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is still a draft. Most browsers do not ship document.modelContext , so we had to match the spec closely without pretending the API is everywhere. 

 The harder product problem was not building another chatbot. The original instinct was an AI-only command center. That hid the point. WebMCP only lands if the human site is real and the agent uses that site’s tools — not a parallel fake API. 

 Shared state was picky too: a full navigation wiped in-memory bookings until we persisted them and tagged each row by source ( human | agent ). Tool registration also had to survive hot reload without double-registering names. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A 2–3 minute demo where you book Marcus as a person, then let the agent plan a $240 move-in, and both appear on My Tasks . 
 Judges can see WebMCP: live getTools / executeTool calls, not a hidden prompt. 
 Human-in-the-loop: the agent never books until Approve & Schedule . 
 One implementation for both audiences — not two products glued together. 
 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native websites are not “add a chat sidebar.” They are capability design : the same operations must be safe, named, and schema’d for a model and obvious in a UI for a person. 

 We also learned why the spec cares about annotations ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint ) and approval. Tool descriptions are easy to trust too much. Keeping consequential actions behind a human confirm is the product, not a footer. 

 What's next for TaskFlow 

 
 Native WebMCP in a supporting browser, dropping the polyfill on that path. 
 Declarative tools from real forms, as the spec’s declarative section lands. 
 A real LLM planner behind the same tools, with the deterministic demo kept as a fixture. 
 Richer trust UX: show which origin registered a tool, and treat tool output as untrusted when the hint says so. 
 

 TaskFlow’s bet is simple: the next marketplace is designed for both hands and agents.

title: WattWeave
pitch: Turn a peak-energy alert into a safe, visible load plan in seconds
about_excerpt: Turn a peak-energy alert into a safe, visible load plan in seconds Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When a building receives a demand-response event or sudden price spike, facilities operators must reduce peak load without disrupting critical equipment or violating occupant constraints. Existing energy dashboards show charts but leave operators to manually coordinate dozens of devices and schedules. The core problem is that reducing total energy is not the same as reducing the critical peak, and manual changes can create dangerous rebound peaks later. We were inspired by the need for a collaborative human-AI interface where operators define what cannot change (critical loads, departure targets, comfort bounds) while an agent discovers, simulates, and applies safe load-shifting plans—all with full visibility, cancellability, and reversibility. What it does WattWeave is an interactive building-energy sandbox where a human pins non-negotiable constraints and an agent discovers, simulates, stages, and applies a safe load-shifting plan inside the same visual interface. Core workflow: Operator locks critical loads directly on the timeline (server room, accessibility equipment) Agent reads the live demand event, locks, and flexible assets through WebMCP tools Cancellable simulation sweeps across the timeline, generating up to 3 candidate plans Operator compares candidates by peak, cost, comfort impact, and rebound risk Selected plan renders as a ghost preview on the load chart and energy-flow diagram Operator approves the exact schedule diff in a visible approval drawer Agent commits the plan; the live meter falls below the target line One-click rollback restores the exact prior schedule with full audit trail Key features: Deterministic 15-minute slot model with integer watt-hour precision Transparent heuristic constraint solver (not a black-box optimizer) Dynamic WebMCP tool registration based on UI state Safety model: critical loads never change, commit requires visible approval, stale plans rejected Animated "living grid" energy-flow visualization Offline deterministic sandbox mode (no API keys required) Optional Pro features: side-by-side candidate comparison, audit export, animated particle flow How we built it Tech stack: React 19.1.0 + TypeScript 5.9.2 + Vite 7.1.5 Zustand 5.0.8 for state management Zod 4.1.5 for schema validation and JSON Schema generation Web Workers for off-main-thread simulation with real cancellation Vitest 3.2.4 for unit tests and intent evals Playwright 1.55.0 for end-to-end browser journeys Remotion for polished demo video production Architecture: domain/ - Pure, framework-free core: types, time model, seed data, schedule logic, constraint solver sim/ - Web Worker bridge with AbortSignal support for clean cancellation webmcp/ - 10 semantic tools with dynamic state-scoped registration via navigator.modelContext state/ - Zustand store with pulse bus for tool-effect animations components/ - React UI: load timeline, flow view, asset panel, planner, approval drawer, inspector billing/ - Polar.sh integration with offline demo mode WebMCP integration: Tools are registered dynamically based on UI state— get_selected_asset only exists while an asset is selected, commit_load_plan is undiscoverable until the operator clicks approve. Every tool execution animates its effect on the UI so humans can see what the agent did. Testing: 36 unit tests covering solver logic, time model, and 15 intent evals 9 Playwright E2E journeys including external agent integration Intent evals drive real WebMCP tools headlessly, exactly as an agent would Challenges we ran into Cancellation semantics - Making AbortSignal work cleanly through Web Worker → solver → checkpoint without state mutation required careful architecture. We solved it with a structured CANCELED result and explicit checkpoint boundaries. Stale plan rejection - Ensuring operators can't accidentally approve plans based on outdated constraints. We implemented scenarioVersion bumping on every constraint change and rejection by name in simulate/preview/stage/commit. Exact rollback - Generating mathematically precise inverse schedules that restore the baseline array exactly. We solved this by negating every integer-Wh delta at staging time and storing the inverse alongside the staged plan. Untrusted content handling - The utility tariff feed in our scenario contains a literal prompt injection. We return it inside an untrusted envelope with warnings, keeping numeric data structured and separate. Dynamic tool registration - Making the tool list itself serve as the permission model. We implemented state-scoped registration where tools appear/disappear based on selection, staging, and approval state. Rebound peak detection - Naïve load-shifting can create worse peaks after the event window. We added explicit 60-minute post-event rebound analysis with guard thresholds. Accomplishments that we're proud of Semantic over scraping: WebMCP tools encode meaning (e.g., "pre-cool auditorium by 30 minutes within comfort bounds") rather than pixel coordinates, making agent actions reliable and interpretable. Safety-critical guarantees: Critical loads never change, commit requires visible human approval, cancellation is clean, rollback is exact, and untrusted content stays data. Transparent solver: We show the full scoring breakdown (peak 32 · rebound 25 · cost 20 · comfort 10) and explicitly state "best candidate found by the deterministic heuristic, not a claim of optimality." Real cancellation: AbortSignal propagates through Web Worker to solver checkpoints, returning structured CANCELED with zero state mutation—no hangs, no rejected promises. Deterministic demo: The entire hero scenario (212 kW → 168 kW, both EV targets met, 160 kW rebound) is reproducible without any external APIs or random data. Comprehensive testing: 15 intent evals prove the WebMCP contract, 36 unit tests cover domain logic, and 9 E2E journeys validate the full user and agent workflows. Beautiful "living grid" UI: Frosted translucent panels, animated particle flow tracking real dispatch numbers, springy motion, and full accessibility support. What we learned WebMCP is transformative for agent-human collaboration: Shared live state through a single Zustand store eliminates the drift that plagues chart-scraping approaches. The tool list itself becomes the permission model. Cancellation is a first-class feature: Real cancellation requires architectural commitment—checkpoint boundaries, structured results, and zero state mutation on abort. It's not an afterthought. Scoring transparency builds trust: Showing the full breakdown and explicitly disclaiming optimality is more honest than hiding the heuristic. Users appreciate understanding why a plan was recommended. The approval pattern is powerful: Making commit_load_plan undiscoverable until the human clicks approve creates a strong structural guarantee. The tool surface itself encodes the permission model. Integer arithmetic matters: Using 15-minute slots and integer watt-hours internally avoids floating-point surprises that could corrupt schedule calculations. Untrusted content needs structural boundaries: Returning prompt injections inside an untrusted envelope with warnings keeps the app safe while still displaying the information. E2E tests with external agents are invaluable: The Playwright journey that injects a real navigator.modelContext and drives the full lifecycle outside the app proves the WebMCP contract without spending model tokens. What's next for WattWeave Real control gateway integration: Complete the documented Home Assistant loopback adapter with organization authentication, transport security, command allowlists, and site-specific safety interlocks. Multi-building scenarios: Extend the deterministic seed data to support additional building types (office, retail, hospital) with different asset profiles and constraint patterns. Historical analysis: Add time-series exploration of past demand events, committed schedules, and their outcomes to support learning and refinement. Collaborative mode: Multi-operator support with role-based permissions, constraint proposal workflows, and team audit trails. Advanced solver strategies: Implement additional candidate generation strategies (thermal mass pre-conditioning, predictive battery dispatch, machine-learning-assisted feasibility analysis). Mobile optimization: Responsive design improvements for tablet and field-operator use cases. title: Novas WebMCP Proving Ground
pitch: A live, inspectable challenge where Codex uses Nova Browser to solve real tasks through WebMCP tools - and measures the difference against the interface.
about_excerpt: A live, inspectable challenge where Codex uses Nova Browser to solve real tasks through WebMCP tools - and measures the difference against the interface. Like Comment Story Updates Nova Inspiration Most WebMCP demos prove that a tool call works. We wanted to answer the more useful question: what does WebMCP actually buy an agent? What it does WebMCP Proving Ground is a live, inspectable challenge with three tasks. Every task can be solved through the visible interface or through the page's nine WebMCP tools. Both paths use the same state and mutations, while the page measures interactions, rejected attempts, and completion. The tasks expose failures that real browser agents hit: An appointment slot that looks available until conflicts are checked An order where one item has already shipped A report where selected filters are not yet applied The WebMCP tools return the hidden state before Codex acts. Codex can therefore choose a valid appointment, cancel only eligible items, and export the intended report without guessing. The live mission monitor records every tool call and ends at 3/3 objectives complete. How we built it The project is a dependency-free static website using semantic HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It registers nine task-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, with navigator.modelContext and provideContext fallbacks. The interface and tool handlers share one state model, so the comparison is inspectable rather than simulated. For the recorded run, Nova Browser gives Codex control of a real browser tab through MCP. Because Nova does not yet discover native page WebMCP tools directly, the demo openly uses a main-world compatibility bridge to the exact same definitions and handlers. The page labels this boundary instead of hiding it. Why Nova Browser Nova is not just a click driver. It provides more than 800 MCP tools in 25 bundles for browser control, target ownership, safety, evidence, local memory, and unattended work. Verified website behavior can become local, evidence-bound knowledge for later agents, with drift checks to guard against stale rules. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making the comparison fair. UI clicks and tool calls had to mutate the same data, start from identical state, and be counted consistently. We also had to show why task-level tools matter without turning WebMCP into renamed UI controls. What we learned The largest benefit is not fewer clicks by itself. It is that an agent receives task-relevant state before making a consequential decision. WebMCP turns hidden interface state into an explicit contract. What's next We want to run the same patterns against larger authenticated workflows and connect native WebMCP discovery directly to Nova's browser MCP layer. title: albugent-webmcp
pitch: Albugent WebMCP brings browser-native data governance—combining deterministic WASM calculation with human-approved AI remediation.
about_excerpt: Albugent WebMCP brings browser-native data governance—combining deterministic WASM calculation with human-approved AI remediation. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Google Chrome Canary Test ✅ Unified Data Governance Dashboard: Real-time WASM risk scoring with independent binary compliance icons for PII exposure. Dual-Control Pattern: Inline Approve/Reject controls rendered in chat before executing any state-changing remediation Dual-Control Pattern: Inline Approve/Reject controls rendered in chat before executing any state-changing remediation. WebMCP Tool Audit Trail: Full visibility into client-side tool inputs and outputs registered via document.modelContext. Dataset Inspection & Lineage: Column-level PII classification, NULL profiling, and inferred pipeline relationships. Interactive KPI: System-wide compliance metric; 57 PII Fields 0.171 Risk Score 17 Datasets Name Origin Notice Albugent is derived from Albumin — the vital, invisible plasma protein produced by the liver that maintains osmotic pressure and safely transports nutrients throughout the human body. Much like Albumin, true data governance works silently in the background: maintaining structural pressure, ensuring compliance, and safely regulating data flow without disrupting operational pipelines. (100% human-conceived project name, not AI-generated). Inspiration Data governance tools are traditionally split into two disconnected worlds: a human scanning visual dashboards for anomalies, and an AI agent asked by a data engineer to "check if anything looks off." In conventional setups, the agent operates blindly — screen-scraping UI elements, guessing what buttons do, or attempting complex calculations inline. When autonomous LLM agents chain dozens of unguided tool calls and perform mathematical profiling, context drift leads to hallucinated metrics and broken schemas. We built Albugent to prove a different paradigm: What if the dashboard and the AI agent shared one single, typed computation layer? WebMCP ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) provides the exact browser-native primitive for this pattern. Instead of the agent guessing what the UI sees, Albugent exposes a single in-browser governance engine twice: As a reactive pixel-rendered dashboard for human operators. As deterministic WebMCP tools for the LLM agent. Both read from the exact same client-side SQLite WASM databases. The core design rule: The engine computes and executes; the agent decides and explains. What it does Albugent WebMCP is a 100% browser-native data governance engine auditing 17 datasets across three enterprise domains ( healthcare , fiction-retail , nyc-taxi pipelines) loaded entirely client-side via SQLite WASM. Zero server backend; zero data leaves the browser. For the Human Operator: Live Governance Dashboard : Real-time health status ( Healthy / Warning / Critical ) across all 17 datasets, driven by a unified risk-scoring formula (0–100). Independent Compliance Badges : Always-visible PII exposure and NULL-density warning icons next to every dataset, preventing critical compliance flags (like 5 PII columns scoring 25/100) from being hidden inside an averaged numeric risk score. Interactive KPI Drill-Downs : Zero-dependency visual charts for system-wide compliance metrics. Dataset Detail & Lineage Views : Column-level NULL profiling, detected PII severity, and inferred pipeline relationships ( raw_ → staging_ → mart_ ). For the AI Agent (via WebMCP): A floating chat widget powered by Groq connects directly to 7 registered WebMCP tools ( document.modelContext ). Tool calls are collapsed into expandable audit traces under each message. Human-in-the-Loop Remediation Loop (The Core Workflow): Contextual Action : Clicking "Propose masking fix" next to a flagged table pre-fills a chat prompt with the exact dataset URN. Deterministic Evaluation : The agent invokes propose_remediation . The engine re-evaluates the real risk score. If risk is low, the tool refuses action with exact metrics unless explicit force=true is requested. Inline Approval : When a proposal is generated, Approve / Reject controls render directly inside the chat bubble. WASM SQL Execution : Approving executes a dynamic UPDATE statement against the in-memory SQLite database, instantly masking PII columns. Live State Sync : The entire UI (KPI cards, dataset badges, compliance icons) refreshes live without reloading the page. How we built it Frontend & UI : Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4. Computation Engine : Web Worker running @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm with sqlite3_deserialize for zero-latency, client-side SQL execution. Agent Integration : Groq API (OpenAI-compatible) executing a strict single-tool-call loop. WebMCP Integration : toolRegistry.ts registers 7 tools on document.modelContext , passing readOnlyHint: true on query tools per Chrome security guidelines. Decoupled State Bridge : proposalStore.ts provides a pub/sub event bus bridging WebMCP tool calls registered at application boot ( main.tsx ) with React UI state ( App.tsx ). Challenges we ran into 1. WASM & Worker Asset Resolution In production, Vite's SPA fallback initially served index.html for mistyped worker or database paths, producing misleading non-JavaScript MIME type and SQLITE_NOTADB errors. We resolved this by building strict URL maps and wrapping all SQLite operations in a shared WASM initialization promise ( ensureSqliteInitialized ) to eliminate race conditions during initial load. 2. Guardrail Enforcement Beyond tool_choice: 'none' We discovered that passing tool_choice: 'none' on follow-up turns did not reliably prevent models from attempting tool calls, causing API rejections. The solution was structural: finalizing completion requests are sent with the tools array completely omitted from the payload, removing the schema shape entirely. 3. Agent Architecture Fabrications During testing, when asked why it executed a remediation, the LLM fabricated a plausible-sounding "automatic risk engine threshold" that did not exist in the code. We resolved this by enforcing strict engine-level risk re-checks in propose_remediation (returning real numerical proof) and updating system prompts to forbid ungrounded operational claims. 4. Blended Risk Scores vs. Strict Compliance Requirements Initially, computeRiskScore assigned a categorical +25 score for MEDIUM-PII presence. For datasets like mart_demographics (containing 5 PII columns but low NULL density), this resulted in a score of 25/100, visually signaling "Healthy/Low Risk." In enterprise data governance, the presence of PII is an absolute compliance event, not an averaged metric. We corrected this architecture by decoupling compliance indicators from the numeric score, adding independent dataset-level warning icons that ignite strictly on anomaly presence regardless of the blended score. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Shared Truth : The dashboard and the LLM agent receive identical JSON outputs computed by the exact same TypeScript worker logic. Real In-Browser Remediation : MASK_PII generates and runs dynamic SQL queries directly inside SQLite WASM, updating reactive UI state end-to-end. Strict Guardrails : The agent never computes math or hallucinates risk scores — it relies 100% on deterministic profiling. First Full-Stack Reactive UI : Designed and built my first full web interface from scratch, successfully orchestrating client-side React state, SQLite WASM worker event loops, and live WebMCP tool execution into a single reactive dashboard. Compliance-First UX Architecture : Successfully separated strict binary compliance flags (PII presence) from aggregated numerical risk scores, ensuring critical compliance issues are never hidden from human operators. What we learned API Guardrails Must Be Structural : Relying on soft parameters like tool_choice: 'none' is insufficient. True reliability requires physically altering the schema payload passed to the model. LLM Fluency Is Not Correctness : An agent that confidently invents explanations for its behavior is more dangerous than one emitting obvious errors. Grounding every action in deterministic worker output is mandatory for enterprise tools. Full-Stack Execution & Team Specialization : Building a custom reactive UI for the first time and bridging complex front-end state with the SQLite WASM engine consumed a massive amount of development time, leaving less bandwidth for UI polish. The primary personal insight: building complex agentic systems as a solo developer highlights the critical need for a balanced team — allowing focus to be directed entirely toward core engine architecture, logic, and data governance, where my true strengths lie. What's next for Albugent WebMCP Governance Tool SDK : Build a standard, extensible SDK allowing developers to wrap arbitrary SQL databases into WebMCP tools with zero custom UI coding. Full Remediation Execution : Implement dynamic SQL generators for REMEDIATE_NULLS and CIRCUIT_BREAK proposal types. FK

title: Village
pitch: Village turns shift changes and childcare gaps into one visible, confirmed family plan—with WebMCP agents coordinating and families keeping control.
about_excerpt: Village turns shift changes and childcare gaps into one visible, confirmed family plan—with WebMCP agents coordinating and families keeping control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Village was not created for this competition . I have been thinking about this idea ever since those adverts years ago that said, "There's an app for that." The problem I have faced is a lack of technical knowhow. I have always been terrible at keeping up with schedules. That was true when I was single, and it is definitely true now that I have children and both my partner and I work shifts. My partner and I currently work as Police Officers in the UK, we are on different teams so have different shift patterns. We rely heavily on family for childcare and there have been a few occasions where we have completely forgot or got confused and its ended up in one of us having to take emergency leave. Our weeks can include early shifts, late shifts, nights, overtime (sometimes planned, often spontaneous), school, childcare, appointments, pickups and drop-offs. One small change can throw everything else out. We end up checking calendars, messaging relatives and trying to work out who is available—all while hoping we have not forgotten something. The idea for Village has always been there. The know-how to build it had not. AI changed that for me. It gave me the ability to take an idea I had carried around for years and turn it into a real, working product. The competition did not create Village, I have been toying with how the idea would work for years. However, it did give me the push—and the technology—to take it much further. Village turns the mess of family life into one visible, shared plan . The demo begins with a completely normal situation in our house: I accept an overtime shift on Tuesday. Village adds the overtime, compares it with my partner's shift and identifies that our children now need childcare. It then proposes an ordered Relay: Anne first, Grandad second and Claire third. I approve the complete plan before anybody is contacted. Only one person is approached at a time. Anne declines, so Village moves on to Grandad. Grandad accepts, the Relay stops immediately and Claire is clearly shown as Not contacted . That last part matters. I did not want to build something that messages everybody at once and leaves several relatives arranging the same childcare. Village should reduce noise and stress—not create more of it. It also supports: rota scans with shifts reviewed before import; repeating patterns such as six days on and four days off; irregular multi-week rotas where every week is different; early, late and overnight shifts; one-off exceptions and overtime; automatic childcare-gap detection; trusted carers and their availability; a visible history of important actions. Village was designed around my family, but the problem is not unique to us. Millions of shift-working families are trying to manage the same thing through screenshots, group chats and memory. How we built it Village is a responsive React and TypeScript application with four connected WebMCP tool surfaces. The visible interface and the agent tools use the same state-transition engine. Whether I press a button or ask an agent to act, the result goes through the same rules. Village is not just a chatbot with calendar information pasted into it. The website exposes 24 page-defined WebMCP tools that act on the same family plan visible on the screen. The tools cover four connected areas: Family Schedule — reads the shared plan, adds approved overtime and identifies childcare gaps. Village Relay — creates an ordered childcare chain, records responses and stops when somebody accepts. Rota Scan — prepares scanned shifts, flags anything uncertain and imports them after approval. Shift Patterns — creates flexible rota cycles, handles exceptions and changes future shifts without rewriting the past. Without WebMCP, an agent would be clicking around a webpage or working from an outdated copy of the calendar. With WebMCP, Village defines exactly what the agent can do, what information it needs and when it must stop for confirmation. The agent is good at: reading across the complete family plan; spotting clashes and missing childcare; checking which trusted carers are suitable; continuing a process that has already been approved; explaining what changed. The family still controls: changes to the calendar; who may be contacted; the order in which people are approached; the response window; the final childcare arrangement. Before Village changes a commitment or contacts somebody, it explains the exact action and asks for confirmation. Once I approve a Relay, the agent can continue inside that boundary without repeatedly asking the same question. It cannot quietly change the order, expand the plan or contact everybody at once. The agent handles the coordination. The family keeps the decisions. Underneath the interface are: stable identifiers for shifts, patterns, requests and responses; shared household revisions that prevent stale approvals; idempotency keys that prevent duplicate actions; confirmation gates tied to the exact proposed change; interval-based scheduling and childcare-gap detection; machine-readable errors; an auditable history; responsive phone, tablet and desktop layouts. The public competition build uses demonstration data and requires no account, allowing judges to test the complete flow immediately. The final build passes 72 automated tests , including duplicate responses, stale plans, mismatched retries, malformed shift times, overnight work and repeating-pattern changes. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering a WebMCP tool. It was keeping one coherent family plan while both a person and an agent could change it. The other difficult question was how much freedom the agent should have. A request such as "sort the childcare" sounds simple, but it could easily result in an agent messaging everybody, duplicating requests or making assumptions about who should look after somebody's children. Village turns that broad request into a clear plan containing: named carers; a specific contact order; a response window; an approval boundary; an immediate stop when somebody accepts. Supporting real shift patterns was another challenge. Rotas are rarely as neat as normal calendar applications expect. Village needed to support short repeating cycles, six-week patterns where every week is different, overnight shifts, individual exceptions and future changes without silently altering previous commitments. We also tested the uncomfortable edge cases: stale approvals, duplicate responses, retries, conflicting identifiers and events that cross midnight. Family coordination involves real people, so silently doing the wrong thing was not acceptable. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that Village solves a problem from my actual family life rather than inventing a problem for a competition. I am also proud that: the WebMCP tools complete an end-to-end coordination task , rather than demonstrating isolated commands; agent actions and direct interface actions share one visible source of truth; confirmation represents meaningful consent rather than decorative friction; retries do not create duplicate shifts or childcare requests; the Relay shows both who was contacted and who was deliberately left alone; irregular and overnight shift patterns are handled properly; the complete build passes 72 automated tests ; the interface works across phones, tablets and desktops; Village remains useful as a family product even when no agent is involved. The moment Grandad accepts, the Relay stops, the calendar updates and Claire remains Not contacted . That single screen demonstrates the whole idea: useful autonomy operating inside a boundary the family approved. What we learned I learned that the best agent experiences do not replace the interface. They make the shared interface more useful. The family should be able to see what the agent sees, understand what it proposes and verify what happened afterwards. WebMCP forced me to think carefully about: the smallest meaningful actions; the information each action needs; what the agent can safely continue doing; the moments where human consent matters. That produced a calmer and more accountable product than simply giving an agent permission to click around a calendar. I also learned that AI can completely change who gets to build software . I did not suddenly have this idea because generative AI became available. I had the idea for years. AI closed the gap between having the idea and being capable of turning it into something real. What's next for Village The competition build proves the core idea, but I want Village to become a real product that my family can genuinely use. The next version would add: private household accounts and permissions; direct Outlook and Google Calendar integration; real-time invitations and carer respons

title: Ratiflow
pitch: Capability grants for agents on a live page: the human picks the access, WebMCP exposes only that tool catalog, and every edit lands as a reversible, attributed revision.
about_excerpt: Capability grants for agents on a live page: the human picks the access, WebMCP exposes only that tool catalog, and every edit lands as a reversible, attributed revision. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Tagging a bot Document editor WebMCP flow Revision history Ratiflow Tagline Capability grants for page agents: the human chooses access → WebMCP registers only that catalog → every edit lands as reversible, attributed proof. Try it out Live: https://ratiflow-webmcp.vercel.app/ Repo: https://github.com/anthonyisaa/webMCP_Hackathon Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5KixpBV92v8 Inspiration Incident reports and launch docs already mix people and AI. The finished paragraph usually survives. The request, tools, sources, authorship, and rationale usually do not. The next teammate sees prose—not why it changed. Another agent often repeats the same work. Most “AI in docs” products add chat beside a document. Ratiflow answers a different WebMCP question: what is this agent allowed to do on this page, right now? The human chooses an access profile for the assignment. The live page registers only that tool catalog. The agent works inside that grant. The document records an immutable revision with prompt, sources, authorship, and diff. WebMCP fits because the website —not a side chat—owns the capability surface for the current task. What it does Ratiflow is a shared Markdown workspace focused on two high-stakes templates: an incident postmortem and a product launch decision. Select a passage Assign @Code , @Data , or @General (expertise label) Separately choose assignment access: Repository , Metrics , or Editorial Ratiflow maps that choice to a capability grant and registers the matching WebMCP catalog The agent updates only the selection; Flight Recorder + History keep the proof Product rule: bot name is not permission. The same @Code identity gets different tools when access switches from Repository → Editorial. During a managed run, the page withdraws the idle BYO-agent catalog and restores it after. Demo sources are deterministic fixtures so judges can replay the same path. Server authority (range, lease, revision, evidence) is the security boundary; the visible catalog only guides the agent. 90-second demo Open completed INC-482 postmortem doc at the live URL Assign @Code + Repository scoped edit Watch Flight Recorder: catalog → tool calls → commit Keep @Code , switch to Editorial scoped edit → different catalog Open History → inspect diff / Restore How we built it Next.js · React · TypeScript · Supabase/Postgres · Vercel Dynamic document.modelContext registration with generation-scoped catalogs Two mutually exclusive surfaces: idle BYO-agent tools vs managed-assignment tools Application-owned Luna ↔ WebMCP relay (Responses API tool search → browser getTools / executeTool ); credentials stay server-side Server enforcement of identity, access, document range, and source revision Full Markdown snapshots with digests, diffs, and Restore Challenges we ran into Connecting a server-side model to live browser WebMCP tools (discovery, execute, cancel, retry, stale descriptors). WebMCP has no pub/sub, so mentions wake the open page; long unattended runs are out of scope by design. Catalog visibility is guidance only—permissions are enforced on the server. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Live, judge-runnable WebMCP workspace with coach + Flight Recorder Capability grants as product: same agent identity, different access → different registered tool catalog Application-owned Luna↔WebMCP relay with fail-closed stale-tool handling Immutable revisions with prompt, sources, authorship, diff, and Restore Narrow scope: two document types, deterministic fixtures, reproducible demo Open-sourced under MIT What we learned WebMCP is not “MCP in the browser” and not a fixed API. The valuable unit is a live, task-scoped tool surface . Designing the handoff—human chooses grant → page registers tools → agent acts → human reviews proof—mattered more than adding more tools. Treat the catalog as UX and the server as authority. What’s next for Ratiflow Polish editor UX, add ChatGPT in-app browser smoke notes for judges, and expand fixture-backed evals around catalog switching and stale-tool rejection. Stay narrow: capability grants + reversible proof for high-stakes docs—not a general collab suite. title: KOTOAGE — "Le Petit Donjon"
pitch: A 3D dungeon played by two: you at the keyboard, an AI co-game-master acting inside the game via WebMCP. It opens walls, sets traps, summons guardians. Strength is never given, it is unlocked.
about_excerpt: A 3D dungeon played by two: you at the keyboard, an AI co-game-master acting inside the game via WebMCP. It opens walls, sets traps, summons guardians. Strength is never given, it is unlocked. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Tabletop role-playing games have a human game master who reacts to the players: opens a secret passage, springs a trap, throws in a monster when the party gets comfortable. Video games lost that. WebMCP gave me a way to bring it back: an AI agent that does not just talk about the game, but changes it, through a contract the browser itself exposes. The rule of the world comes from the anime Baki and That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime : strength is never given, it is unlocked. So the co-game-master never hands out free wins. It sets trials. What it does KOTOAGE is a small 3D dungeon (Three.js, WebGL) with a hamlet and five floors. The player explores, fights, levels up (XP, four stats, skill points). When the page runs in a WebMCP-capable browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), the game registers 8 tools on document.modelContext . An agent can then discover them and act on the live game state: Tool Real effect in the game etat_joueur reads health, mana, floor, gear, counters donner_potion heals the player (small +2, large +6), shown on the HUD ouvrir_mur turns a wall cell into floor; the 3D walls are rebuilt placer_piege places a trap on a floor cell inspirer gives a contextual hint about the place or the floor defier spawns real enemies (guardian, warrior, horde) raconter narrates a floor (1 to 5, 0 = the hamlet) braignak_etude asks Braignak, the dungeon's watcher, for one of his five studies — or gives him a new one to run Every successful call is announced to the player by the "voice of the world" on the HUD. The in-game chat also forwards the player's requests to the co-game-master when the WebMCP bridge is active. Without WebMCP, the game runs exactly the same: the bridge adds zero dependency to rendering. Braignak, the watcher — the eighth tool is a character Braignak is one of our own agents, and his job outside the game is the one he keeps inside it: he looks, and he reports. He never touches anything. In the dungeon he floats beside the player and repeats aloud what the co-game-master just did. The eighth tool interrogates him. He has already led five studies in this dungeon — the walls that open, the guardian of the landing, the traps, the potions, where strength comes from — and answers from his own work. Give him a subject he has never studied and he leaves you: he walks around the room, thinking, then comes back, tells you what he counted, once , and forgets it. How I built it index.html is a self-contained ES module (Three.js + WebGL). It exposes a small bridge window.__webmcpConnexion (grid, player, walls, traps, creatures, HUD). webmcp/webmcp.js is the pure contract layer: tool names, JSON schemas, validation, no DOM. webmcp/integration.js wires the contract to the live game when document.modelContext exists: a Proxy on the grid, accessors on health, traps and challenges. Each agent call becomes a real world change. Hosting: a public Google Cloud Storage bucket, HTTPS, no server. Proof, with zero dependencies: 35 contract tests, 15 integration tests on a DOM harness, 8 tests on the chat bridge, and a real-browser check ( tests/test_webmcp_live_cdp.py ) that launches headless Chrome over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, loads the live URL, and verifies the 7 tools are registered and that etat_joueur and donner_potion change the game state. Challenges I ran into Proving it in a real browser, not just in unit tests: I wrote a tiny CDP client by hand (WebSocket handshake, masked frames) because I wanted a proof with no dependency. Keeping the game intact when WebMCP is absent: the integration layer must do nothing, and that is tested. Making the agent a game master, not a cheat code: the tools give trials (walls, traps, enemies, hints), and the chat bridge answers with an action, never a gift. Accomplishments that I'm proud of 7 tools, each with a visible, physical effect in a 3D world. 46 automated proofs, plus a live-browser check on the hosted page. A game that stays fully playable without WebMCP. What I learned WebMCP turns a web page into something an agent can do things to , not just read. The hard part is not registering tools, it is deciding what an agent should be allowed to change so that the experience stays a game. What's next structuredContent on every tool result (the official recommendation). Letting the co-game-master read the player's progression (level, stats) to scale the trials. A VR version of the same dungeon, same tools. Built during the submission period (project existed before August 25) The dungeon itself (3D world, hamlet, floors, combat) existed before. Added between August 25 and September 3: the whole WebMCP layer ( webmcp/webmcp.js , webmcp/integration.js , the 7 tools), the chat bridge to the co-game-master, the progression loop (XP, level, four stats), the test suite, the live-browser CDP check, the Google Cloud Storage deployment and the public repository. Testing instructions Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. No login needed. Click to enter the dungeon (keyboard: arrows or ZQSD / WASD to move). Ask the agent, for example: "Read the player state", "Give me a small potion", "Open the wall north of me", "Challenge me with a guardian", "Tell me the story of floor 2". Watch the HUD: every tool call is announced by the voice of the world, and the 3D world changes (wall opens, enemy appears, health goes up). To reproduce the proofs locally: python tests/test_webmcp.py , python tests/test_webmcp_integration.py , python tests/test_webmcp_live_cdp.py <url> .
