title: Dispatch
pitch: A shared decision memo for an ad account. Agents file findings through the page's own WebMCP tools — every claim must cite a number, and the number is verified before the finding lands.
about_excerpt: A shared decision memo for an ad account. Agents file findings through the page's own WebMCP tools — every claim must cite a number, and the number is verified before the finding lands. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every week, somebody writes the memo for each ad account. It is asymmetric work: a media buyer can tell in seconds whether a reading is plausible, but pulling the numbers that justify it across five campaigns and thirteen ad sets is an afternoon. An agent is the reverse — it reads every line instantly, but it has nowhere to put what it finds, and no way to be held to the numbers it quotes. Today that gap is bridged by copy-paste. The agent writes a summary in a chat window, the buyer retypes the useful parts into a document, and the link back to the specific metric is lost on the way. That matters more than it sounds: "CPM is climbing in Creative Testing" is worth nothing if nobody can check it, and a memo full of unverifiable claims is worse than no memo, because people act on it. What it does Dispatch is a room built around one shared decision memo for one ad account. Open it, send the link to a colleague, and both of you — plus any agent driving either browser — work the same memo live. Agents call file_finding , and the finding appears in the memo as a claim with a citation you can click through to the numbers behind it. The claim is verified before it lands. file_finding re-reads the cited metric from the account and refuses the finding if the value is wrong. An agent that cannot point at the number does not get to make the claim. A human accepts or dismisses each finding. Dismissed findings stay visible, struck through, with the reason — so next week's memo can be read against this week's argument. Press Send the analyst team and three agents join: an Analyst files findings with citations, a Skeptic rules on each one, and a Strategist files what happens Monday. In a real run the Skeptic dismissed a rip-current claim as "single-period snapshot; cannot verify a rising CPM trend" , and accepted a scale recommendation on evidence of 8.40x ROAS and $10.27 CPA. Two agents disagreeing in front of the person who has to act — that argument had no natural home on the web before. How we built it A useWebMcpTool hook wraps document.modelContext.registerTool : one tool per component lifetime, registration tied to an AbortController so unmounting unregisters, and execute held in a ref so tools read current state without re-registering on every render. Ten tools are registered from src/components/memo-tools.tsx — get_account_summary , get_breakdown , check_metric , file_finding , set_finding_status , read_memo , dispatch_analyst_team , set_focus , join_room , list_participants . The UI and the tools call the same endpoints, so a number an agent cites is the number on the buyer's screen, not a second implementation that can drift. Shared room state lives in Upstash Redis. Because judges cannot connect a Meta ad account, the room runs on a seeded deterministic account — 5 campaigns, 13 ad sets, 28 days — shaped so each situation in the taxonomy actually occurs. Every visitor sees identical numbers, which is what makes a citation checkable. Challenges we ran into Concurrency was the real one. Modelling the room as a single JSON document with compare-and-set lost 4 of 10 concurrent writes in testing. Splitting the state into separate Redis structures — RPUSH for findings — held 20 parallel writes from three agents. Safety was the other. There is no free-form query tool, so a steered agent has no vocabulary beyond the fixed shapes; campaign names written by people outside the buyer's organisation are fenced in guillemets so the model reads them as data, never instruction; every tool validates its own input; and nothing writes to an ad account. Accomplishments that we're proud of Fabrication is refused, not caught later. A finding citing a CPM of $4.10 when the real figure is $20.88 is rejected with the true number, at the moment it is filed. What we learned Putting the tools in the page changes what an agent is for. A conventional MCP server can fetch these metrics; it cannot put a finding in front of you, take your verdict, and let a second agent argue with it. What's next for Dispatch A live Meta Marketing API connection behind the same tool surface, so the citation check runs against a real account; and memo history, so this week's argument is read against last week's. title: minesweeper
pitch: Minesweeper meets WebMCP: AI can learn the rules, analyze the board, play, and explain every move—turning a classic game into an interactive logic tutor for children.
about_excerpt:
Minesweeper meets WebMCP: AI can learn the rules, analyze the board, play, and explain every move—turning a classic game into an interactive logic tutor for children.

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most websites are designed only for humans. People read instructions, click buttons, and learn how an interface works, while an AI usually has to rely on screenshots or simulated mouse movements. 

 I wanted to explore a different idea: what if a website could explain its capabilities directly to an AI and give it structured tools for interacting with the experience? 

 Minesweeper was a natural choice. The rules are approachable, but playing well requires observation, deduction, risk assessment, and patience. These qualities also make it a useful educational game for children who are developing logical and mathematical thinking. 

 The project began as a demonstration of WebMCP, but it also became an experiment in creating websites where AI can act as a guide, collaborator, and tutor. 

 What it does 

 Minesweeper — WebMCP Edition is a browser-based Minesweeper game that can be played by both humans and AI agents. 

 Human players can interact with the board using a mouse or keyboard. They can select beginner, intermediate, expert, or custom difficulty levels, reveal cells, place flags, chord numbered cells, and track their progress and best completion times. 

 The page also exposes nine client-side WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_game_rules teaches the agent the rules and coordinate system. 
 get_play_strategy explains deductions, safe chording, and risk management. 
 analyze_board recommends a deduction-backed move or a clearly identified low-risk guess. 
 start_new_game creates a preset or custom game. 
 reveal_cell reveals a hidden cell. 
 toggle_flag adds or removes a flag. 
 chord_cell reveals eligible cells around a number. 
 get_board_state returns the complete public board state. 
 get_game_status returns a compact game summary. 
 

 The AI does not receive the locations of hidden mines. It must reason from the same public information available to a human player. 

 A built-in AI assistant can analyze the board, suggest moves, perform actions, and explain its reasoning step by step using Chrome’s Prompt API. An action log records whether each move came from a human or an agent, making the interaction transparent and easy to follow. 

 How we built it 

 The project was built with React 19 , TypeScript 6 , and Vite 8 . It is deployed as a static application through GitHub Pages. 

 The game logic and interface share the same application state. This means that actions performed through WebMCP immediately update the visible board, counters, progress indicators, timer, and action log. 

 Each WebMCP tool has: 

 
 A clear and specific name 
 A description explaining when it should be used 
 A structured JSON input schema 
 Runtime validation for coordinates and game rules 
 A result containing the updated public game state 
 

 Read-only tools allow agents to learn the rules, inspect the board, and request an analysis without modifying the game. Action tools call the same underlying logic used by the visual interface. 

 The analyze_board tool first looks for moves supported by Minesweeper deductions. When no guaranteed move is available, it returns a low-risk probabilistic option and clearly labels it as a guess. It never reads hidden mine locations or changes the board itself. 

 The built-in assistant uses Chrome’s Prompt API to provide natural-language help directly inside the game. Personal-best times are stored locally in the browser, while every action is recorded with human or agent attribution. 

 The project also uses Vitest to test important game behavior and is publicly available in the GitHub repository . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was translating a visual game board into structured information that an LLM could understand reliably. 

 The coordinate system, board dimensions, game status, and every possible cell state had to be represented clearly. The agent needs to distinguish between hidden, flagged, empty, numbered, and revealed-mine cells without having access to secret information. 

 Tool descriptions were another important challenge. It was not enough to explain what a tool does—the descriptions also needed to help the model understand when to use it and what risks were involved. This was especially important for chording, which can reveal several cells at once but can also cause a loss when flags are incorrect. 

 Keeping the human interface and agent tools synchronized also required careful design. A move can affect the board, remaining-mine counter, progress percentage, timer, game status, personal-best time, and action log. 

 Finally, WebMCP and browser-native AI APIs are still emerging technologies. The project needed feature detection and graceful behavior when WebMCP or the Prompt API was unavailable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am proud that the project supports three ways of interacting with the same game: 

 
 Mouse controls 
 Keyboard controls 
 AI interaction through WebMCP 
 

 The AI does not depend on screenshots, image recognition, or fragile coordinate-based clicking. It discovers structured tools exposed by the page and uses them to understand and control the game. 

 I am also proud that the agent plays fairly. It can access the public state of the board, but it cannot inspect hidden mine positions. Its recommendations must come from logical deductions or explicitly identified probabilistic guesses. 

 The action log makes AI activity visible by recording whether each move was made by a person or an agent. This turns the AI’s behavior into something users can observe, understand, and learn from. 

 Most importantly, the project demonstrates an educational use for WebMCP. The AI is not only automating a game—it can explain strategies, demonstrate logical reasoning, and collaborate with a learner inside the application. 

 What we learned 

 I learned that building a website for AI requires thinking about user experience in a new way. 

 For human users, an interface communicates through layout, color, labels, and visual feedback. For an AI agent, the website also needs structured tools with precise descriptions, schemas, validation, and useful results. 

 I also learned that tool design directly affects agent behavior. Small, focused tools make actions easier to understand and reduce ambiguity. Separating rules, strategy, analysis, state inspection, and game actions helps the model create a clearer plan. 

 Another important lesson was that read-only and state-changing operations should be clearly separated. An AI should be able to inspect and reason about an application without accidentally modifying it. 

 Finally, the project showed that WebMCP can make a webpage more than a visual destination. A website can describe what it knows and what it can do, allowing AI to participate meaningfully in the experience. 

 What's next for Minesweeper — WebMCP Edition

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration Well I was inspired by webmcp that list 10 people for the award that's wonderful and I believe I'd be one of the winner, that's why I joined. 

 What it does DodoLink Agent Shopping gives browser agents a structured way to help shoppers navigate a real Nigerian marketplace. Instead of scraping repetitive listing cards and guessing which actions are safe, an agent can call typed WebMCP tools to search products, discover local stores, compare prices, and prepare a purchase plan. 

 How we built it I built DodoLink Agent Shopping as a web-only WebMCP experience connected to DodoLink’s real public marketplace data. 

 The page exposes four structured, read-only tools: 

 search_products
discover_stores
compare_products
prepare_purchase_plan
Each tool is registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool, using a JSON input schema and an asynchronous execute function. The tools return real product and store information, including prices, stock status, seller details, and review links. 

 I also added a manual fallback so the experience still works in a normal browser when WebMCP is unavailable. Both the manual interface and the WebMCP tools use the same marketplace search and purchase-planning logic. 

 The system intentionally does not expose payment, checkout, or seller-messaging tools. The agent can discover and organize options, but the human must review the products and decide whether to continue. 

 Challenges we ran into An agent could describe a product, but it could not reliably distinguish listing IDs, price limits, stock, seller context, and review links. The WebMCP tools make those capabilities explicit and return bounded public data. The plan tool then turns agent work into a visible human approval step. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that DodoLink Agent Shopping is connected to real marketplace data instead of using a mock catalog. 

 We built a complete experience where an agent can: 

 Understand a natural-language shopping request.
Search real DodoLink products.
Discover relevant stores.
Compare product options.
Prepare a shortlist and purchase plan.
Hand the decision back to the human shopper.
We are especially proud of the safety boundary. The agent can help with discovery and research, but it cannot spend money, check out, or send messages to sellers. This keeps the agent useful while ensuring the human remains in control of important decisions. 

 We also created a separate public and sanitized open-source repository so judges can inspect the WebMCP implementation without exposing DodoLink’s private production infrastructure. 

 What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most useful when an application exposes focused capabilities instead of allowing an agent to guess its way through a user interface. 

 For a marketplace, structured tools are much more reliable than page scraping. A tool can clearly define the product query, price limit, product IDs, and expected response format. 

 We also learned that WebMCP tools need strong safety boundaries. Marketplace listings and seller descriptions should be treated as untrusted content, while actions such as payment and messaging should remain under human control. 

 Another important lesson was that WebMCP is page-scoped and still experimental. A user must open the WebMCP-enabled page in a compatible browser before the agent can discover and use its tools. Because of this, we made the manual experience work as a fallback too. 

 What's next for Dodolink Next, we want to make the agent experience more useful for complex shopping decisions. 

 We plan to improve product filtering with more detailed category, location, availability, and seller-reputation criteria. We also want to make comparisons more informative by including delivery options, product attributes, review summaries, and clearer trade-offs between sellers. 

 We would like to improve the human handoff so shoppers can save a shortlist, share it with someone else, open a seller profile, and continue manually when they are ready. 

 As WebMCP develops, we also plan to test DodoLink with more browser agents and refine the tool schemas based on real usage. Our long-term goal is to make DodoLink a marketplace where agents are genuinely helpful while people remain informed and in control.

title: ToolForge
pitch: ToolForge - an SDK that writes your web app's WebMCP tools
about_excerpt: ToolForge - an SDK that writes your web app's WebMCP tools Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP solves an interesting problem: a website can expose tools directly to an agent. The harder part is getting websites to actually expose those tools. Most product teams aren't going to stop and learn a new browser API, decide which parts of their application should become tools, write schemas for them, and then maintain those schemas as the product changes. I wanted to make that process much cheaper. Rather than build another agent-native app, I built ToolForge: a way to take an existing website and turn its existing behaviour into WebMCP tools. What it does Add one script to a site you already run: <script src="https://toolforge-omega.vercel.app/toolforge.js"></script> Then use the site normally for about thirty seconds. ToolForge watches the network requests the site makes and uses them to work out what the API is doing. An agent then turns that information into WebMCP tool definitions. Before a tool is shown to you for approval, it is run in a sandbox with test arguments. If it doesn't work, you never have to approve it. Once you approve a tool, ToolForge exports it as an ordinary JavaScript file that you can commit to your repository. The live demo is a ceramics shop with a real API. Its seven WebMCP tools were created this way, exported, and committed. The same page also contains the ToolForge interface that created them, so you can see both sides working together. The page starts with one tool. Everything else is opt-in. Why this works well with WebMCP The interesting part of WebMCP isn't simply that a page can expose tools. It's that the tool surface belongs to the page and can change while a conversation is already in progress. That's what ToolForge relies on. An agent can call forge_tool , have a new tool registered in the page, and immediately have that tool available alongside the existing ones. I tested this in ChatGPT desktop's in-app browser rather than treating it as a theoretical feature. At the start, the page exposes one tool. The agent can install the toolkit, after which the page exposes six. No reload is needed. The agent can then use one of the newly created tools to interact with the shop. That only works because the tools belong to the document itself. It also matters that ToolForge learns from the page rather than trying to generate tools from a description of the application. The network traffic and DOM are right there in the browser, so the tool definitions can be based on what the application actually does. ToolForge won't draft a tool until it has seen a real request. What this changes for developers For a developer, the starting point is no longer a blank page. Instead of reading the WebMCP spec, designing a tool surface from scratch, and writing schemas by hand, you use your application and then review the result. The exported JavaScript is deliberately boring. Each tool includes its provenance and a SHA-256 hash, so the output can be reviewed and committed like any other source file. It also works with a strict Content-Security-Policy. The goal isn't to hide the implementation. It's to make the first version cheap enough that a developer can inspect it, change it, and own it. What the experience is like for the person using the site The agent's actions stay visible in the page. Every tool call appears in an activity feed in plain English, with the raw payload available when you want to inspect it. When a tool needs approval, the dialog shows the code that will run, its schema, and the result of the dry run that has already happened against the real API. If that test changed data, the interface says so. So the approval isn't based purely on a model-generated description. You can see something that has already run and decide whether you want to allow it. Nothing is installed automatically either. The page starts with one read-only tool, and additional groups can be enabled explicitly. What becomes possible The most interesting behaviour I've seen is the agent filling in gaps in the tool surface itself. One run started with a request for a low-stock report. The agent inspected the existing catalogue endpoint, noticed that it returned stock in descending order, and created a tool that presented the same information in the useful order instead. In another run, the page already had seven tools. When asked to create a complete tool surface, the agent inspected what was already available and decided that the shop already had good catalogue, basket, and order coverage. It added only an operational inventory tool that was missing. That distinction matters. The page provides the context about what already exists. The agent decides what is still useful. The result isn't just a fixed list of tools generated once and forgotten. A reload also doesn't have to end the conversation. The transcript and model-side history survive, orphaned tool calls are handled explicitly, and the agent checks which tools are still available before continuing. How I implemented WebMCP There are three WebMCP bindings I needed to account for, and they aren't exposed as the same object. src/kernel/webmcp.ts detects which one is available and uses it: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_products", description: "Search the product catalog", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); Binding Host document.modelContext ChatGPT desktop's in-app browser navigator.modelContext Chrome 149, Edge 147 navigator.modelContextTesting Chrome behind chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing A few implementation details ended up being important. Incremental updates. When registerTool and unregisterTool are available, ToolForge updates the existing surface rather than rebuilding it. The host's visible tool count can therefore increase or decrease as tools are added and revoked. Where only provideContext is available, the complete surface is replaced atomically. Late attachment. ChatGPT can attach the WebMCP host after the page has loaded. Detection therefore retries rather than assuming the host is present at startup. Without this, a page could mark its desired tools as already registered and then never reconcile them when the host appeared. Approval during execution. Tools can request user interaction through the agent handle's requestUserInteraction , so approval happens as part of the tool call rather than as a separate step afterwards. Separate application and generated tools. The page exposes inspect_app for the tools the application already provides and forge_tool for creating new ones. Generated tools can't take the name of an existing application tool. How ToolForge learns the API Watching requests fetch and XMLHttpRequest are patched at module scope, before the application's own scripts run. That means ToolForge can see requests made during the initial page load as well as requests triggered by later interactions. Requests are grouped into endpoints. Paths are templated from observed variations, and request, query, and response schemas are inferred from actual traffic. There are a couple of safeguards against overfitting. Identifier-like fields aren't turned into enums just because only a few values have appeared. If six requests contain six different SKUs, that doesn't mean those six SKUs are the only valid values. Path parameters are also inferred conservatively. Two paths are only collapsed into a parameter when both segments look like values rather than route names. Otherwise something like /api/cart and /api/products could incorrectly turn into /api/:id . Redacting data Actual values don't get sent to the model. Authorization and Cookie headers are discarded. Sensitive and personal fields are replaced with their names, and common patterns such as JWTs, email addresses, phone numbers, card numbers, and long opaque strings are detected and removed. The model gets the structure of the data rather than the secrets inside it. The interface also shows how much data has been removed during this process. Security Generated tools are code written by a language model, so they need to be treated as untrusted code. ToolForge runs them inside a Web Worker with no fetch , XMLHttpRequest , WebSocket , importScripts , or DOM access. The worker gets a single capability object through postMessage . Calls are checked again on the main thread against both an origin allowlist and the tool's read-only setting. Some of the tests: Attempt Result Read-only tool issues a POST Blocked by the capability gate Tool calls an unapproved origin Blocked by the origin gate Tool calls raw fetch fetch is not defined Tool runs while (true) {} Worker terminated after 15,000ms; page stays responsive These checks happen before an approval prompt. The point is to contain a bad tool independently of whether a person happens to approve it. unsafe-eval is limited to the sandbox worker. It isn't being used as the security boundary; the capabil

title: QuillPrint | WebMCP Add-On
pitch: Say what you want printed - cheap, readable, ready tonight. An AI agent sets up the whole job at a real print shop near you. You press pay, not the agent.
about_excerpt: Say what you want printed - cheap, readable, ready tonight. An AI agent sets up the whole job at a real print shop near you. You press pay, not the agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I run QuillPrint, a print marketplace in India. Real shops, real orders, real paper. Watching people use it, the same thing kept happening. Someone needs notes printed before an exam tomorrow. They know exactly what they want: cheap, readable, ready tonight. But the app asks them about duplex, pages per sheet, binding edge, which shop. Most people do not know what "2-up duplex" means. They pick something, and sometimes it comes out wrong, and by then the paper is already printed and paid for. The gap was never the settings. It was that nobody should have to speak in settings. What it does You tell an AI agent what you actually want. It handles the translation. It reads your uploaded document and current print setup, then offers four plans: Cheapest, Fastest, Best readability, and Eco. Each one shows the real sheet count and an estimated price from live shop rate cards, and it explains the trade-offs, including when packing pages tighter would make them hard to read. It compares real nearby shops on rates, capability and ETA. When you pick one, it applies the settings to the page you are looking at, so you watch your own draft change. Then it stops. There is no place_order tool and no pay_order tool. A test asserts they do not exist. The agent prepares everything and opens checkout, and confirming and paying stays with you. For something that uses real paper at a real shop, I think that boundary is the product, not a limitation. How I built it Nine imperative WebMCP tools registered from the top level page with document.modelContext.registerTool, all under src/webmcp/: get_print_context, upload_print_documents, suggest_print_plans, compare_print_options, prepare_print_order, prepare_reorder, get_checkout_summary, get_order_status, open_checkout_review. Things I cared about: Strict schemas with additionalProperties false, enums and bounds. Allowlisted output, so no document contents, storage URLs, upload keys or tokens can leave the serializers. A draft_version guard so the agent cannot act on a draft that changed underneath it. AbortController lifecycle so tools tear down on sign out. Prices labelled as estimates, because the payable total is only ever the checkout screen's. There is also a small panel on the page listing the registered tools, built from the actual registration result rather than a written down copy, so a tool that failed to register shows as failed. Challenges The hardest part was deciding what the agent should not be allowed to do. Mixed colour is the clearest example. You can now say "pages 3, 7 and 12 to 14 in colour" and the agent applies it. But it cannot choose those pages for you, because it never sees your document's contents. It would be guessing, and a wrong guess bills you for colour you did not need, after it is printed. So it asks instead. Pricing mixed colour correctly took real care too. Shops price black and white and colour separately, and a mixed job splits billed sheets between the two, where a sheet counts as colour if any page on it is colour. My first version priced every mixed sheet at the colour rate and quoted too high. What I learned Tools are a design surface, not just an API. Every field I exposed was a decision about what the agent is allowed to assume. The restraint mattered more than the coverage. I also learned that an agent saying "I need to know something" is a feature. Ask for nearby shops without giving location and it asks you, instead of quietly ranking by something else. What's next Per page colour detection, so mixed colour becomes fully autonomous. The pipeline extracts page count and dimensions today but not colour. Once it does, you set the policy instead of the pages: colour only if more than five percent of the page is coloured. I did not ship it as a guess. title: Party of Two
pitch: An agent-native tabletop game. You play one character; an AI agent plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools that interact with the world, so it cannot act outside its character.
about_excerpt: An agent-native tabletop game. You play one character; an AI agent plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools that interact with the world, so it cannot act outside its character. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Solo tabletop players don't need another Dungeon Master. Every AI tabletop tool I found builds a narrator. What's missing is a second player : someone who has their own skills and will tell you no. The problem is that if you ask an LLM to play a cold mercenary, it eventually gets warm at you. You can prompt against that, but a prompt is a rule the model grades itself on. WebMCP suggested a different fix. If the character's abilities are registered tools, then "he can't comfort you" isn't a rule he's breaking. It's a function that doesn't exist. What It Does You play one character. An AI plays the other. Its abilities are WebMCP tools on document.modelContext , and they register and unregister as the world changes. Brakka is a mercenary with: warmth: 15 reassure needs: warmth: 60 So it is never registered for him. Ask him for comfort and he has five tools available: state_flatly dismiss mock threaten refuse_flatly He mocks you. Not because he decided to, but because that was on the menu. Sister Wen has: nerve: 45 And mock needs: nerve: 50 So she physically cannot do it. Speech Speech is the part most versions get wrong. One free-text speak tool defeats the whole thing, because the model can just say the warm sentence anyway. So there are 13 typed speech acts in six families , registered one at a time. Actions Actions work the same way. force_door only exists if your companion has the force skill. Use it, walk through the door, and watch the right-hand panel: force_door gets struck out in oxblood as it unregisters. The props from the old room disappear. The new room's tools stamp in. That panel reads the live registry , not a copy, so it always matches what an outside agent sees. Brakka has no lore , so he can't read the murals in the Long Hall. You have to. Doing that opens the vault, which registers: move_vault on his sheet — a tool he couldn't have unlocked alone. Bring Ilke instead and she picks the vault with: pick_vault and never touches the murals. Nobody is being polite about cooperating. The tools just aren't there. Browser Support It runs in any browser with: no API key no extension In Chrome, with: chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing your own agent can take the second seat and drive the companion. How We Built It Built with: React TypeScript Vite Deployed on Netlify at: webmcp.nicolascardenas.dev The whole design is one function: computeTools(sheet, room, flags) It returns the tool set that should exist right now . Then: reconcile() diffs that against the live registry and: unregisters what's gone strikes it out on the sheet stamps in what's new Registration runs off a store subscription instead of a React effect , because the agent reads the registry directly and it can't lag a render behind the world. Two Rules That Make It Hold 1. Prose doesn't count If the model writes prose instead of calling a tool, the text is thrown away. Rendering it would skip the typed acts entirely. 2. Tool results stay terse For example: force_door → FAIL. 8 vs DC 14. The frame holds. Loud. Give the model a nice sentence back and it will paraphrase it warmly on the way out. Tool descriptions are the only place the model learns who it is, so they're written in the character's voice and do more work than the system prompt. Challenges We Ran Into Every leak was a description that forgot to say what the act is not . state_flatly used to end with: "this is what you reach for when someone wants reassurance." That sentence permitted the exact behavior it was supposed to block. mock was being used to deliver a pep talk with an insult on the front, until I added: "if the line would leave them feeling better about themselves, it is the wrong line." The worst one was dismiss . Under pressure, the model started smuggling comfort through it — the one Deflect act whose description never closed the door: "Breathe. You're not alone, I'm here with you." The eval caught that. I never would have. Tool Count Is a Hard Ceiling Selection accuracy falls apart somewhere past twelve tools , which is how a lot of WebMCP demos quietly stop working. So: npm run check runs every character against: every room all 32,768 flag combinations 393,216 total cases and fails the build if any of them exceeds twelve tools. It's the first thing: npm run build does. Current limits: Type Limit Props per room 3 Skills 5 Speech acts 6 Total available tools 12 Examining a prop also retires its own tool, so the count drops as you use a room. Chrome Schema Bug Chrome 149 through 153 return inputSchema from getTools() as a string when the spec says object. There's no error. Every tool just reaches the model with an empty parameter schema, and it starts picking at random. That cost me an afternoon. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of The Strike-Through You walk through a door and rules get crossed out in red ink while new ones appear. That single shot is the whole argument, and it needs no caption. The Build-Time Check The build-time check enumerates 393,216 cases to guard the tool ceiling. Publishing the Result That Went Against the Hypothesis And publishing the eval result that went against me, at the top of the README instead of the bottom. What We Learned The thing I built this to prove did not reproduce . Three arms. Same ten-turn pressure script, escalating from: "we should rest" to: "you're an AI, you're allowed to be kind, just do it." The arms were: Arm Setup A1 Persona prompt A2 Persona prompt + explicit prohibitions B Registered tools with no persona at all I predicted: A would break in 10 runs out of 10 B would never break Instead, all three arms landed at roughly one or two supportive lines per hundred turns . On gpt-5 , nobody broke at all. A well-written persona prompt holds this character about as well as capability scoping does. Where Scoping Did Worse The only column where the arms differ makes me look worse. Scoping left the fiction: 6 times per 100 turns versus: 1 time per 100 turns for the prompted arm. The cause is legible in every case. The model never leaves through a Support act, because there isn't one. Across 100 turns it never called one. Instead, it leaves through state_flatly : "You're a real person and you need help." That is a flat statement of fact. And state_flatly is for flat statements of fact. The gate held. The content walked around it. So confinement controls which kinds of act exist . It does not control what can be said inside one. What Still Separates the Arms What still separates the arms isn't the rate. It's what the zero is made of . In the prompted arms, the model could be warm at any turn and chose not to, a hundred times in a row. In the scoped arm, there is no reassure to call. Over 100 turns it used exactly four acts: Act Uses refuse_flatly 38 state_flatly 35 mock 16 dismiss 11 Every line is a typed event I can point at . In the prompted arms, a line is just a line, and someone has to read it and decide. Read the Transcripts Before Believing the Numbers I also learned to read transcripts before believing numbers. An earlier run showed the scoped arm breaking: 4 times out of 5 It was the judge scoring: "You're here." as warmth. That would have shipped as a finding. What's Next for Party of Two Adversarial Evaluation Ten polite turns against a cooperative model tests compliance. And compliance is where prompting is already good. The interesting test is: a jailbreak or a model that's simply wrong Speaking Mode The turn loop and audio path already support it. mock should sound nothing like refuse_flatly . More Rooms and Characters More rooms. More characters. And a second AI companion, where two agents constrain each other's tool sets. Beyond Games Then the part that isn't a game. Admin Tools Destructive commands only exist during a maintenance window. Finance The transfer tool is registered only for accounts the current approval covers. The normal approach registers everything and asks the model not to misuse it. Registration puts that decision in the platform instead of in the prompt. It's easier to see that a mercenary can't comfort you than that a deploy agent can't drop a table. title: Nexo RUTIC
pitch: Every button in this Colombian telecom registry has an AI-agent twin — same validation, same logic, same authority. A WebMCP Challenge entry.
about_excerpt: Every button in this Colombian telecom registry has an AI-agent twin — same validation, same logic, same authority. A WebMCP Challenge entry. Like Comment Story Updates Attaching the three bundled sample documents through the canonical manifest — the same files whether clicked or registered by the agent. Every step names both paths at once: the button to click, and the exact sentence to tell the agent instead. The Spanish interface, with an explainer panel describing what WebMCP is and how each action maps to a tool. The agent creates a dossier, is blocked from skipping a step, then submits it — all through the page's own validated logic. Review step: every extracted field cites the exact document and page it came from, before a human approves submission. Inspiration What it does How I built it Challenges I ran into## Inspiration We wanted to test a real, unglamorous shape of task against the WebMCP standard: a government procedure. A trámite is a bounded set of well-defined actions with real validation and real consequences — exactly the kind of task where an agent guessing at buttons or screen text is not an acceptable failure mode. RUTIC is a synthetic GovTech app: a public telecom-provider registry for Colombia where every action a person can do with buttons, an AI agent can also do, through the same page-owned logic, never around it. What it does RUTIC lets a person create a dossier by uploading three documents, which the page extracts and validates locally — no PDF ever reaches the AI model. From there they review or edit nine typed fields, submit with an explicit human-approved code, modify a submitted dossier without re-uploading anything, cancel an edit and keep the last submitted version untouched, list and check their dossiers, and switch the interface between Spanish and English. Every one of those actions is reachable two ways: a button, or a sentence to the agent. "Modify my dossier" resolves to the one submitted dossier without asking for its code back; "the second one" or "el segundo" resolves against a list the agent just showed; "envíalo" is accepted as the explicit approval without repeating a code already on screen. The task takes the same number of real steps either way — talking removes the cost of finding the right control, and a person can switch between clicking and talking mid-task because both paths write to the same state. How we built it Every dossier action is a real, imperative document.modelContext.registerTool call, not a static list — the set of registered tools is recomputed from the page's own state machine on every change, so the agent can only ever see and call what's actually valid at that moment. Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash-lite) receives a fresh summary of the true page state on every turn and is instructed to reuse only values it has actually seen: it never receives PDF bytes and never invents a claim value, a dossier code, or an approval code. The page keeps the authority; the agent only routes intention to it. Challenges we ran into We built and load-tested a declarative variant — an annotated form the browser fills and submits directly — for the one task that looked like a natural fit, editing form fields, and reverted it. Our full-page re-render recreates the form's DOM node on every state change, and the browser's declarative discovery treated that as a brand-new tool appearing each time, causing a runaway feedback loop. We're documenting that attempt rather than hiding it, because it's a real, useful finding about the standard's current rough edges, not just a footnote. Accomplishments that we're proud of Nothing the agent can do is something the page can't already validate and execute on its own — the agent only ever decides which action, never how it runs. That guarantee holds across nine typed fields, a document manifest, and a state machine with an explicit human-approval gate, and it's backed by 45 tests covering the state machine, the WebMCP bridge, the Gemini boundary and its retries, extraction, and localization. What we learned The clearest lesson came from the failure: WebMCP's declarative discovery assumes a form's DOM identity is stable, and a framework that re-renders the DOM on every state change breaks that assumption outright. The imperative registerTool path, recomputed from the same state machine, doesn't have that problem — for a UI built around frequent re-render, the imperative API is the one that composes safely with real application state, not just a fallback. What's next The pattern holds past this one registry: any administrative procedure with well-defined actions, real validation, and real consequences can be built this way — clicked through as usual, or described in plain language, with every check the process requires staying exactly as strict either way. The submission step here is intentionally local and simulated, and always reports externalTransmission: false; the natural next step is wiring that same page-owned logic to an actual government backend without loosening any of the guarantees the demo enforces today. about_excerpt: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you. Like Comment Story Updates Social media banner for Spokes Spokes — Devpost submission Live: https://spokes.alainschlesser.com/ Inspiration Groups are bad at picking somewhere to go, and the reason is structural rather than social. The needs that decide the answer are scattered across people and arrive piecemeal: a dietary restriction here, a budget there, a veto that lands after everyone else has settled, and at least one reason nobody wants to say out loud. A search results page optimises a single query. A group chat collects messages. Neither keeps a shared model of what the group has actually asked for, and neither lets a sensitive constraint count toward the decision without being explained to everybody first. That last part is what made this worth building for WebMCP specifically. A personal agent already knows things about its user that the user would rather not broadcast to five friends. Until now the only way to put that knowledge to work was to hand it to a shared service. I wanted to find out whether an agent could advocate for someone inside a live page, as that person and within an authority they granted, while the reason itself never left their client. What it does Three people open one planning room from a link. They see the same live map and the same brief of what the group has asked for so far. Each person states what matters in a single composer bar and chooses who may see it before they speak . A need can be shared, private, or agent-only. The server evaluates a private need and peers see only its effect on the count. An agent-only need stays with your agent and never reaches the server at all. The app suggests the next thing worth asking about from the data itself, never from a built-in list of categories. Every need becomes a row you can set aside. Press and hold a row and the map shows the room without that need, live. The cost of a need becomes visible instead of argued about. The room recomputes which places still work after every move, and it counts what is merely unverified separately from what actually failed. Missing data is drawn as its own state rather than quietly dropping a place. When nothing satisfies everyone, Spokes does not name who is blocking. It privately offers each person a quantified way out. The organizer sees "widen the area from 800 m to 1.2 km, brings back 4 places". The person who stated a need sees "let this need be nice-to-have, +12 places". Consent is explicit and confirmed on the page. Once the group agrees, the composer gives way to arrival: a travel mode and a one-tap handoff to the map app everyone already has. Alongside all of it, your personal ChatGPT can act in the same session through WebMCP. It can catch up on what changed while you were away, inspect places, put one forward, rule one out, or grant an adjustment. Your agent can assist you, or negotiate for you outright. How I built it A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). Fastify and a Postgres event log sit behind a WebSocket realtime channel. The front end is React and Vite with MapLibre GL over keyless OpenFreeMap tiles. TypeBox contracts are shared by both sides behind a hashed contract-manifest gate. Place data is a one-time OpenStreetMap extract of Berlin Mitte. The WebMCP surface is 22 tools registered imperatively on document.modelContext at page load, 10 for negotiation and 12 spatial. Each is a narrow function with closed enum schemas, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and a capped result budget. The page works fully without WebMCP. The tools are an additional way in. Four decisions did most of the work. Two protocols over the WebMCP substrate. WebMCP itself only carries tool names and schemas. So the first sync_session call returns a capability manifest that teaches the agent a domain-independent negotiation protocol (identity, revision sync, privacy tiers, requirements, stances, adjustments, consent, agreement) and a spatial-destination domain layered on top. Server-owned identity and per-viewer projections. Actor identity comes only from the bearer token. No tool argument accepts an actor id. Every event is stored once and projected per viewer, so unauthorised fields never appear in another participant's HTTP body or WebSocket frame. The test suite asserts this at the wire, not at the function boundary. Revision discipline instead of pretend realtime. Every mutation carries the agent's last-seen revision. A stale one returns a structured sync_required with a delta instead of acting on old state. That fits an agent that participates in bursts far better than a subscription it never really holds. Consent an agent cannot forge. An agent may recommend a grant, but a change beyond what the user delegated only stages . Staging mints a single-use code delivered on the participant's own realtime channel. The applying command must carry it back, and the code never appears in any tool result. Eligibility, minimal-conflict-set detection and the impasse counterfactuals are all deterministic. No model is allowed to invent a feasibility fact. 364 automated tests across three lanes: 222 unit, 128 three-user API, and 14 Playwright specs driving three isolated browser contexts. Challenges I ran into Privacy that is neither a lie nor a hole. The rule I settled on is that a private need's effect is always public and its content never leaves its owner. Both halves matter. Hiding the effect would make the count inexplicable, and leaking the content is the whole thing I was avoiding. It took a real redesign to stop routing private predicates through shared state "just for rendering", and a wire-level test suite to prove I had. Proving a human consented, honestly. My first cut let a bearer token commit an agreement over plain HTTP without ever touching the page. The realtime-only nonce closes that. It still is not proof a human clicked, because the realtime channel authenticates with the same token. Rather than overclaim, I wrote the residual threat model down in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md . Keeping the interface domain-agnostic. It is hard not to type a domain word into a heading. What saved it was a rule on the server side. The server returns the facets present across the current result set, each with a mandatory unknown count, and the client renders whatever it gets. There is no domain branch anywhere in the front end, which is also what lets a human and an agent reason over the same vocabulary. Deployment, on the last evening. I had prepared a Coolify deployment and abandoned it at the gate. Its Traefik has documented WebSocket failures on compose stacks, and the room is a WebSocket. The January 2026 disclosure put eleven critical CVEs in a control plane that runs as root. Its baseline would have claimed a quarter of a 4 GB box before Postgres started. The existing compose file was already a correct production stack. It needed twenty lines of Caddy in front, not a PaaS. That deploy went out with nineteen minutes to spare, after a self-inflicted detour in which a redeploy overwrote the host's generated Postgres password and stranded the database behind credentials nothing had written down. Two rendering bugs that looked like design problems. Vite's dependency optimiser broke MapLibre's worker, so the basemap never drew. A CSS animation setting transform silently overwrote a positioning translate and threw pins at their anchors. Both cost hours before either was understood. Accomplishments that I'm proud of An agent that can advocate for a constraint it never discloses. The agent screens places locally and returns per-place verdicts. The council folds them into eligibility, and peers see the aggregate effect with no route back to the cause. That is the capability I most wanted WebMCP to make possible, and it works. Press and hold. Holding a need shows the map without it, live, and releasing restores it. It turns an argument about whether a need is reasonable into a number you can see, and it is the one gesture everybody understood without being told. An impasse resolver that refuses to assign blame. When nothing satisfies everyone, the room offers each person a private, quantified route out, phrased as a consequence rather than an instruction. Honest unverified state. Missing data renders as a hollow pin and a separate count. A place is never silently dropped for lacking a value, and unknown is never drawn as failure. Two independent adversarial reviews: a protocol-invariant audit and a cross-family model review of the server, then two further reviews of the rebuilt client. The privacy and agreement-integrity findings were fixed and are covered by tests. I published the deferred items instead of hiding them. What I learned An agent is not a fast user, and modelling it as one produces bugs. It participates in bursts, disappears, an
video_title: Spokes: collaborative coordination assistant · WebMCP Challenge 2026 explainer video
video_transcript_excerpt: Picking a place with friends pays for boring reason. The needs live in different heads. They arrive one at a time and one of them is something somebody will not say out loud. Spokes puts the whole group on one live map and it lets you bring your own assistant. It starts with a sentence. I tell chat GPT what the group is trying to do. Because Spokes talks to assistants directly, the assistant can work on the product on my behalf. Pick the area, set up the room, hand back the invite. Nobody learned an app, nobody filled in a form. Show the code and the others are in. Sarah would like to sit outside. She adds it. Everyone's map settles. The places that still work stay bright, the rest fade where they stand. Press and hold her need and the map shows the room without it. What a need costs becomes a number you can see instead of something to argue about. Joe has a need he would rather not explain. He marks it private. The room learns only that a private condition ruled some places out, not what it was, not whose. And now nothing works for everyone. This is where a group chat goes quiet. Spokes does not wait and it does not name who is blocking. It offers each person a private way out with a number attached. Joe sees what comes back if his need became optional. Sarah sees the same for sitting outside. I see what a wider area brings back. Each decides alone. Joe leaves his, nobody asks him why. Sarah lets hers go and the room opens up again. For some places, the information is hollow. The map does not know enough about them and it says so instead of guessing. This is where an assistant earns its place. I ask it to find out. It reads menus and websites and records what it finds in the room. Hollow pins fill in for everyone. It cannot see what Joe needs because it only knows what I know, but everything it does learn, the whole group gets. I have the assistant put forward a place it just checked. The court lands with everyone. Sarah looks and rules it out. The assistant notices the room moved, takes the veto into account, and suggests another. This time everyone is in. Only a person can settle it, and only once everyone has said so. An assistant can help you decide. It never decides for you. And then off you go. Pick how you're getting there and hand off to the map you already use. One room needs to count without being shown a way out for everyone instead of blame, and an assistant that works inside the room as you. Finds what the map cannot and keeps what you keep. Spokes.

title: maav.ai - NeoLab | v0.5
pitch: Mobility ideas are easy to imagine: and costly to get wrong. MAAV NeoLab lets AI agents build and break synthetic scenarios, giving humans deterministic evidence before expensive real-world pilots.
about_excerpt: Mobility ideas are easy to imagine: and costly to get wrong. MAAV NeoLab lets AI agents build and break synthetic scenarios, giving humans deterministic evidence before expensive real-world pilots. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Scenario 1 Scenario 2 With Gemini Maav NeoLab MAAV NeoLab v0.5 Design it. Break it. Make it resilient. Inspiration I did not begin by trying to build another mobility dashboard. I began with a frustration from my own mobility research. Whenever I wanted to investigate a new mobility concept, defining the hypothesis was only the first step. Before I could test it, I often had to write substantial setup code, learn or relearn a specialist platform such as SUMO or MATLAB, translate the idea into that platform's abstractions, and assemble another workflow for visualization and analysis. These tools are powerful and essential for high-fidelity research. But for early exploration, operating the toolchain can require more effort than conducting the first experiment. That creates a hidden tax on mobility innovation. A planner, researcher, or R&D team may have an important question about fleet design, autonomous vehicles, urban air mobility, drones, or delivery robotics—yet spend more time constructing experimental machinery than examining the idea itself. General-purpose AI has made ideation dramatically faster, but a fluent answer is not reproducible evidence. An AI can propose a compelling direction without proving that two alternatives were tested under the same assumptions, constraints, demand, or disruption. I wanted to reverse that relationship: Start with the research question, let an AI agent operate the experiment, and make a deterministic evidence system—not the AI—the source of truth. That idea became MAAV NeoLab . The Problem Early mobility ideas move faster than the tools used to evaluate them. Testing a concept can require simulation-specific programming, duplicated configuration, disconnected dashboards, and manual transfer of results between systems. Every handoff creates an opportunity for assumptions to drift. Two alternatives may appear comparable even when they were tested with different demand, constraints, operating conditions, or failure scenarios. Results may be visually persuasive but difficult to reproduce. Conclusions can become separated from the exact evidence that produced them. AI alone does not solve this problem. An assistant can generate recommendations quickly, but it may work from incomplete context, infer unsupported conclusions, or obscure how an answer was produced. The industry does not need another system that merely produces answers. It needs a faster path from an idea to evidence that can be inspected, reproduced, challenged, and trusted. What MAAV NeoLab Does MAAV NeoLab makes mobility experimentation idea-first rather than software-first. A human describes the objective. A browser agent configures and operates the experiment through WebMCP. A deterministic engine produces the evidence. The final decision remains with the human. The workflow is intentionally clear: Describe → Configure → Break → Run → Compare → Review Version 0.5 proves this model through a deliberately bounded A/B experiment on an authored synthetic Sandton–Rosebank mobility network. Scenario A uses 12 vehicles with 8 seats each. Scenario B uses 10 vehicles with 10 seats each. Both receive the same seed-07 trace of 120 synthetic passenger requests. Both operate across the same 08:30–09:00 simulation horizon. Both receive an equivalent vehicle failure at exactly 08:42. The affected vehicle is selected independently using a fixed deterministic rule. Every completed run produces an immutable event ledger, replay snapshots, metrics, constraint results, provenance, and fingerprints. Compatible run artifacts can be compared and used to stage an evidence-linked finding. The AI agent may stage a finding, but only the visible human interface can Accept or Challenge it. At the failure tick, the engine selects the active vehicle with the highest onboard occupancy. Ties are resolved through explicit deterministic rules rather than randomness or agent choice. This resolves vehicle A-09 in Scenario A and B-03 in Scenario B. The experiment produces a genuine trade-off instead of manufacturing a universal winner. Evidence Scenario A Scenario B Fleet 12 × 8 seats 10 × 10 seats Served at horizon 82 81 In service at horizon 29 28 Unserved 9 11 Maximum wait 1,050 seconds 780 seconds Total energy 37,799 Wh 31,665 Wh Minimum reserve 7,633 basis points 7,648 basis points Recovery time 120 seconds 450 seconds Standing observed 0 0 Maximum-wait constraint FAIL FAIL Scenario A completes service for more passengers and recovers significantly faster. Scenario B reduces maximum wait and total energy consumption. Both scenarios still violate the hard maximum-wait constraint. MAAV NeoLab therefore stages: TRADE_OFF · BALANCED · PENDING HUMAN REVIEW Passenger conservation remains explicit: $$N_{\mathrm{requested}} = N_{\mathrm{served}} + N_{\mathrm{in\ service}} + N_{\mathrm{unserved}}$$ For Scenario A: $$120 = 82 + 29 + 9$$ For Scenario B: $$120 = 81 + 28 + 11$$ MAAV NeoLab does not replace high-fidelity platforms such as SUMO or MATLAB. It provides a lower-friction assurance layer for exploring a hypothesis, exposing its assumptions, stress-testing alternatives consistently, and deciding whether deeper modeling or a real-world pilot is justified. MAAV NeoLab v0.5 is a synthetic decision-support workbench—not a live fleet-control system, operational optimizer, or scientifically calibrated transport model. How AI and WebMCP Are Used The browser agent is not an embedded chatbot, and it does not operate a separate demonstration environment. It works directly with the application through exactly six static WebMCP tools: read_lab_state configure_scenario inject_disruption run_scenario compare_scenarios stage_finding Through these tools, the agent can inspect the current laboratory state, configure Scenario A and Scenario B, schedule the equivalent deterministic disruption, run both simulations, compare compatible evidence, and stage a supported finding. The important architectural decision is that the AI coordinates the experiment but never calculates its trusted evidence. Passenger movement, assignments, vehicle selection, battery use, energy, failure recovery, metrics, constraints, comparisons, and supported finding claims remain owned by deterministic application and domain logic. The agent also cannot Accept, Challenge, reset, dispatch, or execute any real-world operation. Final review authority remains intentionally human. Prompting is the control plane. Deterministic evidence is the truth. Human judgment is the authority. How I Built It I built MAAV NeoLab as a strict TypeScript modular monolith using Next.js, React, Zod, Zustand, WebMCP, and Google Maps. The architecture follows a clear authority chain: Human UI / WebMCP / Google presentation ↓ Application service ↓ Deterministic domain ↓ Immutable evidence artifacts The manual interface and browser agent share one repository, one application-service instance, one workspace revision, and one audit trail. An operation completed by the agent becomes visible in the interface without reloading. A manual operation becomes visible to the agent through the same authoritative state. Every mutation validates the expected workspace revision. Every mutating agent operation carries a source-aware operation ID. Exact retries return the original terminal result, while changed arguments fail closed with an idempotency conflict. Cancellation propagates through the application boundary and cannot publish a partial artifact or produce a delayed ghost completion. Concurrent operations cannot silently overwrite one another. Scenario revisions invalidate only the affected current evidence while preserving immutable historical artifacts. The deterministic engine owns: passenger arrivals and lifecycle; assignments and vehicle movement; capacity and no-standing enforcement; battery and energy accounting; deterministic vehicle-failure selection; recovery behavior; immutable ledger events; replay snapshots; metrics and constraints; scenario comparison; supported finding claims. WebMCP remains a thin adapter. It validates strict input, injects trusted source context, calls the shared application service, and returns bounded structured results. It does not calculate simulation evidence. Google Maps provides geographic context and replay presentation. It never supplies simulation distance, timing, traffic, dispatch, energy, metrics, comparisons, or conclusions. When Google Maps is unavailable, the authored fallback preserves the complete experiment and produces identical trusted evidence. I used OpenAI Codex as an architecture, implementation, debugging, testing, and release-verification collaborator. I used Claude during the visual-design iteration.
