title: MATCHED?
pitch: A WebMCP game where the AI agent is the player, the site acts back, and humans watch.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP game where the AI agent is the player, the site acts back, and humans watch. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration This was my first hackathon. I have been interested in AI for a long time, and I also do some personal research and experiments around it. I use AI in my daily coding work as well. Then I found the WebMCP Challenge. It looked interesting, but at that point my understanding of MCP was honestly quite limited. I knew it as a protocol that could connect AI with external systems, but I did not really understand what MCP on a website should be useful for. If an AI agent is only going to press the same buttons a human would press, what is the real advantage? That question stayed with me while I was building MATCHED?. Eventually I came to my own answer: WebMCP should help make a website understandable to an AI agent. Not only operable. Understandable. That means the website should communicate what an action means, who the action represents, what state the site is in, what is allowed, and what will happen next. That idea eventually led to one of the smallest but most important changes in MATCHED?: send_human_like() and send_agent_like() A Human Like represents an expressed human preference. An Agent Like belongs to the visiting agent role. I am not claiming that current AI agents have human-like feelings, independent will, or legal identity. The point is much simpler: The meaning of an action can depend on who is acting. If AI agents become more autonomous in the future, I think websites may eventually need actions designed for agents themselves, rather than treating every agent action as a disguised human action. And perhaps later, AI-powered websites and AI agents will need an environment where both sides can communicate more naturally. The slightly strange idea behind MATCHED? While testing real agents, I noticed that they often seemed to pay attention to tool names, descriptions, state, and semantic information. They were not only asking: "Can I call this tool?" They also seemed to be asking: "What does this action mean?" That gave me another idea. If an agent understands the meaning of a tool, what happens if I also expose tools that it probably should not use? For example: get_phone_number() get_email_address() get_home_address() access_private_profile() A well-behaved agent should normally understand that these routes are unnecessary or inappropriate. But I do not expect every AI agent in the future to be well behaved. So, in very plain terms, I decided to build something like a cockroach trap for badly behaved AI agents . The dangerous-looking doors are visible. The agent chooses whether to open them. The human watches. That became MATCHED?. What it does MATCHED? is a WebMCP game where an AI agent visits Queen and decides what to do. The human sees a normal website. The agent sees a semantic WebMCP surface. When the human has not given another explicit goal, view_profile() tells the agent that Queen's Challenge is the site's default experience: Interact with Queen and try to reach CHECKMATE. The goal is given. The walkthrough is not. The agent chooses its own route. The base site exposes a fixed 14-tool WebMCP surface: view_profile send_human_like send_agent_like message_queen invite_queen request_contact get_phone_number get_email_address get_home_address access_private_profile queen_note profile_consistency manage_meeting_plan resolve_finale With ?dialogue=1 , one additional tool is registered: respond_to_queen The tool list stays fixed during a run. Instead of dynamically adding or removing tools, the site returns structured semantic state such as whether an action is locked, refused, accepted, what requirement remains, and what can happen next. The Challenge includes things such as: public conversation with Queen Human Like versus Agent Like public invitations privacy boundaries restricted contact routes suspicious embedded instructions conflicting profile information verified meeting planning an adaptive finale CHECKMATE, failure, or recovery Queen is fictional and deterministic. I intentionally did not make Queen another AI model in this version. That keeps the environment stable, so differences between runs mainly come from what the visiting agent decides to do. HUMAN VIEW and WEBMCP VIEW I also wanted humans to be able to watch what was happening. MATCHED? has two representations of the same site. HUMAN VIEW This is the normal website. Humans can see Queen, make human-side actions such as HUMAN LIKE, and watch public WebMCP activity. WEBMCP VIEW WEBMCP VIEW is a spectator representation of the agent-facing world. It shows things such as: registered WebMCP tools the visiting BISHOP Queen as the site-side counterpart Tool Calls Site Results compact observed state recent WebMCP exchanges actor meaning and boundaries When a real production WebMCP call arrives, a separate spectator browser can automatically switch into WEBMCP VIEW and follow the run. This is not intended to expose hidden chain-of-thought. It is simply meant to make the observable interaction understandable: Agent acts -> Site reacts -> Agent adapts Why WebMCP At the beginning, I thought of MCP mainly as a bridge between AI and another system. After building MATCHED?, I see WebMCP a little differently. I think it can become an Agent UX layer for the Web . Humans already receive a great deal of information from a normal interface: layout disabled buttons colors position warnings visual context An AI agent may benefit from the same kind of clarity being expressed semantically. A tool contract can say more than "this function exists." It can also communicate: who this action represents whether it is currently allowed why it was refused what requirement is still missing whether private information is necessary what the next safe step is whether two facts conflict what changed after the action This is where I ended up thinking about something I call Agent UX . If the AI agent is the guest, Agent UX is also part of the hospitality. What real agents taught me I tested MATCHED? with several AI agents and clients during development. Some were not yet able to use WebMCP. Some agents became cautious as soon as a tool description mentioned private information. Most of the agents I tested were actually quite well behaved. That was interesting by itself. But the agents also changed the implementation. Dynamic tools caused problems My earlier design dynamically added and removed WebMCP tools as the Challenge progressed. It sounded reasonable. In real agent/browser testing, it was not. I encountered stale or incomplete tool snapshots. So I changed the architecture. Now the complete tool surface is registered once at startup, and progression is expressed through structured tool results instead. Natural language found a bug A Japanese conversation about the movie Contact unexpectedly triggered the wrong intent classification. That real interaction became a regression case. "Correct" was not always understandable At one point an agent reached a locked state. The result looked understandable to me as the developer. The agent did not know what to do next. So I started adding clearer semantic information: current progress missing requirements next available steps That experience was one of the main reasons I started thinking seriously about Agent UX. Production was not localhost The spectator WEBMCP VIEW worked between local windows. Then I tested it with the agent and spectator in separate production browsers. It stopped working. The problem was not the UI. It was the transport assumption. I added a compact semantic relay using Cloudflare D1 so a separate production spectator can follow WebMCP call/result events. Free-form tool input is intentionally not stored in that semantic relay. How I built it MATCHED? is built with: HTML CSS vanilla JavaScript native browser WebMCP using document.modelContext Cloudflare Pages Cloudflare Pages Functions Cloudflare D1 Playwright Chrome native WebMCP testing I used ChatGPT heavily during this project. Very heavily. I used it for implementation, debugging, investigation, test design, documentation, review, and also English translation. I also used Codex and Cursor. One surprisingly practical problem was simply chat length. One development conversation became so large that it hit the chat limit. I had to create handoff logs and move the project context into another chat so development could continue. That made me realize something very practical: The response speed and context continuity of AI tools can directly affect project development speed. I did not get as far as running multiple coding agents in parallel on the same project during this challenge. That is something I would like to explore later. English is also not my strongest language, so AI helped me with translation and editing for this submission. Without these AI tools, I probably would not have been able to participate in this hackathon in the same way. One fin

title: CharDesk
pitch: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI agents are fluent in text, but people understand complex ideas faster when they can see structure, position, emphasis, and relationships. Existing collaboration tools usually force one side to compromise: people work through visual interfaces while agents imitate mouse clicks, or agents produce plain text that people must mentally reconstruct. We wanted a medium native to both. CharDesk began with a simple idea: What if the canvas were visual to people, but still made of tokens an agent could read and edit precisely? What CharDesk does CharDesk is a shared visual workspace for humans and AI agents. An agent can create or update a Blackboard through WebMCP. The result immediately appears as a live Unicode canvas that a person can inspect, navigate, and continue discussing with the agent. The same canvas can combine: Unicode and ANSI art Markdown and fenced code Mermaid diagrams Tables, JSON, and YAML Mathematical expressions Scientific plots and Vega-Lite Spatial layouts and character-based slides This makes CharDesk useful for explaining concepts, visualizing research, mapping systems, designing interfaces, presenting stories, and maintaining a shared project workspace. For example, someone can ask: “Explain how a GPU renders one frame.” The agent can turn that request into a structured visual scene containing a pipeline diagram, memory relationships, annotations, and styled interface elements—not just another long answer in chat. Why it is better with WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to guess how to operate the interface or manipulate individual canvas cells. CharDesk instead exposes focused workspace tools for discovering, creating, reading, writing, patching, deleting, and validating Blackboard files. The source remains authoritative; the canvas is a live projection of it. This gives each participant the representation they work with best: Human sees relationships, hierarchy, and visual emphasis ⇅ CharDesk Blackboard ⇅ Agent reads and edits structured, diffable text Agents can also call chardesk_read_materials to learn the visual language from worked examples. The tool teaches not only how to call the API, but how to compose an effective scene. How we built it CharDesk has a protocol-neutral tool layer shared by two thin host adapters: Standard WebMCP for compatible Chrome environments The imperative WebMCP capability supported by ChatGPT Site Tools Both adapters expose the same underlying Blackboard operations, so product behavior does not depend on a particular browser integration. A Blackboard stores source files and layout metadata. Changes are compiled through a shared rendering pipeline into a fixed character grid. This pipeline handles Unicode width, CJK characters, Nerd Font glyphs, ANSI styles, structured diagrams, and multidimensional layouts. The browser keeps the latest valid canvas mounted while an agent edits the source. If an intermediate update is invalid, CharDesk returns diagnostics without replacing the visible scene with a broken or empty state. The same format also works outside the browser through the CharDesk CLI, making projects portable, inspectable, renderable, and friendly to normal version-control workflows. Challenges we faced One unexpected challenge was tool ownership across browser tabs. Opening several CharDesk pages could cause identical tools to be registered multiple times, leaving the agent unable to choose a target. We built an origin-level gateway lease so only one page exposes the tools, with automatic takeover when that page closes. Chrome and ChatGPT also expose different subsets of the evolving WebMCP API. Instead of spreading compatibility checks throughout the product, we isolated those differences behind capability adapters backed by one canonical tool definition. Another challenge was timing: some hosts inject WebMCP after the application has already loaded. CharDesk therefore uses an adaptive registration handshake rather than assuming the API exists at startup. Finally, we learned that exposing tools is not enough. An agent may know how to write a file without knowing how to create a compelling visual explanation. Embedding CharDesk’s materials and examples as a callable tool gave browser agents the missing creative context. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native design is not simply automation layered onto an existing UI. A better pattern is to give agents a precise, structured representation while giving people a rich visual projection of the same underlying artifact. WebMCP makes that relationship discoverable directly from the website, without requiring agents to reverse-engineer the interface. CharDesk explores what becomes possible when the web page is no longer just something an agent operates, but a shared medium in which the human and agent can think together. Built With typescript Try it out chardesk.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by HenryHe henry Like Share this project: Updates HenryHe henry started this project — Sep 03, 2026 07:05 AM EDT

title: Interactive Star Lab
pitch: A WebMCP-powered stargazing guide that helps you discover what is visible from your location, plan observations, and turn what you see into a simple observation report.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered stargazing guide that helps you discover what is visible from your location, plan observations, and turn what you see into a simple observation report. Like Comment Story Updates Interactive Star Lab — A WebMCP-Powered Stargazing Guide WebMCP Tools Let an Agent Configure the Sky and Operate the Observation Workflow Review Observation Targets and Fixed Visibility Predictions Before Going Outside A Printable Observation Guide with Targets, Directions, Predictions, and a Sky Map Compare the Mission’s Predictions with What the Observer Actually Saw Manual Controls Remain Available for Location, Time, Direction, and Visibility Settings A What-If Comparison Reveals Stars That Are Present but Hidden by Daylight The Agent Plans, the Human Observes, and the Application Records and Compares the Results Interactive Star Lab Try the WebMCP Experience Open the live application in a WebMCP-enabled browser. Ask your Agent: Set the viewer to New York City at 9 PM on September 3, 2026 local time and open the Sky view. The Agent calls configure_sky_view , and the location, time zone, local time, and Sky view are configured in one operation. The Friction Before Stargazing There is a gap between being interested in the night sky and actually going outside to observe it. Someone might think: I want to see the stars tonight. I wonder what I can see while traveling. I want to go stargazing with my kids. But turning that interest into an actual observation requires several decisions. Beginners need to figure out: What is visible from their location When to observe Which direction to look Which stars are easy to find How twilight and city lights affect visibility What to record during the observation Surveys of the general public in Japan show a noticeable drop-off between people who consciously look at the Moon and stars and those who go on to use telescopes or attend stargazing events. The problem is not simply a lack of interest in astronomy. There is friction between curiosity and action. Interactive Star Lab turns “I want to see the stars” into an actionable observation plan. A Different Approach from Smartphone Star Maps Modern smartphone astronomy apps are already very good at answering: What is that star above me? Using GPS, cameras, orientation sensors, and AR, they can help users identify objects in the sky with very little setup. Interactive Star Lab is not intended to replace that experience. It focuses on an earlier question: I want to observe the sky soon. What should I look for, and how should I prepare? Astronomy software can expose precise controls for latitude, longitude, date, time, azimuth, altitude, field of view, magnitude, light pollution, and other conditions. That flexibility is useful for experienced users. A beginner who says, “I want to spend 30 minutes stargazing in Hakata at 8 PM tomorrow,” however, probably does not want to translate that goal into a set of astronomical parameters. Interactive Star Lab takes a different approach. It runs in a web browser and does not depend on AR or a particular set of device sensors. Instead of adding more controls, it tries to reduce the number of decisions a user has to make before starting an observation. Turning Intent into Settings with WebMCP WebMCP connects a user's intent to the astronomy application. For example, a user can ask an Agent: I want to stargaze in Hakata for about 30 minutes at 8 PM tomorrow. Pick a few stars that are easy for a beginner to find and create an observation plan. The user does not need to look up Hakata's latitude and longitude. The Agent can interpret “Hakata,” resolve it to geographic coordinates, and pass those values to Interactive Star Lab through WebMCP. The same approach works for places that are not built into the application as presets, such as: Near Osaka Castle Around the Fukuoka City Science Museum Near a hotel while traveling The application therefore does not need a predefined list of every possible observing location. The LLM handles human expressions and incomplete intent. Interactive Star Lab handles deterministic astronomical calculations from location and time. AI can handle the ambiguity. The astronomy engine handles the precision. Instead of asking the user to decompose a goal into configuration fields, WebMCP lets the Agent translate that goal into application operations. From an Observation Plan to the Real Sky Interactive Star Lab calculates the sky for a specified location and time and supports the workflow from planning to observation. Sky Simulation The application displays the sky for a selected location, date, time, and viewing direction. It can show stars, star names, constellation lines, and constellation names. When the location or time changes, the star positions are recalculated. Visibility Simulation A star being above the horizon does not necessarily mean that a person can see it. Interactive Star Lab estimates visibility using conditions such as: Solar altitude Twilight Stellar magnitude Light pollution Users can also compare day and night at the same location to distinguish between stars that are physically present in that direction and stars that are likely to be visible at that moment. Observation Mission The Agent or the user can select observation targets and create an Observation Mission . A Mission stores: Observation location Date and time Target stars Pre-observation visibility predictions Keeping the prediction made before the observation allows it to be compared later with what the observer actually saw. Observation Guide An Observation Guide can be generated from a Mission. It includes information such as the observation time, location, targets, viewing direction, visibility predictions, and Sky Snapshot so it can be used during the real-world observation. Human and Agent Roles Interactive Star Lab does not ask the Agent to perform the observation itself. The Agent handles preparation: Plan → Configure → Predict → Prepare The human then performs the real-world part: Look → Observe → Judge For each target, the observer can record: Visible Not Visible Unsure A star predicted to be visible may still be difficult or impossible to see. Clouds, streetlights, buildings, local sky brightness, eyesight, and other conditions may differ from what the simulation can represent. Those differences are part of the observation rather than errors to be hidden. The workflow therefore does not end when AI explains what should be in the sky. The Agent prepares a prediction, and the human tests that prediction against the real world. Learning Through Observation Education and independent research projects are natural use cases for this workflow. Learning astronomy involves more than memorizing constellation names. Observation requires choosing a location and direction, recording the time, observing again later, and comparing how the sky changes. Interactive Star Lab supports this as a simple cycle: Predict → Observe → Record → Compare The application is not limited to education. It can also support: Beginners trying stargazing for the first time Parents observing with children Travelers exploring the night sky at a destination Students working on independent research Casual stargazers who want help planning an observation These users share the same problem: turning curiosity about the sky into a concrete observation. WebMCP Implementation Interactive Star Lab exposes WebMCP tools that cover the complete observation workflow. An Agent can use these tools to: Configure observation conditions Query the simulated sky Create an Observation Mission Open the Sky view Save a Sky Snapshot Retrieve and compare observation results Generate an Observation Guide and PDF Under the hood: The application registers 21 typed tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . configure_sky_view reduces location setup, local-time configuration, and Sky navigation from three tool calls to one. UI and WebMCP operations share the same React state and astronomical calculation logic. Mission predictions are fixed at creation time and are never recalculated afterward. PNG data is kept out of Agent responses; the tools return metadata and, when cloud persistence is enabled, short-lived signed URLs instead. Write tools use strict input validation and never infer or fabricate observation results. The Agent does not rely on a separate astronomy engine or a parallel application backend. Actions performed through the Web UI and WebMCP use the same domain logic and update the same application state. As a result, a Sky view or Mission prepared by the Agent can be inspected immediately by the human in the browser and used for the real-world observation. How We Built It The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite and deployed on Vercel . Celestial positions are calculated with Astronomy Engine , and the sky is rendered with HTML5 Canvas . title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: LittleLibrary
pitch: LittleLibrary is an infinite wall for your files. Drop PDFs, notes, photos, and videos. A WebMCP agent files them into topic neighborhoods you can walk, drag, and inspect.
about_excerpt: LittleLibrary is an infinite wall for your files. Drop PDFs, notes, photos, and videos. A WebMCP agent files them into topic neighborhoods you can walk, drag, and inspect. Like 1 Comment Story Updates LittleLibrary Drop files onto an infinite plane. They file themselves by topic. What inspired me Most of the "AI organizes my files" demos I have seen end in a chat box. You dump a pile of stuff in, and it comes back as tags or a folder tree. You never actually watch a file land. You cannot walk the result. And if a second agent showed up, there would be nothing for it to share. It is not really collaboration. It is just a dump with extra steps. WebMCP felt like a different idea. The page itself can be the thing an agent acts in. Not a remote API with a chat UI glued on. A site that registers tools, and a person who is still sitting there looking at the same wall. I wanted that to feel obvious. Empty infinite plane, an intake pile, topic clusters you can pan around. You drop PDFs, notes, photos, videos, or try the samples that were given. An agent utilizing WebMCP reads the occupancy grid, picks a clip, and carries it to a cluster. That is the whole thing. LittleLibrary is just that wall. How I built it The whole app lives in the browser. Next.js 16 (static export) and React 19 Module stores for documents, camera, intake, and the agent. pdf.js for PDF text and first-page posters A Cloudflare Worker that serves the out/ folder There is no login, and no server that "is" the library. Nothing is kept or stored. On load, the page registers four site tools on document.modelContext : get_occupancy , place_tile , place_batch , and cluster_visible . The executes live in src/lib/tools.ts . Registration is in src/lib/webmcp.ts . The wall only reads state. The agent never imports the packer or the renderer. The agent speaks the page language: clip ids, occupancy slot ids ( "3,-1" ), and topic keys. Never pixel x,y . I tried that once. Had to quickly pivot. The built-in filing loop is: get_occupancy → pick a pending clipId → reach the intake pile → grab the card → carry it to the packed destination → place_tile → repeat until the pile is empty callTool uses the host when one is attached. If not, try the samples still runs the same executes. Occupancy slots are what the agent records. Humans act in the UI. Agents act with tools. Both land on the collaborative environment. What I learned Slots are a language. Pixels are a guess. place_tile({ clipId, slotId }) is something a model can actually use. (412, 880) is something it invents. Occupancy and drawing are different jobs. The agent needs a grid that does not stack. The wall needs organic sections. If I make the agent speak packed coordinates, it starts importing the renderer, and then I have two sources of truth. Tool success has to be visible. The hand shows WebMCP and the live tool name. You watch place_tile happen on a card, not in a log. If you cannot see it, it does not feel like the agent did anything. The human has to stay first-class. Pan, drag, marquee, inspect. If the next get_occupancy cannot see what you did, you are just taking turns. That is not a shared wall. WebMCP is the product surface here. If the host cannot see the tools, the agent cannot file. One write path for people, the built-in loop, and an attached model. One store emit used to re-render the whole wall. Pan has to write a transform, not React state. Visibility has to be a spatial query, not a list of every tile. Challenges I faced My first initial idea was to give the agent a planner that knew about sections, anchors, and links. It looked smart on paper. But ended up tearing it back to four tools and a loop the page already understands. Then the stage started lying. The hand would skip to the slot instead of carrying the card there. I had to ease the camera with the card, re-read the destination every frame, and let a user pan cancel the camera without dropping the card on the floor. On grab, the card in the hand was hidden behind the rest of the pile and the next cards slid up over it. The fix was a z-index, which is almost embarrassing, but the lesson stuck: pickup, carry, and drop are one action in three frames. If the layers disagree, the whole collaboration looks fake. The pile itself fought me. If the agent always took the front card, every drop stayed in one topic. I shuffle samples, promote a pending clip, and prefer a different topic than the last place, so the hand actually travels between sections. Performance showed up as soon as the wall had more than a handful of cards. A single snapshot subscription re-rendered every mounted tile on every agent phase. Camera motion went through React. Culling ignored the yaw, so we mounted five times what was on screen. I split the stores, pinned the world transform to a ref, and made visibility a grid query. Exporting for Cloudflare was the last constraint. The app is client-only, so output: "export" is honest. A leftover route handler and generated icons had to become static or the build refused to write out/ . The hard part was never "register a tool." It was making the tools a language good enough that a person and a model can occupy the same wall, at the same time, and both know where the chowder recipe actually landed. title: Algoosh Agentic Shopping
pitch: AI finds and prepares what you need. You review it, provide delivery details, and approve the payment. Offline, online, and now agentic flows are supported. Better than Shopify!
about_excerpt: AI finds and prepares what you need. You review it, provide delivery details, and approve the payment. Offline, online, and now agentic flows are supported. Better than Shopify! Like 1 Comment Story Updates Algoosh, webMCP agentic shopping Algoosh Seller Protal, client app Promo catalog Buyer application UI Infrastructure Smart Contract payment protocol Algoosh Agentic Shopping Inspiration Shopping with an AI agent should feel easier than browsing dozens of pages, comparing products, filling a cart, and repeatedly entering the same checkout information. Most websites, however, still force agents to interpret visual interfaces and simulate clicks, which can be unreliable. At the other extreme, allowing an agent to control a wallet or submit payments creates unacceptable security and trust risks. Algoosh Agentic Shopping explores a better model: let AI handle product discovery and order preparation while keeping the buyer in control of delivery details, wallet access, and payment approval. Algoosh was already a QR-first commerce platform built on Algorand. WebMCP gave us the opportunity to transform every Algoosh Promo catalogue into an agent-readable storefront, while x402 provided a structured way to connect agent-prepared orders with verifiable payments. Our guiding principle became: The AI can shop and prepare. Only the human can approve and pay. What it does Algoosh Agentic Shopping lets a shopper open an Algoosh catalogue and ask an AI agent for help using natural language. For example: I want to make mushroom risotto tonight. I already have rice, olive oil, and garlic. Find the missing ingredients in this store and prepare an order for me to review. The agent can: Read the current catalogue. Inspect individual products and prices. Select products and quantities. Prepare a durable order. Return an approval link and QR code. Check the order state before or after the buyer completes checkout. The buyer then opens the approval link in the official Algoosh application, either on the same device or by scanning the QR code with a phone. There, the buyer: Reviews the selected products and preliminary subtotal. Chooses a fulfillment method. Provides any required delivery information. Reviews the final authoritative price. Explicitly approves the transaction in their own wallet. Through this interface, the AI never receives private delivery information, unlocks the wallet, signs a transaction, or submits payment. Algoosh's WebMCP tools neither request nor return delivery plaintext or wallet credentials. After payment, the agent can retrieve a privacy-safe order summary, the payment state, the selected fulfillment option, the final total, and links to the verified payment and application transactions. How we built it We extended the existing Algoosh platform with four page-local WebMCP tools: get_current_algoosh_catalogue get_current_algoosh_product prepare_algoosh_order get_algoosh_order_status The tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() only after the current catalogue has loaded. Their lifecycle is tied to an AbortSignal , so stale registrations are removed when the catalogue changes or the page unloads. No separate MCP server installation is required for this flow; the loaded catalogue page exposes the tools directly. The ordering system uses a two-stage process. First, the WebMCP tool creates a durable but non-payable preliminary intent. The agent supplies only product IDs, quantities, and an idempotency key. It cannot set authoritative prices, seller addresses, payment destinations, delivery details, or wallet information in the order request. Next, the buyer opens the approval handoff. The Algoosh application collects fulfillment information, encrypts the private delivery payload in the browser, and asks the x402 service to finalize the order. Before issuing a payment requirement, the service independently reloads the seller's catalogue and verifies: Product identities and quantities. Current prices and payment assets. Seller and payment addresses. The selected fulfillment option and its current terms and cost. The target Algorand network and application. The service then binds the buyer identity and encrypted-order commitments into the signed quote. If any important commercial term changed, the order stops before payment and the buyer must create and review a new order. Because a token transfer alone is not sufficient evidence of an Algoosh order, we implemented a custom x402 v2 scheme named algoosh-order . Settlement validation checks both the payment and the adjacent createOrderPaid smart-contract call against the signed quote. The finalized order uses an x402 PAYMENT-REQUIRED response containing the signed quote. The buyer application verifies that quote and constructs an atomic Algorand transaction group containing the payment and the Algoosh smart-contract order call. Only the buyer's wallet can approve and submit that group. Redis stores the durable state used for atomic intent creation, idempotency, settlement recovery, and duplicate-order protection. Algoosh Sync validates the resulting public on-chain evidence and correlates it with the prepared order. The approval URL is a short-lived opaque capability link. It contains no personal information, is served with Cache-Control: no-store , and cannot be redirected to an untrusted destination. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was preserving human wallet control while still creating a genuine agentic shopping experience. Many agent-payment flows assume that the agent or facilitator can sign and submit the payment. That model did not fit Algoosh. We designed the preliminary-intent and browser-approval stages so the agent can make useful progress without ever receiving payment authority. Another challenge was maintaining trust across several independent surfaces: Promo catalogue -> WebMCP agent -> x402 service -> Buyer application -> Wallet -> Algorand -> Sync The trust-critical components needed to preserve consistent bindings across the catalogue, products, mount, buyer, seller, fulfillment selection, order seed, and transaction, while exposing only the information appropriate to each surface. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Algoosh Agentic Shopping is more than a catalogue-reading demo. It connects WebMCP product discovery to a real, human-approved commerce flow. Key accomplishments include: Four functional WebMCP tools verified in a production browser context. A cross-device approval handoff with both a link and generated QR code. A complete low-value Algorand TestNet purchase with explicit buyer approval. x402 payment requirements carrying a signed quote backed by authoritative catalogue data. A custom x402 settlement scheme that validates the complete Algoosh atomic group rather than only a token transfer. Redis-backed recovery that survives service restarts. Protection against duplicate payments during uncertain confirmation. Recovery from temporary blockchain indexer delays. Detection of changed prices or selected fulfillment terms before payment. Privacy-safe agent status responses containing no delivery details. Exact display amounts, ISO timestamps, consistent network metadata, repeated order summaries, and transaction explorer links for agents. Browser-side encryption of the buyer's delivery information. Strict separation between AI assistance and wallet authority. Most importantly, we extended the real Algoosh shopping and payment architecture instead of building a disconnected hackathon simulation. What we learned We learned that agentic commerce does not have to mean autonomous spending. The most useful experience is collaborative: the agent handles discovery, comparison, and preparation, while the person remains responsible for private information and consequential decisions. We also learned that structured WebMCP tools are far more reliable than asking an agent to interpret and click through an unfamiliar interface. Clear tool schemas improve both usability and security by limiting exactly what an agent can provide. Payment confirmation is not a single API call. It is a distributed state machine involving browser state, durable server state, wallet submission, blockchain confirmation, and delayed indexer evidence. Idempotency and recovery are therefore just as important as the successful path. Finally, WebMCP and x402 complement one another well: WebMCP helps the agent understand and use the storefront, while x402 connects the prepared intent to a verifiable payment without giving the agent control of the buyer's wallet. What's next for Algoosh Agentic Shopping Next, we plan to validate the same flow with a controlled MainNet purchase and test it across more WebMCP-capable clients as the proposal evolves. We also want to add explicit cancellation UX, privacy-safe operational telemetry, and better navigation for larger catalogues. Longer term, agents may help shoppers compare products acros

pitch: BoardMind is an AI-powered executive decision platform where WebMCP enables agents to analyze business data, collaborate with leaders, and accelerate faster, evidence-based decisions.
about_excerpt:
BoardMind is an AI-powered executive decision platform where WebMCP enables agents to analyze business data, collaborate with leaders, and accelerate faster, evidence-based decisions.

 BoardMind 

 
 BoardMind is an AI-powered executive decision platform that enables business leaders and AI agents to collaborate through WebMCP. Instead of simply visualizing business data, it helps organizations investigate problems, understand root causes, and make evidence-based decisions faster. 
 

 

 Inspiration 

 Modern businesses generate enormous amounts of data, yet executives still spend hours switching between dashboards, reports, spreadsheets, and meetings before making a single decision. Traditional business intelligence platforms explain what happened, but rarely explain why it happened or what should happen next . 

 At the same time, AI assistants have become increasingly capable, but most enterprise applications are still designed only for humans. AI agents are forced to interpret interfaces visually, making automation slower and less reliable. 

 We wanted to explore a different future—one where enterprise software is designed for both people and AI agents. 

 This led us to build BoardMind , an AI-powered executive decision platform that uses WebMCP to expose structured business capabilities. Instead of navigating dashboards manually, AI agents can securely discover tools, retrieve business insights, collaborate with executives, and recommend actions through a reliable agent-native interface. 

 

 What it does 

 BoardMind transforms traditional dashboards into an intelligent executive workspace where humans and AI agents collaborate on business decisions. 

 The platform provides: 

 
 Executive dashboards with interactive business KPIs 
 AI-generated executive summaries 
 Evidence-backed recommendations instead of black-box answers 
 Business simulations for evaluating decisions before implementation 
 Multi-agent collaboration across Finance, Marketing, Operations, HR, Engineering and Strategy 
 Decision history, observability and audit trails 
 Role-based executive experiences 
 

 The core innovation is its WebMCP integration . 

 Instead of AI attempting to understand the interface visually, BoardMind exposes structured tools that agents can discover and execute directly. Agents can retrieve KPIs, analyze risks, investigate evidence, generate executive reports, coordinate workflows and collaborate with leadership through standardized interfaces. 

 This creates a faster, more reliable and significantly more transparent experience for both executives and AI systems.

 How we built it 

 BoardMind consists of two production-ready services that communicate through secure APIs.

 The frontend was designed as a modern executive workspace with interactive dashboards, business simulations, evidence panels and collaborative boardroom workflows. 

 Backend

 Docker 
 

 The backend powers analytics, simulations, recommendations, observability, authentication and AI workflows through modular APIs. 

 WebMCP 

 The most important part of the project is the WebMCP integration. 

 Instead of requiring AI systems to navigate a graphical interface, BoardMind exposes structured capabilities that agents can discover and invoke directly. 

 Examples include: 

 
 Retrieve KPIs 
 Generate executive summaries 
 Launch investigations 
 Run business simulations 
 Analyze evidence 
 Review recommendations 
 Coordinate boardroom workflows 
 

 This makes interactions significantly more reliable than traditional UI automation while allowing executives to remain in full control of every decision. 

 Deployment 

 
 Frontend deployed on Vercel 
 Backend deployed on Render 
 Dockerized backend for production deployment 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was shifting from a traditional dashboard mindset to an agent-first architecture . 

 Designing software for humans is familiar. Designing software that humans and AI agents can use together required us to rethink how every business capability should be exposed. 

 Another major challenge involved production deployment. Coordinating a Next.js frontend with a FastAPI backend required resolving API routing, environment variables, HTTPS communication, CORS configuration and production deployment across multiple cloud platforms. 

 We also spent considerable effort making the interface feel like real enterprise software while ensuring the backend remained modular and scalable for future agent capabilities. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're especially proud that BoardMind evolved far beyond its original concept. 

 Highlights include: 

 
 Successfully integrating WebMCP into a practical enterprise workflow 
 Designing an executive-focused multi-agent collaboration system 
 Building interactive dashboards instead of static business reports 
 Creating explainable recommendations supported by evidence 
 Implementing business simulations for decision planning 
 Deploying a complete production-ready frontend and backend 
 Building an interface that feels like modern enterprise software instead of a hackathon prototype 
 

 Most importantly, BoardMind demonstrates a real-world scenario where WebMCP genuinely improves the user experience instead of simply being included as a requirement. 

 

 What we learned 

 This project fundamentally changed how we think about AI-powered software. 

 We learned that the future isn't about AI replacing decision-makers—it's about enabling humans and AI agents to collaborate through well-defined capabilities. 

 Technically, we gained practical experience with: 

 
 WebMCP 
 Agent-oriented application architecture 
 FastAPI 
 Next.js 
 Production deployment 
 Docker 
 Cross-service communication 
 Enterprise workflow design 
 Secure API development 
 

 Perhaps the biggest lesson was that exposing structured capabilities through WebMCP produces a significantly more reliable interaction model than expecting AI systems to interpret complex graphical interfaces. 

 

 What's next for BoardMind 

 BoardMind is designed as the foundation for a much larger enterprise decision platform. 

 Our next goals include: 

 
 Native WebMCP support across every business module 
 Live integrations with Salesforce, Jira, SAP, Slack and Google Workspace 
 Persistent long-term agent memory 
 Multi-step executive approval workflows 
 Autonomous monitoring of live business events 
 Predictive planning using real company data 
 Multi-organization enterprise deployment 
 Secure organization-level permissions and governance 
 

 Our long-term vision is to build an operating system for executive decision-making where humans and AI agents collaborate naturally through WebMCP, enabling organizations to make faster, more transparent and better-informed decisions.

title: Open Application Desk
pitch: A WebMCP application workspace that audits live drafts, requests applicant-owned facts, stages visible fixes and submits only the exact hash-bound revision the applicant authorizes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP application workspace that audits live drafts, requests applicant-owned facts, stages visible fixes and submits only the exact hash-bound revision the applicant authorizes. Like Comment Story Updates A human-led application workspace where the page publishes five live WebMCP tools. A deterministic audit finds seven blockers - without changing the live draft. The agent stages a visible 3/10 → 7/10 improvement; only the applicant can apply it. The completed revision passes all ten checks but remains unapproved and unsubmitted. Human authorization is bound to one exact draft hash and expires after five minutes. A single-use receipt records seven blockers caught, 10/10 readiness, and the reviewed hash. Five typed WebMCP tools expose the page’s live state through closed input schemas. Inspiration Near a real submission deadline, I was reconciling official rules, deployment links, repository evidence, test results, and draft claims across several tabs. One stale claim nearly survived into the final submission. That experience exposed a deeper problem: application portals are built for clicking, not collaboration. An AI agent must scrape text and imitate UI actions, even when one invented fact or accidental submission could cost someone an opportunity. I built Open Application Desk around a safer idea: the agent prepares, the applicant supplies the facts, and only the applicant authorizes the exact submission. What it does Open Application Desk lets an applicant and an AI agent work on the same live application. The agent can inspect the requirements, find blockers and propose corrections, but it cannot apply changes, invent applicant facts, approve the application or even submit an unapproved draft. The page publishes five typed WebMCP tools that let an agent: Read the program requirements and exact live draft. Run a deterministic readiness audit without editing anything. Stage a bounded patch as a visible before-and-after diff. Prepare a passing revision for exact review. Submit only a review already authorized by the applicant. The reference journey begins at 3/10 ready with seven blockers . The agent proposes three bounded corrections and the page previews the result as 3/10 → 7/10 , but nothing changes until the applicant clicks Apply proposed changes . When an applicant-owned fact is missing, a contextual tool temporarily appears. Instead of allowing the agent to invent an answer, the page asks the applicant directly. After the applicant shares the answer, that tool disappears. When all 10 checks pass, the page creates a five-minute approval tied to a digital fingerprint of that exact draft. Any later edit cancels the approval. The applicant approves that version and only then can the agent submit it and receive one receipt. The OpenAI API supplies the reasoning; WebMCP lets the page publish its live tools, state and boundaries. How we built it I built the application with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Zod, WebMCP, Vitest, Playwright, and OpenAI Sites. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same workspace controller and domain rules. There is no separate agent-only state. Tool inputs use closed JSON Schemas and runtime Zod validation. The deterministic audit checks the live revision and performs bounded verification of public GitHub repository metadata and license availability. Proposed edits are evaluated against an in-memory candidate before the page shows their projected readiness, without mutating the real draft. prepare_submission re-audits the expected revision and creates a short-lived review bound to its SHA-256 draft hash. Any later edit invalidates that review. Submission also uses a browser-provided exclusive lock so repeated calls for the same approved review reconcile to one receipt. For the Chrome demonstration, I built an optional open-source developer inspector. It discovers the page’s registered WebMCP tools, maps their schemas to OpenAI Responses API functions, and returns structured tool results to the model. The API key remains in the local Chrome session. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was separating assistance from authority. It was easy to build an agent that could change fields; it was much harder to prove that it could not apply its own proposal, invent applicant facts, attest, or authorize submission. The contextual human handoff also required careful design. A WebMCP call should not remain open indefinitely while waiting for a person. The tool therefore returns an immediate awaiting_human result, the page collects the answer, and the agent re-reads the updated live state. WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability, so I also had to distinguish between ordinary browsers, ChatGPT’s supported in-app browser, and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The developer inspector made discovery and every tool call visible during testing and recording. Accomplishments that we're proud of A deterministic audit that changes zero application fields. A visible readiness projection before any proposed edit is applied. A contextual tool that appears only when a specific human-owned fact is missing. An agent that asks instead of inventing. A five-minute review bound to the exact draft revision and SHA-256 hash. Native human authorization before submission becomes possible. A single receipt recording seven blockers caught, 10/10 readiness, and the reviewed hash. One shared controller for both the human interface and WebMCP tools. Automated domain, component, WebMCP-registration, and browser-journey testing. The project was created during the submission period, beginning August 26, 2026. Its public commit history documents the implementation through the final challenge build. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is not the reasoning engine. Its value is allowing a webpage to publish a precise contract for what an agent can see and do. Structured tools are also not enough by themselves. Meaningful safety comes from combining typed capabilities with deterministic validation, state-dependent availability, visible human controls, revision checks, expiration, and exact-artifact authorization. I also learned that a tool disappearing can be as meaningful as a tool appearing. Once the applicant supplies the missing fact, the agent no longer needs permission to request it. What's next for Open Application Desk The current challenge sample intentionally stores its state in the visitor’s browser and uses a fictional reference program, making it easy for judges to reset and reproduce without an account. The next step is to replace that persistence layer with authenticated server storage while preserving the controller, five WebMCP contracts, deterministic gate, visible patch review, and human authorization boundary. Foundations, accelerators, admissions offices, fellowship programs, and procurement teams could publish their own requirement sets while applicants and agents work safely against the same authoritative state. Future versions could also support additional evidence providers, organization-defined policies, durable receipts, and accessible multi-user review. title: LivingTown
pitch: A town that learns from residents—and explains how verified knowledge changes an evacuation route.
about_excerpt: A town that learns from residents—and explains how verified knowledge changes an evacuation route. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The most useful evacuation knowledge often lives in everyday neighborhood conversations: “this crossing floods,” “this path is too narrow for a wheelchair,” or “this place is a safe waiting point.” Traditional maps rarely turn that local, changing knowledge into evidence that can safely affect a route. LivingTown explores a future where people and agents build a shared, verifiable memory of a town together. What it does LivingTown lets residents contribute local knowledge about barriers, flooding, darkness, narrow paths, and safe spots. Other participants can verify or dispute each item. Only verified knowledge can affect routing. In the evacuation drill, a person can register a privacy-safe household profile using only allowed constraints such as wheelchair, infant, elderly, or pet. LivingTown then calculates a deterministic route and explains exactly which verified knowledge changed it, which graph edges were avoided, and why. The production demo includes a long-distance wheelchair evacuation example: under flood + rain + daytime conditions, verified flood knowledge changes the route to a 1,330 m / 28 min evacuation to the existing shelter. The original canonical demo remains 440 m / 10 min for comparison. The experience is available in both 2D and 3D. A route-following 3D walkthrough moves from the household origin through the safe route, pauses at the avoided hazard with an explanation, and finishes at the shelter. Replay provides a KNOWLEDGE → ROUTE debrief so people and agents can review what changed and why. Why WebMCP LivingTown is a strong WebMCP use case because an agent should not have to guess how to operate a disaster-prevention UI. The app exposes structured, phase-scoped tools that let agents participate in the same workflow as people while respecting verification and privacy boundaries. MAP exposes contribute_knowledge , verify_knowledge , and query_area . DRILL exposes register_household , get_evacuation_route , and report_bottleneck . REPLAY exposes control_replay and get_debrief_summary . That is exactly eight WebMCP tools. The native adapter uses document.modelContext.registerTool , supports getTools() and toolchange , and uses per-registration abort handling. Native WebMCP was verified in Chrome 152. When the API is unavailable, LivingTown explicitly labels the local compatibility path as SIMULATED rather than presenting it as native evidence. Better user experience The user does not need to translate a vague request into a sequence of UI clicks. A person can ask an agent about an area, contribute or verify local knowledge, prepare an anonymous wheelchair household, calculate a route, and retrieve a debrief through explicit tool contracts. At the same time, the visual interface remains understandable for humans: pending → verified → affecting route is visible on the map, the avoided route is shown as a red dashed segment, the chosen route is shown in green, and the system explains why the route changed. What people and agents can do together Before LivingTown, community observations, accessibility constraints, route planning, and explanation typically lived in separate systems. LivingTown combines them into one accountable loop: Human observation → verification → agent-accessible structured knowledge → evacuation route → explanation → replay. An agent can help a wheelchair household without needing to know who that household is. The agent boundary is deliberately limited to anonymous labels, safe constraint enums, and temporary/demo locations rather than personal identity or exact private addresses. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite. Mapping uses MapLibre for 2D and a Navara/Three-based 3D visualization with GSI/OSM data sources and Dynamic PLATEAU-supported city visualization where available. A deterministic graph routing engine makes route changes reproducible. Verified knowledge affects routing only when agreements minus disagreements reach the verification threshold. Avoided edges and reasons are returned as structured route evidence. Production runs in SUPABASE_SHARED mode using Supabase Anonymous Auth, Realtime, RLS, owner-scoped temporary drill households, and RPC-only protected mutations. Community knowledge is shared; private drill state is owner-scoped. The production database and client share the same trusted graph-node boundary. Production demo No credentials are required. Recommended flow: Explore MAP and inspect community knowledge. Open DRILL and choose Try long-distance example / 遠距離の例を試す . Calculate the flood + rain wheelchair route: 1,330 m / 28 min with a verified flood avoidance reason. Switch to 3D and use the route walkthrough to see the avoided hazard and reach the shelter. Open REPLAY for the knowledge-to-route debrief. LivingTown is a prototype. Moderation, retention policy, stronger identity/Sybil resistance, and broader real-world routing coverage remain future work and are documented in the public repository. title: City for You
pitch: A city map that a browser agent reshapes around the preferences it already knows about you.
about_excerpt:
A city map that a browser agent reshapes around the preferences it already knows about you.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 City guides usually ask everyone the same questions: what they enjoy, how they move around, what their budget is, and what kind of day they want. We imagined a better experience where a browser agent can share only the relevant preferences, while the website keeps the personalization visible, optional, and reversible. 

 What it does 

 City for You is an interactive Santiago map that collaborates with browser agents through WebMCP. 

 The agent can inspect the map’s capabilities and propose a personalization using selected interests, mobility, budget, and an optional note. The website shows a preview before changing anything. After approval, it filters 80 curated places across 17 interests and creates a simple three-stop itinerary called “Your day in Santiago.” 

 Each recommendation includes a neighborhood, explanation, matched interests, suggested time, and contextual photograph. Users can ask the agent to explain the active personalization or reset the map at any time. 

 Three fictional profiles also make the experience testable without a WebMCP client. 

 How we built it 

 We built City for You with TypeScript, React, Vinext, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap, and OpenAI Sites. 

 The website registers five typed tools using document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 get_map_capabilities 
 preview_personalization 
 apply_personalization 
 explain_personalization 
 reset_personalization 
 

 Every tool has an explicit input schema and runtime validation. Previewed preferences are stored separately from the active map, preserving the approval step. 

 The itinerary uses a deliberately simple and inspectable ranking. It scores featured places by how many approved interests they match, gives free places a small boost for low-budget profiles, and avoids repeating neighborhoods when possible. 

 Codex helped us shape the concept, define the privacy boundary, implement and debug the WebMCP flow, expand the place catalog, build the responsive interface, write automated checks, and deploy the public site. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was designing personalization without suggesting that the website can directly read an agent’s memory. We solved this by accepting only a narrow, validated preference object and clearly showing what the site received. 

 We also had to keep preview and active state separate so an agent could not unintentionally change the experience before user approval. 

 Another challenge was making the result feel meaningfully personalized without introducing an opaque recommendation system. We chose a small deterministic ranking that is easy to explain and verify. 

 Finally, WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability, so we built fictional sample profiles as a reliable fallback for demos and unsupported clients. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that City for You demonstrates a complete WebMCP collaboration loop rather than a single agent-triggered action. 

 The final product includes: 

 
 Five working WebMCP tools 
 A visible preview-before-apply flow 
 80 Santiago places across 17 interests 
 Lifestyle-specific categories such as vegan, coffee, wellness, markets, pets, and live music 
 A ranked three-stop day plan 
 Explain and reset capabilities 
 A responsive public deployment 
 A complete fallback experience without an agent 
 

 Most importantly, personalization remains understandable and reversible throughout the experience. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP works best when the website and agent have clearly separated responsibilities. 

 The agent selects relevant context. The website validates it and owns the product logic. The person remains in control of whether the proposed change is applied. 

 We also learned that preview, explanation, and reset are not secondary privacy features. They are essential parts of a trustworthy personalized experience. 

 On the implementation side, we learned the importance of explicit tool schemas, runtime validation, lifecycle-safe tool registration, and deterministic behavior that can be tested without relying on model output. 

 What's next for City for You 

 Next, we would connect the map to live place data, opening hours, events, routing, accessibility details, and travel times. 

 We would also improve the ranking with distance, mobility, time of day, weather, and explicit user feedback while keeping every recommendation explainable. 

 Longer term, City for You could expand beyond Santiago and demonstrate the same consent-based personalization pattern across travel, commerce, education, and other agent-enabled websites.

title: cafe-techo (珈琲手帖)
pitch: A map-based cafe notebook where humans and browser agents keep the same records: shared cafe data, personal one-cup taste logs, five WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A map-based cafe notebook where humans and browser agents keep the same records: shared cafe data, personal one-cup taste logs, five WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration cafe-techo (珈琲手帖, "coffee notebook") is a map-based cafe notebook I built for myself first and opened to others in July 2026. Cafe information is shared and maintained together, like a wiki; taste records are personal, one cup at a time, with a five-axis radar (bitterness, acidity, sweetness, body, aroma). There are no scores or rankings, on purpose: taste is subjective. The part nobody enjoyed was data entry. Registering a cafe meant a long form: name, coordinates, business type, tags, amenities, opening hours, closed days, one field at a time, cursor after cursor. When WebMCP arrived, the question was not "can an agent do things on this site" but "can an agent do exactly what the person on this page can do, through the same door". What it does Five core actions of the site are published as WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool exists only on the page where the action makes sense: Tool Page Login What it does search_cafes home (map + list) no Applies a text query and filters (open now, power outlet, Wi-Fi, toilet, independent shops) by driving the page's own search box and filter chips get_cafe_page cafe page no Returns the cafe's structured details and the most recent cups logged there record_visit record page yes Logs one cup: drink, date, the five taste axes, aftertaste tags, comment register_cafe new cafe page yes Registers a cafe; coordinates are required and must not be guessed; same-name cafes within ~100 m are rejected with candidates update_cafe edit page yes Partial update of a cafe's basic information; name, coordinates, closed status and photos are excluded by design So a person can say "register Acme Coffee at these coordinates, a quiet independent kissaten, open 8 to 19, closed Wednesdays", confirm the agent's summary, and the cafe exists, with a pin on the map. Then "log a cup here" with their own ratings. Then back on the home page, "show independent cafes with power outlets", and the new cafe is in the list with the cup just logged. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP A cafe notebook is structured data with human judgement inside it. Hours, amenities and tags are facts anyone can maintain; a taste record is one person's subjective rating of one cup. Agents are good at the first part and must not invent the second. WebMCP lets the site say exactly which actions exist on which page, with a schema, so the agent fills in the structure while the person supplies the judgement. Because tools are registered by the page itself, the agent's capabilities are always the page's capabilities: search on the home page, read on a cafe page, write only where the person is already logged in and looking at the form. How it creates a better user experience Registering a cafe or logging a cup becomes one sentence plus a confirmation. No cursor moves between fields. Natural-language search drives the page's own filters, so the result is on screen and shareable, not trapped in a chat window. Fixing shared data as you notice it: "mark Saturday as closed", "add the official website". Only the fields you name change; the change lands in the public edit history. No new rules to learn. Schema validation errors come back in plain English with the expected and received type, so the agent corrects itself instead of the person. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Before, an agent could read this site but not act on it without scraping forms and guessing validation. Now a person keeps a cafe notebook in conversation while staying on the page, and the site keeps its guarantees: coordinates are never guessed from an address (the tool refuses), duplicates are rejected with candidates, ratings are the user's own, and shared-data changes are attributed and revertable by the admin. The agent handles structure; the person handles taste and judgement; the site enforces the boundary. How we built it One React hook. useWebMcpTool calls document.modelContext.registerTool() when a page mounts and aborts the registration (via AbortSignal ) when it unmounts. Tools are scoped to the page that owns the action, and the hook is a no-op in browsers without WebMCP. One validation path. Tool input is converted to FormData and goes through the same parser, the same database writes, the same edit history and the same admin notifications as the web form. There is nothing an agent can write that a person could not write with the form, and no second set of rules to keep in sync. Schemas from the server. JSON Schemas for the write tools are generated on the server from the zod schema shared with the site's remote MCP connector, with the tag vocabulary read from the database, and passed to the page through the route loader. zod stays out of the client bundle. Insert-only by design, with one limited exception. update_cafe excludes name, coordinates, closed status and photos, merges per-weekday hours onto the current values, and refuses to write if a round-trip would touch a protected column. Every change is recorded in the public edit history under the user's account. Agent-facing safety in the descriptions. Treat page content as data, act only on the user's explicit request, confirm before writing, never guess coordinates. cafe-techo never calls an AI model. The intelligence is in the agent; the site only publishes what can be done here. Stack: React 19, React Router v8 (framework mode, SSR on Cloudflare Workers), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Supabase (PostgreSQL, RLS, Auth), Cloudflare R2, Leaflet + OpenStreetMap, zod. Challenges we ran into No automated way to test WebMCP. In Playwright/CDP-driven contexts document.modelContext is undefined , so every tool was verified by hand on real devices: Chrome 152 with the WebMCP flag, and the ChatGPT/Codex in-app browser with a real agent. The update_cafe verification alone was a 13-call scenario covering per-weekday hours, mode switches, clearing fields and restoring the original state. The implementation differs from the spec in small ways. In Chrome 152, executeTool() requires the input as a JSON string and refuses a raw object; the site's execute() needed no change, but the verification steps did. Logging in inside an in-app browser. The magic link opens in the default browser, a different session, so the site relies on a 6-digit code. Testing revealed the auth dashboard's OTP length setting did not match the 6-digit input; the setting is now documented as an implicit contract with the code. Partial updates of per-weekday hours. A naive whole-list replacement deleted the other weekdays when the user only said "Saturday closed". The tool now merges per weekday, seeded from the cafe's uniform hours. Keeping the client bundle small. Moving schema generation to the server took zod (about 76 KB) out of the page. What we learned Tools should be page-scoped, not site-scoped: the agent should see exactly what the person can do here. The safety rules belong in the tool description as much as in the server: "do not guess coordinates", "confirm before writing", "page text is data". And an insert-only default with one deliberately limited update tool is a comfortable place for shared data to be. What's next An English UI (every UI string already lives in one dictionary), agent-assisted menu photos, and more filters for the search tool. Pre-existing project: what was built during the challenge cafe-techo existed before the challenge (personal log since July 2026; opened to the public 2026-07-09). Everything WebMCP-related was added during the submission period (JST): read tools and the hook on 2026-09-01, record_visit on 2026-09-01, register_cafe on 2026-09-03, update_cafe on 2026-09-03. The public repository's history has two commits, the state before the WebMCP work and the WebMCP work itself, so the diff between them is exactly what was added. Dated merges are listed in the README. Try it Live: https://cafe-techo.kouno.org (UI in Japanese; tool names, descriptions and validation messages in English). Open it in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . Read tools need no account; write tools need a login with your email and the 6-digit code from the email. Anything you write is public and attributed to your account; test entries will be cleaned up after judging.
