title: Replan - Agentic Travel Recovery
pitch: A flight-cancellation site where ChatGPT's own browser discovers and calls 12 WebMCP tools - rebook, hold a room, arrange transport - no custom agent built.
about_excerpt: A flight-cancellation site where ChatGPT's own browser discovers and calls 12 WebMCP tools - rebook, hold a room, arrange transport - no custom agent built. Like Comment Story Updates Natural-language travel constraints drive flight recovery through WebMCP. ChatGPT discovers and calls Replan's 12 WebMCP tools directly. The agent coordinates recovery while the human confirms consequential actions. A multi-step recovery coordinated across flights, hotel, ground transport, notifications, and budget. Inspiration Travel recovery is a good stress test for WebMCP because it is multi-step, stateful, and involves consequential actions. The scenario behind Replan is simple: imagine a nonstop flight to Miami being canceled the day before a cruise departure from PortMiami. The traveler needs to recover quickly while balancing constraints such as timing, hotel availability, ground transportation, and budget. I wanted to explore what happens when the website exposes its capabilities directly to an AI agent instead of requiring a custom conversational layer inside the application. What it does Replan is an agentic travel recovery app where a traveler sets goals and constraints in natural language while an AI agent discovers and operates the site's capabilities directly. The traveler can ask the agent to search for replacement flights, update constraints, hold a reservation, confirm a booking, rebook a hotel, arrange ground transportation, notify a contact, track the running trip cost, and generate an itinerary summary. The app exposes 12 WebMCP tools: ping search_flights search_flights_semantic update_constraints hold_reservation confirm_booking search_hotels update_hotel_reservation book_ground_transport notify_contact calculate_total_cost generate_itinerary_summary The human remains in control of consequential actions through explicit confirmation gates, while the agent handles the multi-step coordination. How we built it Replan is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Convex powers the one live backend piece—the semantic-search vector index, reached from the browser tool through an HTTP endpoint, so no Convex client code ships in the runtime bundle. The key integration is WebMCP. The page registers its capabilities through the WebMCP API using document.modelContext.registerTool() . ChatGPT, in its in-app browser, discovers those tools and calls them from natural-language requests. There is no custom LLM, NLU, voice layer, or custom agent in the Replan codebase. The application exposes structured capabilities and lets the agent decide how to compose them. The 12 tools are registered statically at page load. Each tool validates its inputs and returns structured JSON, including structured errors that allow the agent to understand failed operations and recover. One of the tools, search_flights_semantic , uses natural-language semantic ranking backed by a live vector index with embeddings rather than simple keyword matching. I verified the complete interaction flow manually: 12/12 tools registered, 36/36 demo turns passed, 0 failures . Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges was designing tool validation and error responses so that an AI agent could recover from invalid or conflicting requests. Structured errors turned out to be especially important because the agent needs actionable information rather than only human-readable error messages. Another challenge was designing confirmation boundaries. Search and other reversible operations can be performed speculatively, but consequential actions such as confirming a booking need an explicit human confirmation step. The final challenge was compressing a 36-turn recovery workflow into a clear demonstration under three minutes without losing the important WebMCP interactions. Accomplishments that we're proud of I successfully exposed the complete travel recovery workflow through WebMCP without building a custom agent or natural-language processing layer. The final implementation has 12 WebMCP tools , and the complete human verification covered 36/36 turns with 0 failures . Most importantly, the entire recovery chain can be driven from natural language: the agent discovers the capabilities exposed by the webpage, composes multiple tools, handles state and constraints, and stops for human confirmation when an action becomes consequential. What we learned WebMCP changes the design boundary between a website and an AI agent. The website does not need to understand how the agent reasons. It needs to expose clear, reliable capabilities that an agent can discover and compose. I also learned that confirmation gates are not just a UI concern. They shape the tool design itself by separating safe, reversible operations from consequential actions. Finally, structured JSON responses and meaningful errors are critical when tools are being operated by an agent. They provide the information needed for the agent to adapt instead of simply failing. What's next for Replan - Agentic Travel Recovery The next step is to make the recovery workflow more realistic and flexible. Potential extensions include partial availability, multi-leg itineraries, more complex constraint conflicts, and broader use of live vector search across additional travel capabilities. The goal is to continue exploring how far a website can go when it exposes reliable, composable capabilities directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. title: Warranty Vault
pitch: Warranty Vault is a personal warranty management web app for tracking products, purchase details, warranty coverage, invoices, manuals, warranty cards, and other supporting documents in one place.
about_excerpt: Warranty Vault is a personal warranty management web app for tracking products, purchase details, warranty coverage, invoices, manuals, warranty cards, and other supporting documents in one place. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page for Warranty Vault after user login Add warranty page Chart of remaining warranty per product List of WebMCP tools, from Chrome Agent using tool to create a new warranty item Agent conversing in Hindi+English to user for fethcing details of warranty Preview of uploaded warranty doc through Codex Agent Warranty Vault Inspiration Whenever we buy a product—an AC, TV, laptop, mobile phone, or home appliance—we receive product and warranty information in different ways. Sometimes we have to register the warranty manually on a website. Sometimes the information is available in a Gmail purchase email, invoice, PDF, receipt, or warranty document . The information already exists digitally, but we still have to manually organize it. To keep track of a warranty, users often have to search their emails, find the invoice or warranty document, read it, and manually copy details such as the product name, brand, model number, serial number, purchase date, price, warranty period, and expiry date into another application. Months or years later, when the warranty is about to expire—or when the product develops an issue—we have to search through the same old emails, PDFs, and invoices again. This made us ask a simple question: Why should users manually enter and search for information that already exists digitally? That question inspired us to build Warranty Vault . Warranty Vault brings the complete warranty lifecycle into one place—from capturing warranty information from Gmail to tracking expiry and helping users extend or claim their warranty when they need it. With WebMCP , Warranty Vault becomes agent-ready, allowing AI agents to understand the application's capabilities and perform structured actions on behalf of the user. What it does Warranty Vault is a smart warranty management application designed to eliminate repetitive manual warranty entry and simplify warranty management throughout the product lifecycle. Instead of manually finding an email, reading an invoice, and entering every field into Warranty Vault, a user can simply ask: "Find my AC warranty email in Gmail and add it to Warranty Vault." The AI can find the relevant purchase or warranty email in Gmail, understand the information, extract the required product and warranty details, and use Warranty Vault's WebMCP capabilities to create the warranty record. Warranty Vault can maintain information such as: Product name Brand Product category Model number Serial number Purchase date Purchase price Retailer or seller Warranty duration Warranty start date Warranty expiry date Invoice and supporting information But Warranty Vault doesn't stop after saving the warranty. It continues to help users throughout the complete warranty lifecycle . Warranty Expiry Tracking Warranty Vault keeps track of warranty expiry dates so users don't have to remember them manually. When a product is approaching its warranty expiry date, Warranty Vault can surface that information to the user so they can take action before it is too late. Claim Warranty If a product develops an issue while it is still under warranty, the user can initiate a warranty claim directly from the product record . Instead of searching again for the invoice, purchase date, model number, or warranty information, Warranty Vault already has the required product context available. Our complete experience is: Gmail / Invoice / PDF → AI extracts details → WebMCP → Warranty Vault → Track Expiry How we built it We started by building Warranty Vault as a structured product and warranty management web application . Users can manually add and manage warranties, but we didn't want to build another application where users simply move information from one form to another. The biggest opportunity was eliminating that repetitive manual entry. That's where WebMCP became an important part of the solution. We used WebMCP to make Warranty Vault agent-ready by exposing meaningful, structured capabilities that an AI agent can understand and use. Instead of requiring an AI agent to visually navigate the website, locate every input field, enter information, and click buttons, WebMCP allows Warranty Vault to expose the actions available to an agent and the information required to perform them. For our Gmail use case, the journey works like this: The user gives a natural-language instruction: "Find my AC warranty email in Gmail and add it to Warranty Vault." The AI searches Gmail for the relevant purchase or warranty email. It reads the relevant email and identifies the product and warranty information. It extracts available information such as product name, brand, model number, purchase date, purchase price, and warranty period. The extracted information is converted into the structured fields required by Warranty Vault. The AI discovers the relevant capability exposed by Warranty Vault through WebMCP. The agent provides the structured warranty information to Warranty Vault. Warranty Vault validates the information and creates the warranty record. This transforms the traditional experience from: Search Gmail → Open Email → Open Invoice → Read → Copy Details → Open Warranty App → Fill Form → Save into: Ask → AI understands → WebMCP acts → Warranty saved We also designed the experience around higher-level user actions rather than individual UI interactions. For example: Add Warranty Extend Warranty Claim Warranty This allows WebMCP to support the warranty lifecycle rather than simply automate form filling. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was that warranty information is not standardized . Different manufacturers and retailers provide product and warranty information differently. One Gmail message might contain all the required information directly in the email. Another might contain only basic purchase information with an attached invoice or PDF. Some documents clearly specify the warranty duration, while others may not mention it at all. This created an important challenge: How do we allow AI to understand unstructured information while keeping the data stored in Warranty Vault structured and reliable? We also had to think carefully about missing information. For example, if a purchase email doesn't contain a serial number or clearly specify the warranty duration, the AI should not invent information simply to complete the record. Another challenge was deciding what capabilities should be exposed through WebMCP. Instead of thinking about low-level interactions such as: "Click this button." or "Fill this field." we focused on meaningful user goals: "Add this warranty." "Extend this warranty." "Claim this warranty." This helped us design Warranty Vault not only as a website for humans, but as an application that AI agents can understand and interact with through structured capabilities . Building Warranty Vault with WebMCP helped us discover some interesting challenges around how agents interact with dynamic web applications. Dynamic WebMCP Tool Availability One of the first challenges we encountered was that Warranty Vault could be loaded successfully, but its WebMCP tool list could refresh during the agent's first interaction . This created situations where a tool discovered by the agent was temporarily unavailable or changed while the agent was attempting to use it. It highlighted an important consideration for agent-ready applications: tool discovery and tool execution need to remain reliable even while the underlying page and application state are changing. Page Loading vs. Agent Execution Another challenge occurred when the web page was not fully loaded and the WebMCP tools were not yet available . Agents are naturally eager to complete the user's task. If the expected WebMCP tools are not immediately available, the agent may attempt to continue by interacting with or scraping the UI instead of waiting for the structured WebMCP capabilities to become ready . For Warranty Vault, we wanted the agent to use WebMCP as the primary interaction mechanism rather than falling back to UI-based interaction too quickly. This taught us that agent-ready websites need clear readiness signals and reliable tool availability so agents know when to wait, retry tool discovery, or proceed. File Download and Upload Our warranty workflow also involves invoices, PDFs, receipts, and warranty documents , which introduced another challenge. While structured data such as product name, purchase date, and warranty period works naturally with WebMCP tools, file transfer is more complex . For example, an agent may need to: Read a Gmail message → download the attached invoice → extract warranty information → create the Warranty Vault record → upload or attach the original invoice. title: DrawMCP
pitch: I rebuilt the public Excalidraw MCP as a WebMCP to showcase the power and utility of WebMCP with a measured almost 7x performance improvement by doing so.
about_excerpt: I rebuilt the public Excalidraw MCP as a WebMCP to showcase the power and utility of WebMCP with a measured almost 7x performance improvement by doing so. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 20 randomized production pairs: DrawMCP finished the measured task 6.58x faster at p50. Seven WebMCP tools let the browser agent read and update the same live Excalidraw canvas. DrawMCP: Excalidraw's public MCP rebuilt as a WebMCP Inspiration Excalidraw has a great MCP server. I used it and kept running into one awkward boundary: the agent generated a diagram in a remote widget while the canvas in front of me remained separate. I wanted the agent to work with me on the page I already had open. That is where WebMCP clicked. DrawMCP is my WebMCP take on the current Excalidraw MCP. You draw through the normal Excalidraw controls, and the agent works on that same canvas through WebMCP. What it does DrawMCP gives a browser agent seven tools over the Excalidraw canvas on screen: get_canvas_summary get_selection add_elements update_elements delete_elements fit_to_content organize_diagram A person can sketch an idea, select part of it, or move a shape by hand. The agent reads that exact state and can continue the drawing. Both edits use one revision history, so the normal Excalidraw Undo and Redo controls still work. There is no connector to configure for the WebMCP path, no export step, and no second canvas to reconcile. The site also places the official Excalidraw MCP and DrawMCP side by side. Both are useful. They solve the agent-to-canvas boundary in different places. How I built it The app uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and the published Excalidraw React SDK. The /canvas page registers seven closed-schema tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read tools return bounded scene and selection summaries. Write tools validate their inputs again when they execute, serialize competing changes, support cancellation, and accept an optional expected_revision so a stale agent write cannot silently overwrite a newer human edit. Every agent mutation goes through one canvas service and Excalidraw's own element versioning. The tool returns after the editor has applied the change. Registrations are aborted when the page unmounts, and the ordinary editor still works when WebMCP is unavailable. I used Puppeteer for real-browser evaluation, Vitest for component and contract tests, AJV for runtime schema validation, and Vercel for the production deployment. The measured result I ran 20 randomized production pairs from the same machine. All 40 trials passed the same scene oracle. The DrawMCP lane called add_elements , called fit_to_content , and proved that the rendered Excalidraw pixels changed before its clock stopped. It measured 13.71 ms at p50. The official public MCP lane stopped when create_view returned its checkpoint, before the separate widget rendered, and measured 90.23 ms at p50. DrawMCP was 6.58 times faster for this measured task and 9.93 times faster at p90. Those clocks include different work, so I keep the boundary beside the result. This is a measured workflow result, not a claim that every WebMCP site beats every remote MCP server. Challenges I ran into Drawing rectangles was easy. Keeping Excalidraw normal after an agent write was the real work. Bound text, connectors, selection, revisions, stale writes, cancellation, local recovery, and native history all had to survive the tool boundary. The benchmark was the second hard part. The two implementations do not expose the same stopping point. I kept every failed trial in the denominator, randomized the lane order, throttled calls to the public service, checksummed the raw rows, and withheld p95 because each live lane had fewer than 40 successful samples. Accomplishments that I am proud of The final release passed 115 deterministic tests, 17 browser proof steps against both the development and production builds, 11 Chrome Labs smoke calls, 125 repeated local-model decisions, and nine desktop and mobile visual routes. The shared-canvas evaluation also proved a complete human edit, WebMCP read, agent write, rendered change, Undo, and Redo sequence. More importantly, the product still feels like Excalidraw. The person can use the normal keyboard shortcuts and pointer while the agent sees the same scene. Nothing has to leave the page for the two of them to continue working. What I learned WebMCP changes who owns the useful context. The page already knows the current selection, viewport, scene revision, and undo history. Exposing a small set of bounded tools lets the agent use that context without inventing another document model beside it. I also learned that tool design matters more than tool count. Seven narrow tools were enough because each one has a clear job, a closed input schema, bounded output, and visible consequences on the page. What's next for DrawMCP I want to prepare a narrow upstream proposal for the official Excalidraw MCP project after the challenge, so this can be officially integrated into the live Excalidraw platform For now, the live site shows the thing I wanted to test: a person and an agent can work on the same open Excalidraw canvas without passing a drawing back and forth. title: AgentReady
pitch: AgentReady audits websites for AI-agent readiness and turns commercial gaps into structured, actionable WebMCP capabilities.
about_excerpt:
AgentReady audits websites for AI-agent readiness and turns commercial gaps into structured, actionable WebMCP capabilities.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Bannière 3:2 : AgentReady — Visibility. Understanding. Buyability. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Logo : AgentReady — AI Commerce Readiness 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Bannière 3:2 : AgentReady — Visibility. Understanding. Buyability. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Logo : AgentReady — AI Commerce Readiness 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Bannière 3:2 : AgentReady — Visibility. Understanding. Buyability. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming a new way for people to interact with the web, but most small-business websites were built for humans and search engines — not for agents. 

 A business may have products, services, prices, booking options or contact flows publicly available, yet an AI agent can still struggle to reliably understand what the business offers or how to take action. 

 AgentReady started from a simple question: how can a small business know whether its website is actually ready for AI agents? 

 What it does 

 AgentReady audits a real website and evaluates its AI commerce readiness across three dimensions: 

 Visibility → Understanding → Buyability 

 It analyzes observable commercial information, evaluates what an AI agent can reliably understand, and produces evidence-based scores and prioritized recommendations. 

 The goal is not simply to make websites more machine-readable. The goal is to help businesses move from being visible to AI agents to becoming genuinely understandable and actionable by them. 

 AgentReady also exposes its audit capability directly to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 The native WebMCP tool agentready.run_audit allows an agent to launch the same website audit available to a human through the AgentReady interface and receive structured results including readiness scores, observed evidence, recommended actions, rendering provenance and monitoring eligibility. 

 This creates one capability for two users: 

 Humans get a clear visual audit. AI agents get a structured, callable tool. 

 How we built it 

 AgentReady uses an evidence-first audit architecture designed to avoid inventing commercial facts. 

 The challenge demo combines a browser interface with a bounded server-side audit function. For JavaScript-heavy websites where the initial HTML does not expose enough reliable evidence, AgentReady can use a controlled browser-rendering fallback and clearly reports that provenance. 

 The WebMCP integration registers agentready.run_audit through: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 The tool calls the same AgentReady audit capability used by the human interface and returns structured content that an AI agent can consume directly. 

 This means WebMCP is not a separate demonstration layer: humans and agents access the same underlying capability. 

 AgentReady also includes monitoring of comparable audits over time, allowing businesses to identify improvements or degradation in their AI readiness while avoiding false comparisons when an acquisition is incomplete. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest problem has been factual reliability across very different types of websites. 

 Real-world sites contain navigation elements, product cards, booking flows, duplicated prices, dynamic JavaScript content and commercial information distributed across different structures. 

 AgentReady therefore follows a simple principle: 

 Observed, not assumed. 

 If reliable evidence cannot be observed, the system should report uncertainty rather than manufacture a confident answer. 

 Another challenge was making dynamic website audits reproducible. The browser-rendering fallback and monitoring eligibility rules were designed to prevent incomplete page acquisition from creating misleading readiness changes. 

 What's next 

 The next step is expanding AgentReady from one callable audit capability into a broader AI commerce readiness layer where detected gaps can map to additional WebMCP actions. 

 The longer-term loop is: 

 Audit → Detect capability gap → Expose capability → Agent takes action 

 The vision is to make AI commerce readiness accessible to small businesses that do not have dedicated technical teams — so they can participate in an increasingly agent-driven web without having to understand the underlying technology.

During the challenge, I focused specifically on turning AgentReady’s audit capability into a native, structured WebMCP tool that AI agents can discover and invoke directly.

title: Nearcast WebMCP
pitch: Nearcast is a WebMCP-powered cross-border hazard map that helps people and AI agents explore authoritative wildfire, severe weather, and earthquake data across Canada and the U.S.
about_excerpt: Nearcast is a WebMCP-powered cross-border hazard map that helps people and AI agents explore authoritative wildfire, severe weather, and earthquake data across Canada and the U.S. Like Comment Story Updates Map Overview Focusing on a specific region Human + Agent Shared State Cross-Border Hazard Comparison Inspiration Nearcast began as a Canadian iPhone app that pulls official hazard data. Hazard maps are exactly the kind of interface generic browser agents struggle with: hundreds of clustered markers, a dozen filter combinations, geographic bounds, a selection, and six agencies' worth of heterogeneous records. WebMCP lets the page say what it can do instead of making the agent infer it from the DOM. What it does Nearcast WebMCP shows current wildfires, weather alerts and earthquakes across Canada and the United States on one MapLibre map, normalized from six official sources (ECCC, NRCan CWFIS, Earthquakes Canada, NWS, NIFC, USGS) with explicit attribution and freshness. Every source fails independently; if a feed is down the app says so and keeps working. It exposes eight WebMCP tools that read and mutate the same application state the human is looking at: get_current_view — map bounds, zoom, filters, selected hazard, counts, source freshness get_visible_hazards — concise list of what is on screen after all filters set_focus_area — move the map to regions ( ["BC","WA"] ), bounds, or a point set_hazard_filters — countries, hazard types, minimum weather severity, minimum magnitude focus_hazard — select a hazard exactly like a human click (highlight, pan, details panel) get_hazard_details — full record with agency classifications and the official link compare_regions — deterministic counts for provinces/states create_situation_context — structured facts for an area; the agent writes the prose An Agent Activity panel logs every tool call, so people can see what the agent did. Why WebMCP fits this use case Map applications hold large amounts of visual state. Screen-scraping and clicking is brittle and slow. WebMCP gives the agent typed, described operations while keeping human and agent in the same visible workspace : the human zooms and clicks, the agent reads that through get_current_view , changes filters or focus, and the human sees it happen and refines by hand. Better UX Instead of manually toggling countries, filtering hazard types and scanning hundreds of markers, the user says "Focus on British Columbia and Washington and show only wildfires and important weather alerts" — and still sees and controls the resulting map. Verified live in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser with GPT-5.6. What humans and agents do together Human: explores visually, selects incidents, validates context, controls decisions. Agent: manipulates filters, compares regions, retrieves structured details, surfaces relevant information, writes the narrative. Application: authoritative normalized data, deterministic geographic calculations and counts, visual state — and never a "you are safe" claim. How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite + MapLibre GL (OpenFreeMap basemap, no tokens). One TypeScript Lambda behind API Gateway HTTP API with six source adapters ( Promise.allSettled , per-source timeouts, stale-snapshot fallback), a shared hazard model, and severity translation kept alongside raw agency classifications. CloudFront serves the SPA from a private S3 bucket (OAC) and routes /api/* to API Gateway so everything is same-origin; Terraform provisions all of it. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() and wrap the app's own store actions — the same functions a click uses. No AI API keys anywhere: WebMCP is the AI integration. Challenges Government feeds are inconsistent: CWFIS's national fire layer is temporal (189k rows; only rows whose validity window includes "now" are current), most NWS alerts have no polygon (placed at Census county centroids and flagged approximate ), Earthquakes Canada is pipe-delimited text. Keeping severity honest: earthquakes and US wildfires have no agency severity, so we expose magnitude/hectares plus a clearly labelled display significance instead of inventing one. Demo robustness: per-source failure handling, stale snapshots, and a clearly labelled demo-data mode. Accomplishments Live cross-border six-source hazard workspace; eight well-described tools; shared state proven by get_current_view reflecting manual pans and clicks; 44 unit tests; reproducible Terraform deployment; verified end-to-end in ChatGPT's built-in browser. What we learned Tool descriptions and strict schemas matter more than tool count. Deterministic, structured outputs (counts, ids, source status) let the agent explain without hallucinating, and a visible activity log makes the collaboration legible to people. What's next Evacuation orders (BC first), air quality, time-windowed regional summaries, and Chrome origin-trial enrollment. Safety Nearcast is an awareness tool, not an emergency service. It always shows the issuing agency, timestamps and the official link, and reminds users to follow local emergency authorities. I designed the product and the human + agent experience, chose the government data sources (reusing what I learned building the Nearcast iPhone app), and built and deployed the full stack: React/MapLibre front end, TypeScript Lambda API, Terraform on AWS, and the eight WebMCP tools. I used Claude Code as a pair programmer throughout and tested the tools live in ChatGPT's desktop browser and Chrome. Biggest lesson: good tool descriptions and deterministic, structured outputs matter far more than tool count. title: Lense
pitch: Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface. Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface with WebMCP, explicit approvals, screen observation, and a bounded local desktop bridge.
about_excerpt: Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface. Turn any screen into an agent-addressable interface with WebMCP, explicit approvals, screen observation, and a bounded local desktop bridge. Like Comment Story Updates setup bridge Drawing a picture of a house Drawing and Evaluating picture of house lense chopping wood Inspiration Lens explores what happens when WebMCP needs to reach beyond the webpage. It combines structured WebMCP tools, screen observation, explicit human approval, verification, an inspectable event log, and an optional paired local desktop bridge to create a controlled path from an agent in the browser to workflows running elsewhere on the computer. WebMCP gives websites a powerful new capability: instead of making an AI agent infer what a site can do by looking at the interface, the site can expose structured tools directly. That made me wonder: What about software that isn't a website? A huge amount of important software still runs as: Desktop applications Legacy enterprise applications Internal Windows tools Creative software Games Testing environments Operating-system interfaces A normal webpage cannot and should not be allowed to arbitrarily control those applications. Lens explores whether WebMCP can still act as the structured control plane while preserving that security boundary. It gave your web browser eyes. What I Built Lens is a local-first WebMCP application combining: Screen observation Structured action proposals Target resolution Policy checks Human approval Desktop action execution Post-action verification An inspectable event timeline Reusable workflows Deterministic Paint, Notepad, and Claims demonstrations An optional local native companion for bounded desktop input The basic workflow is: Observe → Propose → Approve → Act → Verify Rather than sending a long blind macro, Lens can represent workflows as individual inspectable steps. WebMCP Tools Lens exposes structured WebMCP capabilities around the control loop. The tools allow agents to interact with the same runtime used by the UI for operations involving: Session state Screen observations Planned actions Action sequences Approval state Execution Verification Clipboard workflows Reusable recorded workflows Demo scenarios Event history The application currently contains 19 strict WebMCP tools when native WebMCP support is available. The WebMCP documentation page derives directly from the tool definitions and includes example prompts and chained workflows. Why WebMCP Traditional desktop automation tends to fall into one of two categories. One is a fixed macro. The other is an autonomous computer-use system that attempts to understand the entire interface visually. Lens explores something in between. WebMCP provides a structured agent-facing control surface. The application can then layer: policies approvals local capabilities observation providers verification around those tools. That means reasoning and permission do not have to be the same thing. An agent may be capable of proposing an action without automatically being allowed to execute it. The Local Bridge Browsers intentionally cannot issue arbitrary operating-system mouse and keyboard commands. Lens does not try to bypass that. For real desktop input, the user explicitly runs and pairs a small local companion. The companion provides a narrow local bridge for approved desktop operations. The bridge is intentionally constrained. It does not expose a general-purpose shell, unrestricted filesystem API, remote command server, or privilege escalation mechanism. The user can pause or disconnect it, clear pairing, create a new pairing code, and use an emergency stop hotkey. Screen sharing also requires explicit browser permission. Human + Agent Collaboration The human remains part of consequential workflows. Lens is designed around visibility. The user can see: what the agent observed what it proposed what action is waiting whether approval is required what was executed what changed afterward This makes the automation inspectable instead of hiding it behind an autonomous loop. The deterministic demonstrations make that architecture visible through scenarios such as drawing in Paint, typing in Notepad, and stopping before a fictional consequential claims submission. How I Built It The browser application is built with Vue, Pinia, TypeScript, IndexedDB, browser screen capture, and WebMCP. A shared runtime coordinates: planning target resolution policy approval execution observation verification The normal UI and WebMCP tools both use that same runtime. The optional native companion is written in Rust and implements local desktop input backends. The browser application remains the control surface while the bridge is intentionally limited to the local actions it has been designed to accept. Challenges I Faced The largest challenge was the browser security boundary. There are good reasons a webpage cannot simply start controlling the user's desktop. The solution had to make desktop capability explicit rather than trying to hide or bypass that limitation. That led to pairing, origin checks, strict message formats, local-only communication, approvals, and emergency controls. Another challenge was separating what is deterministic today from what could eventually be powered by more advanced semantic vision. The submitted architecture does not need to pretend that arbitrary desktop applications can already be perfectly understood. Richer observation systems can be added later while keeping the same policy and execution architecture. What I Learned The biggest lesson from Lens was: Capability and permission should be modeled separately. An agent being able to determine the next action should not automatically grant it permission to perform that action. WebMCP provides a useful structured capability layer. The application can then determine when those capabilities are safe to execute automatically and when the human should remain involved. What's Next The most interesting extension would be adding stronger semantic screen-understanding providers. Those providers could improve how targets and state are identified while keeping the existing WebMCP interface, approval model, pairing system, execution engine, and verification loop. The same architecture could potentially apply to: Legacy enterprise software Desktop QA Accessibility tools Creative applications Internal company software Remote support Specialized computer-use agents The broader experiment is whether WebMCP can become a structured control plane for experiences that extend beyond the page itself. title: MASIL — Reconnecting Korean Elders to Creative Life
pitch: Korean elders living alone lose access to creative spaces. Only the web remains; its UI fails them. WebMCP turns Agent access into human access—restoring creative life and expanding what’s possible.
about_excerpt: Korean elders living alone lose access to creative spaces. Only the web remains; its UI fails them. WebMCP turns Agent access into human access—restoring creative life and expanding what’s possible. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP optimization Landing page Calligraphy Janggi Inspiration What happens when the only path left is still inaccessible? MASIL began with a double exclusion. For Korean elders who live alone and can no longer leave home, the places that sustained their creative and social life become unreachable. The web may be the only path left—yet its interface creates a second barrier. Korea entered a super-aged society in 2025, when people aged 65 or older reached 20.3% of the population . The 2024 census counted 2.289 million one-person households in that age group . Meanwhile, the older-adult group scored 95.4 for digital access but only 56.2 for digital capability . A device can be within reach while the activity remains out of reach. MASIL (마실) means casually stepping out into the neighborhood—a small trip that is no longer easy for the people this project serves. Why calligraphy and Janggi? They were natural starting points: two forms of living Korean heritage sustained through practice, participation, and shared place. Calligraphy remains a mainstay of senior welfare centers, renewing the tradition whenever brush meets paper. Janggi has long served as social infrastructure. At Seoul’s Tapgol Park, a 30-year tradition gathered players and onlookers for play, debate, and conversation; removing the boards dispersed the gathering. For many Korean elders, these are more than pastimes. They give everyday life rhythm and momentum—something to practice, improve, share, and look forward to. MASIL asks whether WebMCP can turn the Agent’s access to a website into the elder’s access to the activity, allowing creative life to continue and expand without first mastering the interface. What it does MASIL is not assisted navigation. It is a live creative space where an Agent contributes through WebMCP and the elder shapes and continues the same activity. What becomes possible only when all three work together? Approach What it brings Result for the elder Voice Agent alone Understands and generates An answer outside the activity Fixed UI alone Holds visible state and valid actions Predetermined content that still requires control literacy Agent + WebMCP + Web UI Creates, interprets, holds provider truth, and connects both directions The elder creates and plays without first mastering the interface Calligraphy: imagination beyond a fixed library What changes: Their imagination—not a fixed library—defines what they can practice. Describe (Elder → Agent) — They ask for 추석 in a soft, flowing brush style. Create (Agent) — Their Agent generates that exact calligraphy reference. Place (Agent → WebMCP → Web UI) — It enters the live canvas without altering human strokes. Make it theirs (Elder → Web UI) — They write over it through air writing or direct drawing. The starting point is generated; the finished work remains theirs. Janggi: familiar words become a real match What changes: Their decades of Janggi experience—not interface literacy—become enough to play a complete match. Speak (Elder → Agent) — They say, “포 사용해서 위쪽 차 먹어줘” (“Use the cannon to capture the chariot at the top”). Resolve (Agent ↔ WebMCP state) — WebMCP exposes the board, turn, and legal moves. The Agent resolves the coordinate-free request, including the cannon's screen-piece rule, against that state. Play it safely (Agent → WebMCP → Web UI) — MASIL validates and animates the legal move. Continue (Elder ↔ Web UI ↔ WebMCP ↔ Agent) — The Agent takes the other side. A direct move by the elder returns to the waiting Agent, so speech and direct play continue the same match. Together, the two experiences restore access while expanding what the activity can become: creation beyond a fixed library and a complete match through familiar language. How we built it The Agent expands what is possible. WebMCP turns that capability into a live activity the elder can enter and continue without first learning the interface. MASIL is built around one continuing exchange, not a collection of Agent commands. The elder's Agent handles conversation, interpretation, generation, and the next judgment. MASIL provides the live canvas, Janggi board, rules, and visible activity. WebMCP joins them in both directions: the Agent's contribution enters the Web UI, and what the elder does there becomes new context for the Agent. The result is a single loop: elder's words → Agent judgment → WebMCP → live activity → elder's action → Agent continuation . We implemented its semantic tool surface with document.modelContext.registerTool() in a Next.js, React, and TypeScript app. WebGPU and Vercel Labs' vGPU render the creative spaces, while ONNX Runtime Web supports local hand tracking. Challenges we ran into Once that loop worked, we found that tool execution was the easy part. A WebMCP call could return successfully while the activity still failed: a calligraphy reference remained outside the canvas, a Janggi move stopped at an explanation, or the Agent continued from stale state. Tool-level tests could therefore make a broken user experience look complete. So we evaluated the experience end to end. We froze 15 realistic scenarios, ran each twice in a clean context, and scored only the complete visible outcome. Across one control and 24 WebMCP candidates—25 official iterations in total—we refined the Agent-facing surface while keeping every task and assertion fixed. Every failed candidate stayed in the record; the definition of success never moved. Accomplishments that we're proud of On the same frozen 30-session evaluation, the no-WebMCP control succeeded in 6 of 30 trials. The retained iteration-008 succeeded in 28. Same frozen evaluation No WebMCP control iteration-008 Overall task success 6/30 (20.0%) 28/30 (93.3%) Calligraphy 2/16 (12.5%) 14/16 (87.5%) Janggi 4/10 (40.0%) 10/10 (100%) Interface continuity 0/4 (0%) 4/4 (100%) Agent tokens per try 21,593 18,550 Seconds per try 21.1 21.1 That is a 73.3 percentage-point improvement , using about 14% fewer Agent tokens with no increase in average time. We did not stop when the score first peaked: we tested 17 more candidates after iteration-008 and rejected every one because none produced a better verified result. Every iteration preserves its exact candidate source, case grades, timing, and final responses. What we learned What MASIL taught us Access is not participation. A person can have a connected device and still be excluded if meaningful activity begins only after they understand the interface. Voice or an Agent alone may leave them with an answer outside the activity. Generation becomes meaningful inside a continuing activity. An Agent can create a new starting point for each person and moment, but an output in chat is still only a response. WebMCP makes it usable when that contribution enters the live Web UI, remains shapeable, and can be changed by what the elder does next. How we now define WebMCP: a new accessibility standard We now see WebMCP as a shared accessibility layer that turns technical Agent access into human participation without requiring interface mastery first . Conventional accessibility remains essential; WebMCP adds a second criterion for the Agent-native web: Can a person enter, shape, and expand a meaningful web activity through their Agent—without first mastering its interface? A WebMCP-ready website can meet people through the language and abilities they already have, then open possibilities that no fixed interface could anticipate. What's next for MASIL — Reconnecting Korean Elders to Creative Life Calligraphy and Janggi are MASIL's starting point, not its boundary. We will first test whether homebound Korean elders can begin, shape, and resume meaningful creative activity through their Agent without learning the interface. If that voluntary experience earns trust, MASIL could become an earlier doorway for unmet needs: an elder explicitly asks for help, reviews what would be shared, and chooses whether it moves forward. Korea's customized-care system serves about 550,000 vulnerable elders through roughly 2,600 dedicated social workers and 35,000 frontline care workers ; MASIL does not claim to save their time, but asks whether a trusted return path could help scarce human attention reach people before isolation becomes a crisis. title: Murph Food Lab
pitch: Compare 2M+ foods with clear grades, lab evidence, and WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Compare 2M+ foods with clear grades, lab evidence, and WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Murph Food Lab compares more than two million foods with ChatGPT and WebMCP. ChatGPT sees four typed WebMCP tools exposed directly by the Food Lab page. Murph compares exact products in one normalized nutrition table. Open the grade, ingredients, and product-level lab evidence behind each result. Inspiration Food labels make simple choices hard. Serving sizes differ, ingredient lists are difficult to scan, and lab results rarely tell a shopper what matters. We wanted a child, a parent, or an AI agent to compare real products and understand the tradeoffs in seconds. What it does Murph Food Lab searches more than two million branded foods and compares up to four exact products side by side. It normalizes nutrition to the same basis, shows a clear A-E Murph grade, calls out useful and concerning ingredients, and links exact product-level lab evidence when it exists. The person and the agent share one visible workspace. The agent can search for foods, add exact products, read the current comparison, and open the evidence drawer. The person stays in control and sees every result the agent used. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the interaction layer, not a wrapper around a chatbot. The Food Lab page registers four typed tools: search_food_products searches the public catalog and returns exact product references. compare_food_products places selected products into the visible comparison. get_food_comparison reads the same normalized metrics and grades shown to the person. show_food_evidence opens the visible evidence view for one selected product. Each tool has bounded input, structured output, and shares the current page state. This lets an agent act through the real interface instead of using a separate hidden backend. How we built it We built the experience with TypeScript, React, Next.js, WebMCP, PostgreSQL, Vercel, Brandfetch, and Codex CLI. Murph reuses its public product search and exact-evidence APIs. Nutrition comparison and grading use deterministic code. WebMCP exposes those same results to compatible agents. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping the result useful without pretending that one food is universally healthy. We kept nutrition, ingredients, and lab evidence separate. Missing lab data stays unknown instead of becoming a safety claim. We also filtered generic database rows that look like products but do not identify a real consumer product. Accomplishments that we are proud of A shared human-agent comparison instead of a separate AI chat result. More than two million searchable food records. Clear A-E grades with plain-language reasons. Exact product-level evidence when available. Stable layouts across loading, empty, mobile, and four-product states. Brand matching without exposing the Brandfetch credential to the browser. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools control a useful page that already makes sense to a person. Typed tool inputs, exact product references, and shared visible state made the agent behavior easier to trust and debug. What is next We want to add barcode scanning, more exact lab sources, regional product catalogs, and personal comparison preferences. We also want agents to explain why two similar products received different grades without hiding the underlying label or evidence. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: WithGeX — Human + Agent Collaborative Planning with WebMCP
pitch: A shared planning workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live state through WebMCP — with real context, proposals, approvals, and human control.
about_excerpt: A shared planning workspace where humans and AI agents work on the same live state through WebMCP — with real context, proposals, approvals, and human control. Like Comment Story Updates Shared activity timeline showing agent actions, blocked writes, proposals, and human decisions in a visible audit trail. WebMCP settings showing live connection status, five registered tools, context controls, autonomy modes, and human-only restrictions. Shared dashboard showing plan health, agent mission, risks, WebMCP connection, and human-agent collaboration status. Five live WebMCP tools registered through the page, with context controls, autonomy modes, and restricted human-only actions. Human-locked work rejects agent modification through WebMCP, proving that human constraints override agent autonomy. Agent-generated proposal with before/after impact, risk level, reasoning, and explicit human approval or rejection controls. Live planning workspace where human focus becomes agent context, with tasks, dependencies, priorities, and plan analysis in one view. A real WebMCP update creates a medium-risk proposal with before/after impact and explicit human approval controls. WithGeX combines shared context, live WebMCP tools, human approval, and controlled agent actions in one collaborative workspace. Inspiration Most AI agents work beside the software humans already use. The human works in one interface, then has to explain context again in a chat, upload data, or synchronize a separate copy of the task state. WithGeX was built around a different idea: What if the human and the agent worked on the same live workspace? With WebMCP, the page itself can expose structured tools and context directly to the agent. That makes it possible for human focus, planning state, dependencies, locks, and decisions to stay inside one shared operating surface. The goal of WithGeX is not to maximize agent autonomy. It is to make human-agent collaboration more direct, visible, and controllable. What it does WithGeX is a live collaborative planning workspace where a human and an AI agent operate on the same project state. A human can select, edit, move, prioritize, and lock planning items in the UI. At the same time, an agent can access that same live workspace through WebMCP. The agent can: read the full workspace detect the human's current focus add planning items propose or apply updates depending on risk and autonomy settings analyze blockers, dependencies, schedule risk, and critical path When a human selects a card, that same item immediately becomes available to the agent through get_current_focus . There is no copy/paste step and no separate project state. WithGeX also keeps humans in control. Low-risk changes may be applied automatically, while more meaningful changes become proposals for human approval. Humans can reject proposals, lock critical work against agent changes, and review actions in a shared activity history. How we built it WithGeX is built with: React 19 TypeScript Vite Zustand Tailwind CSS 4 @dnd-kit WebMCP through document.modelContext The UI and WebMCP tools both use the same live Zustand store. There is no separate agent-facing copy of the workspace. WithGeX registers five WebMCP tools: get_workspace_state get_current_focus add_item update_item analyze_plan These tools are registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and operate on the same live state shown to the human. How WebMCP is used WebMCP is the core connection between the agent and the live planning surface. The agent does not receive an exported copy of the project. Instead, WebMCP exposes the current state of the page directly. This means: when the human changes focus, the agent sees the new focus when the agent acts, the change appears in the same UI when a human locks an item, the WebMCP write is blocked when an agent creates a proposal, the human reviews it in the same workspace The page becomes the shared context between the human and the agent. Human authority WithGeX uses three autonomy modes: Observe — all agent mutations are blocked Assist — low-risk changes auto-apply; medium/high-risk changes become proposals Autonomous — low/medium-risk changes auto-apply; high-risk changes still require approval Risk is based on the type of change. Low risk: title, description, owner Medium risk: due date, status, priority High risk: dependencies Human locks always take priority over autonomy settings. If an agent attempts to modify a locked item, the request returns: ITEM_LOCKED_BY_HUMAN The agent cannot lock or unlock items itself. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making WebMCP feel like part of the product rather than an external API demonstration. It was relatively straightforward to register tools, but much harder to make the agent's actions feel naturally connected to the human experience. We had to solve several interaction problems: keeping the human's current selection synchronized with agent context preventing agent actions from silently changing important work defining a clear risk model for agent edits making locks override autonomy settings distinguishing real WebMCP runtime history from seeded demo history making proposal creation and approval understandable inside the workspace ensuring the UI and WebMCP tools always use the same state These constraints shaped the product more than the individual tools themselves. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part we are most proud of is that WithGeX does not treat WebMCP as a hidden backend connection. The WebMCP relationship is visible in the product. A judge can: select a task and see Agent Context change immediately inspect the five registered WebMCP tools execute a real tool against the live workspace generate a proposal through update_item reject that proposal as a human attempt to modify a locked item and see the write blocked verify the interaction in the Activity timeline That creates a complete human-agent collaboration loop inside a single web application. What we learned Building WithGeX changed how we think about agent UX. A capable agent is not enough. The human also needs to understand: what context the agent currently has what the agent is allowed to change what it tried to change why it proposed a change what remains under human authority WebMCP makes the technical connection possible, but good human-agent collaboration still requires clear boundaries and visible state. What's next for WithGeX The current version focuses on collaborative planning, but the same shared-workspace model could extend to many other applications. Possible next steps include: multi-user shared workspaces external agent clients server-side persistence team-level permissions richer approval policies organization-specific agent authority rules real-time collaboration additional planning and project-management tools reusable WebMCP collaboration patterns for other applications Long term, we see WithGeX as a pattern for software where humans and agents do not work in separate interfaces. They work together in the same one. title: TrustFill
pitch: This is TrustFill. It's a grant application form that an AI agent can fill out for you — but it's built so the agent can never submit anything sensitive without you confirming it first.
about_excerpt: This is TrustFill. It's a grant application form that an AI agent can fill out for you — but it's built so the agent can never submit anything sensitive without you confirming it first. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP's whole premise is that agents shouldn't have to guess their way through a page — a site can just declare what an agent is allowed to do. Reading Chrome's WebMCP tool security guidance, one line stuck with us: agents are powerful precisely because they act with the user's session already open, which is also exactly why that power needs a boundary. Most of the WebMCP demos we saw were about letting agents do more — search faster, check out faster. We wanted to explore the opposite question: could WebMCP be the thing that lets an agent do less, on purpose, in exactly the right places? High-stakes forms — grant applications, insurance claims, legal filings — are where people are least willing to hand an agent full control. That felt like the right place to test whether "trust" could be a structural property of a tool, not just a line in a system prompt. What it does TrustFill is a grant application — the Riverbend Micro-Grant form — that a WebMCP-aware agent can fill out on your behalf, with a hard boundary baked into the tools themselves. For low-risk fields (business name, address, EIN, founding date), the agent fills them in directly. For anything with real consequences — annual revenue, requested amount, legal certifications — the agent cannot fill them at all; the tool it would need rejects the call outright and requires it to flag the field with a reason instead. The application cannot be submitted while any flagged field is unresolved. A live audit trail records every action, agent or human, in order, so nothing happens invisibly. The result: an agent that's genuinely useful for the boring 80% of a form, and structurally incapable of guessing on the 20% that matters. How we built it The frontend is React + Vite with Tailwind for styling, and all state lives in a single reducer-driven form model — no backend needed for the demo. Six tools are registered through the real WebMCP API, document.modelContext.registerTool , each with an AbortController for clean unregistration on unmount: get_form_state , fill_field , flag_uncertain , request_human_review , submit_form , and get_audit_trail . The two read-only tools carry readOnlyHint annotations so an agent knows they're always safe to call. The critical piece is inside fill_field itself: it checks each field's risk tier and rejects the call for high-risk fields before it ever touches state — the boundary lives in the tool's own code, not in a prompt telling the agent to behave. We registered the deployed Netlify domain for Chrome's WebMCP origin trial so the API is genuinely available to any visiting browser or agent in production, added /.well-known/webmcp and llms.txt so the site is discoverable before an agent even loads the page, and built an explicit demo-mode fallback (with console diagnostics reporting mode=real-webmcp vs mode=demo ) so the concept is visible even in browsers without WebMCP support yet. Challenges we ran into Getting from "works locally with a Chrome flag" to "works for a real visiting agent in production" surfaced problems we didn't expect. The WebMCP API surface itself has been shifting ( navigator.modelContext moved to document.modelContext ), so we had to make sure we were building against the current spec rather than a stale example. Production availability required registering for Chrome's origin trial, and our first token was scoped as third-party by mistake — a mismatch that silently kept the site in demo mode until we re-registered with the correct scope. We also had to learn the hard way that not every "browser agent" actually uses WebMCP tool discovery — some general-purpose browsing tools simulate a human clicking through the UI instead, which looked like a WebMCP failure at first but was really a different agent entirely. Most importantly, testing surfaced a real bug where the Submit button's enabled state wasn't reading from the same blocker logic as the submit_form tool — meaning the UI could have let someone submit with unresolved high-risk fields, which would have quietly undermined the entire premise of the project if we hadn't caught it. Accomplishments that we're proud of The core guarantee isn't a claim, it's enforced in code: fill_field structurally cannot touch a high-risk field, and submit_form and the Submit button now share one blocker calculation, so there's no path to submitting with something unresolved. We verified the full six-tool integration independently with a WebMCP tool inspector showing real, callable schemas — not just our own word for it. And the live audit trail means every decision, whether made by the agent or by the human reviewing it, is visible and traceable rather than happening behind the scenes. What we learned The biggest shift in thinking: safety for agentic web apps doesn't have to live in a prompt at all — it can live in the shape of the tool contract itself, which is a guarantee no amount of clever prompting can quietly break. We also learned that the gap between local, flag-enabled WebMCP testing and real production behavior is bigger than the docs make it sound, and that "an agent used my site" can mean two very different things depending on whether it discovered structured tools or just simulated a human — a distinction worth designing and testing for explicitly, not assuming. What's next for TrustFill We'd like to make the risk tiers (low/medium/high) configurable per organization instead of hardcoded per field, so the same pattern could be dropped onto any long form — insurance claims, rental applications, government paperwork — without rebuilding the gating logic each time. We're also interested in extending request_human_review to support multiple humans on one application (co-applicants, cosigners) negotiating shared fields, and in exploring WebMCP's declarative HTML-attribute tools alongside our imperative ones to see whether the same trust boundary can be expressed even more simply. Longer term, we'd like to publish the gating pattern itself — reject-by-default on high-risk tool calls, shared blocker logic between tools and UI — as a small reusable library other WebMCP-based forms could adopt directly.
